pools.title: The Comparative Method
pools.covers: reading §2.1, §2.1.1, §2.1.2 · lecture 2.1 slides the_horizontal_move, frog_and_human, ninety_five_percent, the_arithmetic

items.stem: As this book uses the term, what is the comparative method?

options.text: The practice of setting systems or situations side by side and asking what their similarities and differences reveal.
options.why: Correct. The book uses the phrase widely, covering every case where two measurements are made to inform one another.

options.text: The practice of taking a single system apart by asking what problem it solves, by what procedure, and in what physical stuff.
options.why: That describes decomposition, Marr's three levels, which is the vertical method that comparison complements rather than replaces.

options.text: The practice of changing one variable deliberately and observing what happens to a second variable being measured.
options.why: That describes an experiment, one design inside the second family of comparison rather than the general method itself.

options.text: The practice of judging a capacity against the world the animal in question actually senses and acts on.
options.why: That describes the Umwelt standard of §2.2.5, a corrective to ranking rather than a definition of the method.

items.stem: Which term names the practice of setting systems or situations side by side and asking what their similarities and differences reveal?

options.text: comparative method
options.why: Correct. It is arguably the field's primary engine of inference, and most claims in the book are underneath claims about a similarity or a difference.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That is the strategy of using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether they agree, from §2.4.2.

options.text: synthetic method
options.why: That is studying a mind by building a system that does the thing and seeing what building it requires, from §2.4.1.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That is the process that produces analogies, two lineages arriving at one solution from different starting points.

items.stem: How does this book's use of the phrase comparative method differ from the sense it often carries in evolutionary biology?

options.text: The book's sense is wider, covering any case where two measurements inform one another, not only traits compared across species.
options.why: Correct. The narrower biological sense is just the comparison of traits across species, which §2.2 takes up in its own right.

options.text: The book's sense is narrower, covering only comparisons made inside a single laboratory experiment rather than across whole organisms.
options.why: Reversed, and wrong about the content: the book's sense is the wider of the two, and experiments are one family inside it.

options.text: The book's sense concerns living systems only, while evolutionary biology extends the phrase to designed machines as well.
options.why: Reversed again. Comparison with machines is a large part of this book, and the biological sense is the one restricted to species.

options.text: The book's sense concerns how deep a resemblance runs, while evolutionary biology uses the phrase for where a resemblance came from.
options.why: Depth and origin are two of the three questions the method asks; neither is what separates the two usages of the name.

items.stem: In a table whose rows are Marr's three levels and whose columns are human and frog vision, what separates reading down a column from reading across a row?

options.text: Down a column is Marr's analysis, one system asked three questions; across a row is the comparative method, one question asked of two systems.
options.why: Correct. Decomposition runs vertically through a single system and comparison reaches horizontally to another, so the table shows both at once.

options.text: Down a column is the comparative method, since Marr's three levels are what the two systems are being compared on; across a row is decomposition.
options.why: The two are swapped. A column holds one system at three levels, which is decomposition; a row holds one level across two systems.

options.text: Down a column gives the frog's visual system and across a row gives the human's, so direction names which of the two animals is meant.
options.why: The animals are the columns, so both are read downward; direction distinguishes the two methods, not the two species.

options.text: Down a column gives the computational level and across a row gives the implementational one, so direction names which level is in play.
options.why: All three levels appear in every column. A level is a row, and neither direction is a way of selecting one.

items.stem: A student reads Lettvin's description and concludes that a frog has a crude, cut-down version of human vision. What does §2.1.1 conclude instead?

options.text: The frog is solving a different problem, finding a small moving insect and striking, and its machinery fits that problem well.
options.why: Correct. The comparison shows a difference in the problem being solved, not a deficit measured against the human case.

options.text: The frog is solving the same problem a human visual system solves, with far fewer neurons available to solve it with.
options.why: That is the deficit reading in another form. The chapter's point is that the computational-level problems themselves differ.

options.text: The frog's visual system is genuinely cruder, though the chapter argues that crudeness is not a fair basis on which to rank whole species.
options.why: The chapter does reject ranking, but not by conceding crudeness. It denies that the frog is a worse version of anything.

options.text: The frog's visual system cannot usefully be compared with a human's, because the two lineages diverged too long ago.
options.why: The chapter compares them at all three levels on the same page. Distant relatedness limits inheritance claims, not comparison.

items.stem: A frog surrounded by freshly killed flies can starve to death. Which feature of its visual system does §2.1.1 give as the reason?

options.text: Its eye is largely a device for finding a small dark thing moving as an insect moves, so a motionless fly may not register.
options.why: Correct. The problem the frog's vision is built around involves movement, and a still fly falls outside it entirely.

options.text: Its eye has too little resolution to separate a fly from the ground it happens to be lying on at the time.
options.why: Acuity is not the issue the chapter raises. A moving fly of exactly the same size is caught reliably by the same eye.

options.text: Its retina sends output to the optic tectum, which has no pathway of its own to the circuits that control feeding.
options.why: The tectal route is what drives the strike. The chapter names it as where the work gets done, not as a missing connection.

options.text: Its visual system builds a general description of surfaces and objects first, which takes far too long to be useful for a strike.
options.why: That describes human vision's computational problem. Very little general description gets built in the frog, which is the contrast.

items.stem: A study reports that two species solve a puzzle box at almost identical rates. On §2.1.2's account, what has to be settled before anything follows about how either species thinks?

options.text: Why the two rates are alike, since one and the same relationship is compatible with several quite different explanations.
options.why: Correct. A comparison cannot interpret itself, and what an agreement licenses depends entirely on why the agreement is there.

options.text: Whether the two rates are alike to a high enough level of statistical precision to count as a genuine match at all.
options.why: Sharpening the measurement does not help until the candidate explanations are separated. A precise match is just as ambiguous.

options.text: Which of Marr's three levels the puzzle box task is best described at, before either of the species is tested on it.
options.why: Naming a level matters later, at the depth question, and it does not settle why two measured rates came out alike.

options.text: Whether the two species were tested by one laboratory, using identical apparatus and identical scoring rules from the first trial onward.
options.why: Procedural matching is good practice, and it leaves every one of the competing explanations of an agreement wide open.

items.stem: A person and an image model are each right about 95% of the time and agree with each other on 95% of photographs. Why does §2.1.2 treat the 95% agreement as far less impressive than it sounds?

options.text: Two independent systems each right 95% of the time would already agree about 90% of the time, leaving five points unexplained.
options.why: Correct. It is the surplus over what independence alone produces, not the raw agreement, that actually calls for an explanation.

options.text: A person and a model that agree about a photograph are usually right about it together, which makes the whole figure uninformative.
options.why: Being right together is exactly the baseline the arithmetic computes, and the surplus above that baseline still needs a cause.

options.text: Inherited training labels explain everything, since a model trained on human labels has simply been handed the answers in advance.
options.why: Inherited labels are one live explanation of the surplus, not a reason the raw figure is unimpressive before that is established.

options.text: Accuracy and agreement are measured on different scales, so the two 95% figures cannot meaningfully be set against one another.
options.why: Both are proportions of the same test set, and the chapter does set them against each other to get its baseline.

items.stem: §2.1.2 closes by naming the central skill the module exists to teach. Which of these is it?

options.text: Working out why a relationship between two systems is there, rather than stopping once it has been noticed.
options.why: Correct. Noticing similarity is the easy part, and the chapter treats diagnosing the why as the actual scientific work.

options.text: Noticing similarities between systems that other researchers have overlooked or dismissed as coincidental.
options.why: People are already extremely good at noticing similarities, which the chapter names as the easy half of the job.

options.text: Measuring a similarity accurately enough that its size can be reported as one reliable and replicable number.
options.why: A number is where the problem starts rather than where it ends, which is what the 95% agreement case is written to show.

options.text: Choosing which of Marr's three levels a similarity between two systems ought to be described at.
options.why: That is the depth question of §2.1.4, one of three diagnostic questions rather than the skill they are all in service of.

items.stem: Four studies: one times the same people under two display conditions, one contrasts crow and chimpanzee planning, one tracks a capacity from six months to two years, and one matches human errors against a model's. On §2.1's account, what do all four have in common?

options.text: Each sets two measurements beside each other so that the two can inform one another, which is what the comparative method is.
options.why: Correct. §2.1 opens by claiming the field is built on comparison, and lists exactly this spread of cases as its ordinary forms.

options.text: Each compares two different biological species in order to reconstruct what the common ancestor of the two was like.
options.why: Only the crow and chimpanzee study compares species, and reconstructing an ancestor is a further step the others cannot take.

options.text: Each takes a single system apart by asking Marr's three questions of it, before any second system is brought into the picture.
options.why: That is decomposition, the vertical method. All four of these studies reach horizontally to a second measurement.

options.text: Each manipulates one variable deliberately and observes the effect of that manipulation on a second variable.
options.why: Only the display-conditions study manipulates anything. The other three compare things the researcher did not arrange.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 works the agreement arithmetic over 400 photographs, with each of two independent systems right on 380 of them. On how many of the 400 do the two return the same verdict, and what does the lecture take from that?

options.text: 362, about 90.5%, which is the agreement two systems that have never met already produce between them.
options.why: Correct. Against that baseline an observed 95% is roughly four and a half points of surplus, and the surplus is what needs explaining.

options.text: 380, or 95%, which is the agreement that each system's own accuracy rate produces entirely on its own.
options.why: 380 is how many each system gets right individually. Agreement between the two is a separate count, and it comes out lower.

options.text: 200, or 50%, which is the agreement two unrelated systems produce when there is nothing at all linking them.
options.why: Fifty per cent would be the baseline for two systems guessing at chance, not for two that are each usually right.

options.text: 19, about 4.75%, which is the surplus agreement left over once independence has been properly accounted for.
options.why: 19 is how many one system gets right and the other does not. The surplus is a difference in percentage points, not that count.

items.stem: §2.1.2 offers four candidate explanations for a person and an image model agreeing on 95% of photographs. Which one attributes the agreement to the model having inherited our answers?

options.text: The model was trained on photographs that people had labeled, so human confusions were built into its lessons from the start.
options.why: Correct. That is the inheritance route, and it is the one that makes the agreement uninformative about how the model works inside.

options.text: The photographs that both systems get wrong are simply the hard ones, and neither of the two inherited anything at all from the other.
options.why: That is the shared-difficulty explanation: the items themselves account for the pattern, with no transmission between the systems.

options.text: The two systems really do work alike, the model building up from edges toward shapes and failing at the very same point.
options.why: That is the genuine-similarity explanation, the interesting one, and precisely what an agreement rate cannot establish.

options.text: Some of the agreement is luck, since two systems that are each usually right will very often say the same thing.
options.why: That is the chance explanation, and the arithmetic shows it accounts for about ninety of the ninety-five points.

items.stem: §2.1.1 states the computational-level problem for human and for frog vision. Which pair gives them correctly?

options.text: Human vision recovers a general description of surfaces and objects able to serve many tasks; frog vision finds a small dark thing moving as an insect moves, and strikes.
options.why: Correct. The human problem is general-purpose description and the frog's is narrow detection and action, and that difference is the point.

options.text: Human vision recovers a description of surfaces and objects; frog vision recovers much the same description, at a lower resolution and rather more slowly than a human visual system manages.
options.why: That is the deficit reading the section rejects. The frog builds very little general-purpose description at all, at any resolution.

options.text: Human vision detects local edges and orientations; frog vision detects whole objects that stay recognizable from a new angle or in new light.
options.why: Edges are the early stages of the human algorithm and viewpoint-stable objects are its output. Neither belongs to the frog.

options.text: Human vision routes its output through a large hierarchy of cortical areas; frog vision routes most of its output to the optic tectum.
options.why: Both halves are true and both are implementational rather than computational: they say in what stuff, not what problem.

items.stem: Two systems agree on almost every item and differ on a handful. §2.1.2 says that signature fits two quite different arrangements. Which are they, and what follows?

options.text: Two genuinely different procedures that mostly converge, or two nearly identical ones differing by a random step, and from outside these are indistinguishable.
options.why: Correct. The agreement rate is the same either way, so telling them apart means dropping to the algorithmic and implementational levels.

options.text: Two systems trained on the same body of data, or two trained on different bodies of data, and the size of the residue tells us which of the two we are looking at.
options.why: The residue is the same size in both of the arrangements the chapter describes, so its size cannot do that work.

options.text: Two systems solving one and the same problem, or two solving different problems, and the disagreements say which problem each solves.
options.why: Disagreements are informative about mechanism, but the chapter's point here is that this signature alone identifies neither.

options.text: Two systems measured carefully, or two measured carelessly, and only replication with better instruments can separate the cases.
options.why: Measurement quality is not the issue. Both arrangements are real and produce identical numbers however well they are measured.

items.stem: A press release reports that a new model "agrees with human judges 88% of the time" on a labeling task, where the human judges are right about 90% of the time and the model is right about 90% of the time. In a short paragraph, say what a reader should make of the 88% figure, using the reasoning of §2.1.2.
items.answer: Two independent systems each right about 90% of the time will already agree a great deal, simply because both are usually right. Counting the cases where both are right and the cases where both happen to be wrong the same way, that baseline is roughly 82%. So an observed 88% is not 88 points of evidence for similarity; it is about six points more than two systems that had never met would produce. Those six points of surplus are the only part of the figure that calls for an explanation, and a surplus that size is still compatible with the model having inherited human labels during training, with both systems finding the same items hard, and with a share of plain chance. The number on its own settles none of that.
rubric: States that two independent systems each about 90% accurate would already agree at a high rate, and gives a baseline near 82%.
Identifies the surplus over that baseline, rather than the raw agreement, as the quantity that needs explaining.
Names at least one alternative explanation the figure cannot rule out — inherited training labels, shared item difficulty, or chance.
Concludes that the reported figure does not by itself show the model works the way a person does.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how decomposition and comparison relate to one another as methods, and say what a field with both can ask that a field with only one of them cannot.
items.answer: Decomposition is the vertical method. It takes a single system and asks three different kinds of question about it: what problem is being solved, by what procedure, and in what physical stuff. Comparison is the horizontal method. It holds one of those questions fixed and reaches sideways, either to a second system or to the same system under different circumstances. The two are complementary rather than competing. A field with decomposition alone can say in detail what a capacity is, but has no way to ask what else in the world has anything like it. A field with comparison alone can notice that two systems resemble each other and cannot say at which level the resemblance holds, which is exactly what separates a real similarity from a surface one.
rubric: Identifies decomposition as one system examined at three levels, and calls it vertical or equivalent.
Identifies comparison as one question carried across to another system or another condition, and calls it horizontal or equivalent.
States that the two methods are complementary rather than alternatives to each other.
Says what having both allows: asking what a capacity is and also asking what else has anything like it.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 flags one thing about the name comparative method straight away, saying it will otherwise cause confusion within two days. What is the warning?

options.text: In evolutionary biology the phrase means something narrower — the comparison of traits across species — so it does less work in a biology paper than it does here.
options.why: Correct. The lecture flags it before Wednesday precisely because Wednesday is the lecture that uses the narrower sense.

options.text: In evolutionary biology the phrase means something wider, covering any two measurements made to inform one another, so it does more work there.
options.why: Reversed: the wide sense is this book's, and the biological sense is the restricted one.

options.text: In historical linguistics the phrase means the comparison of two languages, which is where evolutionary biology borrowed the name from.
options.why: The lecture says the borrowing ran the other way, with linguistics taking the name from biology.

options.text: In cognitive psychology the phrase means comparing two experimental conditions, which is the second family rather than the general method.
options.why: No such usage is flagged, and the warning the lecture gives concerns the narrower biological sense of the term.

items.stem: Having shown the frog-and-human table, lecture 2.1 tells the room to hold onto one thing in particular. What, and why?

options.text: That nothing in the table says the frog is a worse version of us, because the pull to read a difference as a deficit is very strong.
options.why: Correct. The lecture says the following meeting is almost entirely about resisting that pull.

options.text: That the frog's visual system is simpler, because simplicity is what makes it a useful first case for the comparative method.
options.why: Simplicity is not the lesson, and the lecture is explicit that the frog is solving a different problem well rather than a shared one poorly.

options.text: That the table has three rows and two columns, because the shape of it is what distinguishes decomposition from comparison.
options.why: The shape is explained on the same slide and the thing the room is told to hold onto is the anti-ranking conclusion.

options.text: That Lettvin described the frog's eye in the 1950s, because the age of the finding shows how long the method has been productive.
options.why: The date is given in passing, and what the lecture asks the room to carry forward is the conclusion rather than the provenance.

pools.title: Three Questions to Ask of a Resemblance
pools.covers: reading §2.1.3, §2.1.4, §2.1.5, §2.1.6 · lecture 2.1 slides question_one_origin, question_two_depth, question_three_precision, three_questions

items.stem: When two systems resemble each other, §2.1.3 says the resemblance can come from three broad sources. What are they?

options.text: Shared origin, shared problem, and coincidence.
options.why: Correct. The three are inheritance from a common source, independent arrival under the same constraint, and no real connection at all.

options.text: Shared origin, shared mechanism, and shared behavior.
options.why: Shared mechanism and shared behavior are answers to the depth question, which asks at which level a match holds rather than where it came from.

options.text: Homology, analogy, and convergent evolution.
options.why: The first two are §2.2.2's names for shared origin and shared problem; convergent evolution is the process producing the second, not a third source.

options.text: Behavioral equivalence, mechanistic equivalence, and engineering convenience.
options.why: Those are §2.3.1's three modes for the natural-versus-artificial case, and only the first two are about resemblance at all.

items.stem: Two species share a capacity. What does §2.1.3 say follows about their common ancestor, on the shared-origin answer and on the shared-problem answer?

options.text: Shared origin lets us reason about the ancestor; shared problem licenses no inference about the ancestor at all.
options.why: Correct. Saying the trait arose twice independently is precisely the claim that the ancestor did not have it.

options.text: Shared origin licenses no inference about the ancestor; shared problem lets us reason about what the ancestor faced.
options.why: The two are swapped. Inheritance is what makes an ancestral claim available, and independent arrival is what removes it.

options.text: Both answers let us reason about the ancestor, though shared problem supports a weaker and more hedged version of the claim.
options.why: Shared problem does not support a weakened ancestral claim. It supports the positive claim that the ancestor lacked the trait.

options.text: Neither answer licenses any claim about an ancestor, because ancestral states can only ever be inferred from fossil evidence.
options.why: The chapter's whole point about the tree is that ancestral states are inferred from the pattern of traits across living species.

items.stem: A student calls the shared-problem answer the disappointing one, since it costs us the ancestor. What does §2.1.3 say we get in exchange?

options.text: That the pressure was real, that it is a good candidate for a computational-level explanation, and that the capacity is what solving it looks like.
options.why: Correct. The section treats this as arguably more interesting than the ancestral claim, not as a consolation for losing it.

options.text: That the two systems are likely to be far more closely related than the phylogenetic tree suggests, since independent arrival at the same solution is very unlikely.
options.why: Independent arrival is exactly what shared problem asserts, and the chapter treats it as common wherever a problem has few good solutions.

options.text: That the resemblance is probably a coincidence after all, since a shared problem does not by itself explain a detailed similarity.
options.why: Coincidence is the third and separate answer. A shared problem is a real cause, and the chapter treats it as the informative one.

options.text: That the capacity is an adaptation in both of the lineages, which settles the question of what the trait is for in each of them.
options.why: The section makes a claim about the problem rather than about either lineage's history, and §2.2.7 warns against reading every trait as an adaptation.

items.stem: §2.1.4 asks how deep a resemblance goes. What kind of answer does that question take?

options.text: The name of the Marr level at which the match holds — what the systems do, how they do it, or what they are made of.
options.why: Correct. Two systems can match only in behavior, or down to the algorithm, or all the way to the implementation.

options.text: A number saying how many of the measured dimensions the two systems turned out to match on when they were compared.
options.why: That is closer to the precision question, and §2.1.5 insists precision is a separate axis from depth rather than a version of it.

options.text: A judgment about whether the resemblance was inherited, arrived at independently, or is a coincidence between the two.
options.why: That is the origin question of §2.1.3. Depth asks where the match sits, not where the match came from.

options.text: A statement of which of the two systems is the better solution to the problem that both of them are engaged in solving.
options.why: The chapter rejects ranking as a use of comparison, and depth is a structural question rather than an evaluative one.

items.stem: §2.1.4 adds a case that runs the other way from a merely behavioral match. Which is it?

options.text: Two systems built from nearly the same materials can still be doing entirely different jobs with those materials.
options.why: Correct. Depth is not a ladder on which sharing the hardware implies sharing the function; it has to be asked at each level.

options.text: Two systems that match at the implementational level must also match at the algorithmic and computational levels above it.
options.why: That is the ladder reading the section exists to block, and the chapter gives the counterexample rather than the rule.

options.text: Two systems that match behaviorally have thereby been shown to match at the algorithmic level as well, if only loosely.
options.why: That is surface matching, named in §2.1.8, and it is the error the depth question is meant to make visible.

options.text: Two systems made of different materials cannot be compared at the implementational level, so only the top two levels apply.
options.why: Comparing implementations across different materials is exactly what multiple realizability makes interesting, and the chapter does it.

items.stem: What separates the depth question from the precision question in §2.1.5?

options.text: Depth asks at which level two systems match; precision asks how finely the match is specified at whatever level is being looked at.
options.why: Correct. The two are independent, which is why a claim can be shallow and precise, or deep and vague.

options.text: Depth asks how finely two systems match; precision asks whether the match holds at the computational, algorithmic or implementational level.
options.why: The two are swapped. Naming a level is the depth answer, and the fineness of the specification is the precision answer.

options.text: Depth asks whether the two systems match at all; precision asks how confident we should be that the reported match is not chance.
options.why: Statistical confidence is a different worry, addressed in §2.5.1. Precision here is about how finely the claim is stated.

options.text: Depth asks how far back in time a shared trait can be traced; precision asks how exactly the ancestral state can be reconstructed.
options.why: Both halves belong to the origin question rather than to either of these two, and neither is about history at all.

items.stem: A paper reports that people and a model "behave alike" on a categorization task. What does §2.1.5 say that claim actually amounts to?

options.text: That the two matched on the things that happened to get measured, not that they would match in every possible circumstance.
options.why: Correct. A behavioral match is a claim about the dimensions someone looked at, and looking at more of them tends to surface differences.

options.text: That the two match at the computational level and could not match any more precisely than they already have been shown to.
options.why: A behavioral match names a level, which is the depth answer, and says nothing about how precisely that match has been pinned down.

options.text: That the two would behave alike in any circumstance sharing the same computational description as the ones already tested.
options.why: That is the stronger reading the section is written to block: a match on what was measured does not generalize to what was not.

options.text: That the two have been shown to differ in no respect at all, since any real difference would have shown up in the measurements.
options.why: Differences tend to surface only when someone looks harder, so an unfound difference is not the same as an absent one.

items.stem: §2.1.5 says precision is not a matter of yes or no. What is it a matter of instead?

options.text: How finely we looked before we stopped looking, since looking harder at the same things tends to surface differences.
options.why: Correct. That is why a comparison which has survived a lot of looking is worth more than one that has survived very little.

options.text: Whether the instruments available were sensitive enough to register a difference of the size the theory predicted.
options.why: Instrument sensitivity is a practical limit; the chapter's point is about how far anyone chose to push the comparison.

options.text: Whether both of the two systems were described at the same Marr level before any of their behavior was compared with one another.
options.why: Describing both at one level is the depth question doing its work, and the chapter keeps that axis separate from precision.

options.text: How many independent research groups have replicated the match between the two systems using their own procedures.
options.why: Replication is valuable and it repeats a comparison at the same grain rather than making the claim any finer.

items.stem: §2.1.5 says the three questions cross rather than nest. Which pair of cases does it give to show it?

options.text: Two systems that share an origin but drifted into different mechanisms, and two that arrived independently at nearly the same machinery.
options.why: Correct. Origin does not fix depth in either direction, which is why every combination has to be checked rather than inferred.

options.text: Two systems that share an origin and therefore must share a mechanism, and two that arrived independently and therefore share nothing at all.
options.why: Those are the inferences the section denies. The whole point of the crossing is that origin does not settle depth.

options.text: Two systems matching precisely at the behavioral level, and two matching precisely at the implementational level as well.
options.why: Both are precision claims at a single level, so the pair shows nothing about how the three questions relate to one another.

options.text: Two systems compared by one method and agreeing, and two compared by two methods and disagreeing with one another.
options.why: That is §2.4's material on converging operations and disagreement, which is a different family of comparison entirely.

items.stem: A team does the hard work, gets down to the mechanism, and finds that two systems genuinely share one. What does §2.1.5 say happens next?

options.text: The shared mechanism is itself a resemblance, so the origin question comes back: inherited, independently arrived at, or chance?
options.why: Correct. That is what makes the three questions a loop rather than a checklist that can be finished.

options.text: The depth question has been answered at the lowest level available, so the comparison has gone as far as this method can possibly take it.
options.why: Reaching the mechanism answers depth and immediately raises a fresh instance of the origin question about the mechanism itself.

options.text: The precision question becomes the only one left, since a mechanism can always be described more finely than it has been.
options.why: Precision does remain live, and the section's actual move is that the shared mechanism sends us back to the first question.

options.text: The comparison is complete, because a shared mechanism is the strongest evidence a comparison of two systems can produce.
options.why: A shared mechanism is a finding rather than a conclusion, and the section treats it as the start of another round of questions.

items.stem: A researcher finds a difference between two experimental conditions. According to §2.1.6, where can that difference have come from?

options.text: From the change deliberately introduced, from something else that varied alongside it, or from chance.
options.why: Correct. The same three-way shape as the origin question, with the candidate answers adapted to a comparison across conditions.

options.text: From the change deliberately introduced, from a shared origin between the conditions, or from convergent evolution.
options.why: Shared origin and convergence are answers for comparisons across systems, and neither applies to one system measured twice.

options.text: From the change deliberately introduced or from measurement error, these being the only two possibilities in a controlled study.
options.why: Something else varying alongside the manipulation is the third and most important possibility, and §2.5.1 names it a confound.

options.text: From the change deliberately introduced, from the level of description chosen, or from the precision of the instruments used.
options.why: Level of description and instrument precision belong to the other two questions rather than to the sources of a difference.

items.stem: Two entirely different ways of measuring the same mind agree with each other. What does §2.1.6 list as the possible reasons?

options.text: Both are tracking something real, both share a blind spot, or the agreement was due to chance.
options.why: Correct. The shared blind spot is the one that makes agreement between methods less conclusive than it first appears.

options.text: Both are tracking something real, both were designed by the same laboratory, or the agreement was due to chance.
options.why: Shared design is not one of the chapter's candidates, and two methods from one laboratory can still have unrelated weaknesses.

options.text: Both are tracking something real, or one inherited its assumptions from the other during the course of its development.
options.why: Inheritance is an answer for comparisons across systems; the chapter's third candidate here is a blind spot the two methods share.

options.text: Both are tracking something real, both are measuring at the same Marr level, or the two measurements were not independent.
options.why: Measuring at one level is not a reason for agreement, and the chapter's own list names a shared blind spot rather than dependence.

items.stem: What does §2.1.6 name as the classic error of the comparative method, and who makes it?

options.text: Mistaking one candidate explanation for another, and it is not a beginner's error — serious careers have been built on relationships of the wrong kind.
options.why: Correct. The section is explicit that experience does not protect against it, which is why the diagnostic questions are worth the trouble.

options.text: Failing to measure a resemblance precisely enough, and it is a beginner's error that disappears with better training in research methods and statistics.
options.why: Precision is one of the three questions rather than the classic error, and the section denies that experience makes anyone immune.

options.text: Comparing two systems that are far too distantly related for the comparison to license any inference at all about either one of them.
options.why: Distant relatedness rules inheritance out and leaves the comparison perfectly informative, as the octopus and crow cases show.

options.text: Choosing the wrong Marr level to describe a resemblance at, which is a bookkeeping error rather than a substantive one.
options.why: A mismatch of levels does cause trouble, and the error the section names is mistaking one candidate explanation for another.

items.stem: §2.1.6 previews how two domains name the questions. Which question gets formal names across species, and which gets them across the natural and artificial divide?

options.text: Across species the origin question gets names, as homology and analogy; across the natural and artificial divide the depth question does, as behavioral and mechanistic equivalence.
options.why: Correct. The vocabulary changes between domains while the same three questions keep coming back underneath it.

options.text: Across species the depth question gets the names homology and analogy; across the natural and artificial divide it is the origin question that does, as behavioral and mechanistic equivalence.
options.why: The two are swapped. Homology and analogy are claims about history, and the equivalences are claims about the level a match holds at.

options.text: Across species the precision question gets names, as homology and analogy; across the natural and artificial divide the depth question does, as convergence and divergence.
options.why: Homology and analogy answer the origin question, and convergence is a process rather than a name for a mode of equivalence.

options.text: Across both domains it is the origin question that gets formal names, since where a resemblance came from is the only question a name can settle.
options.why: Behavioral and mechanistic equivalence say nothing about history at all, which is exactly what makes them depth vocabulary.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 illustrates the three answers to the origin question with word pairs. Which pair was given as the case of a shared problem rather than a shared origin?

options.text: English cuckoo, Japanese kakkō and Hindi kuku, three unrelated languages imitating one bird that says its own name.
options.why: Correct. No borrowing and no common source: the three converged because they were all solving the same imitative problem.

options.text: English brother and German Bruder, which descend from a single ancestor language that no longer exists anywhere.
options.why: That is the shared-origin case, and the lecture used it to show that the likeness is a family resemblance quite literally.

options.text: English much and Spanish mucho, which mean nearly the same thing and sound nearly the same by pure accident.
options.why: That is the coincidence case: much comes from Old English mycel and mucho from Latin multus, with no connection at all.

options.text: English comparative and its use in evolutionary biology, where the same term does narrower work than it does in this book.
options.why: That is the naming point from the previous slide, and it is about a term of art rather than about a resemblance between languages.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 gives a bodily example of two things built from nearly the same materials while doing entirely different jobs. Which is it?

options.text: The muscle in the heart and the muscle in the bicep, which are made of much the same stuff and do very different work.
options.why: Correct. Shared material tells us almost nothing about what either one is for, which is why depth has to be asked rather than assumed.

options.text: The human eye and the octopus eye, which are both camera eyes and arrived at that design from entirely separate starting points.
options.why: That is the analogy case from §2.2.2, where two lineages solve one problem the same way rather than one material serving two jobs.

options.text: The retina and the optic tectum in the frog, which are both made of neurons and handle different stages of the same task.
options.why: Those are two stages of one visual system rather than two systems doing different jobs with a shared material.

options.text: The corvid brain and the mammalian brain, which are built on plans that diverged before either group had much of a brain at all.
options.why: Those are two different plans rather than one shared material, and the lecture uses them for convergence rather than for depth.

items.stem: §2.1.5 pairs a loose and a precise version of the same claim at each level. Which pair does it give for the behavioral level?

options.text: Loose: both can on average make the same kind of distinction. Precise: both make the same pattern of errors, on the same items, in the same proportions.
options.why: Correct. The loose and precise versions are both behavioral claims, which is what shows precision is a separate axis from depth.

options.text: Loose: both build from simple features toward complex ones. Precise: both compute the same features at the first stage, in the same order.
options.why: That is the pair the section gives for the algorithmic level, one level down from the behavioral one.

options.text: Loose: both are built from cells that signal electrically. Precise: both use the very same molecules to carry those signals, with the same timing, in the same arrangement.
options.why: That is the pair for the implementational level, and it is the deepest of the three rather than the behavioral one.

options.text: Loose: both solve the same problem. Precise: both solve it by the same procedure and in much the same physical material as each other.
options.why: That pair moves down through the levels, which makes it a depth contrast rather than a precision contrast at one level.

items.stem: A paper claims that two species "use the same navigation strategy," giving as evidence that both reach a goal by an indirect route rather than a straight line. In a short paragraph, state what has and has not been established, using the depth and precision questions.
items.answer: The claim rests on a behavioral match, so what has been established sits at the computational level: both species get to the goal, and both do it by an indirect route. That is the depth answer, and it is shallow. Nothing has been shown about the procedure either species runs or the machinery it runs on. The precision is also low: an indirect route is about the loosest behavioral description available, far short of the same errors on the same trials in the same proportions. And because depth and precision are independent, the shallowness does not follow from the vagueness or the other way round — the claim could have been made precisely at this shallow level, by reporting matched error patterns, and it was not. So "the same strategy" overstates what an indirect route supports, and what would sharpen it is either measuring more finely at this level or reaching down to the next one.
rubric: Identifies the evidence as a behavioral match, and names the level as computational or the depth as shallow.
States that nothing follows about the procedure or the machinery from a behavioral match alone.
Judges the precision as loose, and says what a more precise behavioral claim would look like.
States that a claim can be shallow and precise, or deep and vague — the two axes being independent.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the shared-problem answer removes the ability to reason about a common ancestor, and say what §2.1.3 argues we learn in its place.
items.answer: Shared problem means the two lineages arrived at the capacity separately, each under its own pressure. Asserting that is the same as asserting that the common ancestor did not already have the trait, since if it had, the trait would have been inherited rather than built twice. So there is no ancestral state left to reconstruct from the resemblance. What comes back in exchange is a set of claims about the problem rather than about the history: that the pressure was real rather than invented after the fact, that the problem is a good candidate for a computational-level explanation, and that this capacity is what solving that problem looks like. The section argues this is arguably the more interesting finding, not a consolation prize.
rubric: States that shared problem asserts independent arrival in each lineage.
Explains that independent arrival is the claim that the ancestor lacked the trait, so no ancestral inference is available.
Names at least two of what is gained instead: the pressure was real, the problem is a computational-level candidate, the capacity is what solving it looks like.
Reports the section's evaluation that this is not simply the weaker finding.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 says the picture of the three questions matters, and specifically that it is three panels side by side rather than a flowchart. Why?

options.text: The questions are not three steps taken in order — they cross, so every combination is possible and all three have to be asked.
options.why: Correct. The lecture adds the loop: a shared mechanism is itself a resemblance, which sends us back to the first question about it.

options.text: The questions are equally important, and a flowchart would suggest that the first one matters more than the two that follow it.
options.why: Relative importance is not the issue. What a flowchart would misrepresent is that answering one question constrains the answers to the others.

options.text: The questions are asked by different disciplines, and a flowchart would suggest a single researcher answers all three of them.
options.why: No division of labor is claimed, and the point of the layout is about the logical relationship between the questions.

options.text: The questions can be answered in any order, though a flowchart would suggest starting with whichever is easiest to measure.
options.why: Order of convenience is not what the layout denies; it denies that answering them in sequence is the right picture at all.

pools.title: Three Families, Four Failures, and the Stakes
pools.covers: reading §2.1.7, §2.1.8, §2.1.9 · lecture 2.1 slides three_families, four_ways_to_get_it_wrong, we_do_it_to_ourselves, never_neutral

items.stem: What is anthropomorphism?

options.text: Projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned that description.
options.why: Correct. The dog assumed to look guilty and the chatbot taken to mean what it says are the chapter's two examples.

options.text: Refusing an animal a capacity it plainly has, because granting it feels unscientific rather than cautious.
options.why: That is anthropodenial, the opposite error, named by de Waal and introduced alongside anthropomorphism in §2.2.6.

options.text: Treating the human case as the reference point, so every other mind is described by what it lacks by comparison.
options.why: That is anthropocentrism, which the chapter calls subtler than anthropomorphism and often a good deal more damaging.

options.text: Assuming that every trait must be a finely tuned solution to some problem the organism's ancestors faced.
options.why: That is unconstrained adaptationism, the third of the named errors, and it concerns explanation rather than attribution.

items.stem: Which term names projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned that description?

options.text: anthropomorphism
options.why: Correct. Its opposite number is anthropodenial, refusing an animal a capacity it plainly has because granting it feels unscientific.

options.text: anthropocentrism
options.why: That is treating the human case as reference point, default, or "normal", so other minds are measured by how near they come.

options.text: unconstrained adaptationism
options.why: That is the habit of assuming every trait must be a finely tuned solution to some problem the organism faced.

options.text: surface matching
options.why: That is the assumption that what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside.

items.stem: What is anthropocentrism?

options.text: Treating the human case as the reference point or default, so that every other mind is measured by how near it comes to a human one.
options.why: Correct. The chapter calls it subtler than anthropomorphism and often more damaging, because it shapes which questions get asked at all.

options.text: Projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description, as with a dog assumed to be looking guilty.
options.why: That is anthropomorphism. Anthropocentrism does not over-attribute a capacity; it makes the human case the yardstick for every other.

options.text: Judging a capacity against the world the animal in question actually senses and acts on, rather than against the world as we happen to see it.
options.why: That is the Umwelt standard from §2.2.5, which the chapter offers as the corrective to anthropocentrism rather than as its name.

options.text: Assuming that similarity in behavior between two systems is good evidence about the machinery inside either of them.
options.why: That is surface matching, the theme running under all three named errors rather than one of the three itself.

items.stem: Which term names treating the human case as the reference point or default, so every other mind is described in terms of what it lacks?

options.text: anthropocentrism
options.why: Correct. It is the error behind the ladder of intelligence, and §2.2.5 says it is hard to shake even once it has been named.

options.text: anthropomorphism
options.why: That is projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description, which is over-attribution rather than ranking.

options.text: unconstrained adaptationism
options.why: That is treating every trait as a finely tuned solution, which turns adaptive explanation into a game that always wins.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That is the process producing analogies, two lineages arriving at one solution from different starting points.

items.stem: What is unconstrained adaptationism?

options.text: The habit of assuming every trait must be a finely tuned solution to some problem, which makes even contradictory explanations sound correct.
options.why: Correct. The test for it is whether the explanation offered would have accommodated the opposite result just as comfortably.

options.text: The habit of assuming that a trait is a byproduct of some other structure rather than something natural selection acted on directly.
options.why: That is closer to Gould and Lewontin's corrective in §2.2.7 than to the error, which runs in the opposite direction entirely.

options.text: The habit of explaining a behavior by appeal to a higher mental process when a simpler process would account for it just as well.
options.why: That is what Morgan's Canon warns against, a guard against anthropomorphism rather than a name for adaptive over-explanation.

options.text: The habit of assuming that a trait present in two species was inherited from a common ancestor rather than arrived at twice over, independently, in each lineage.
options.why: That is a specific error about origin, corrected by the phylogenetic tree, rather than the general habit of adaptive storytelling.

items.stem: Which term names the habit of assuming every trait must be a finely tuned solution to some problem, so that even contradictory explanations sound correct?

options.text: unconstrained adaptationism
options.why: Correct. §2.2.7 takes it up again as the source of just-so stories, and Tinbergen's four questions are offered as the corrective.

options.text: surface matching
options.why: That is the habit of assuming what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside, which is the theme running under this error rather than the error itself.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That is the process producing analogies, in which two lineages converge on one solution from different starting points.

options.text: reverse inference
options.why: That is the move from a brain region being active during a task to the task having involved the process that region does.

items.stem: What is surface matching?

options.text: The assumption that what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside.
options.why: Correct. The chapter names it as the common theme running underneath anthropomorphism, anthropocentrism and unconstrained adaptationism alike.

options.text: The assumption that two systems built from the same materials must be doing much the same job with those materials.
options.why: That is a real error the depth question blocks, and it runs from the inside outward rather than from the outside inward.

options.text: The assumption that a resemblance between two species was inherited rather than arrived at separately by each of them.
options.why: That is a mistake about origin, which the phylogenetic tree exists to settle, rather than a mistake about depth.

options.text: The assumption that a difference between two experimental conditions was caused by the manipulation the researcher chose.
options.why: That is what a confound defeats, and §2.5.1 rather than §2.1.8 is where the chapter takes up that particular error.

items.stem: Which term names the assumption that what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside?

options.text: surface matching
options.why: Correct. It is the theme under the other three named errors, and §2.3.2 diagnoses the whole Turing–Searle exchange as an instance of it.

options.text: behavioral equivalence
options.why: That is a match between two systems in what they do judged from outside, which is a finding rather than an unwarranted assumption.

options.text: anthropomorphism
options.why: That is projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description, one special case of the broader error.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That is using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether the results they give agree.

items.stem: §2.1.8 says surface matching is an error about two of the three questions in particular. Which, and why?

options.text: Depth and precision: two systems that behave alike get treated as alike underneath, when the only dimensions checked are the ones that happened to be measured.
options.why: Correct. Assuming a behavioral match runs deeper than it does, on the strength of a loose set of measurements, is both errors at once.

options.text: Origin and depth: two systems that behave alike get treated as having inherited the behavior from a common source they never actually shared.
options.why: Surface matching says nothing about history. It is the leap from outward behavior to inward machinery, whatever the origin turns out to be.

options.text: Origin and precision: two systems measured loosely get treated as related to each other, when a finer measurement would have shown that the relationship was a coincidence.
options.why: Coincidence is one candidate answer to the origin question, and surface matching is a mistake about how far a behavioral match reaches.

options.text: Precision alone, since depth is settled the moment two systems have been shown to produce the same outputs from the same inputs.
options.why: Producing the same outputs settles only that the match holds at the top level, which is exactly the assumption at issue.

items.stem: Shoppers shown several identical pairs of stockings in a row chose the rightmost far more often, and explained their choice by the knit and sheerness of the fabric. Why does §2.1.8 include the study?

options.text: To show that surface matching is a mistake we make about ourselves, crediting a decision to reasoning when a simpler process explains it.
options.why: Correct. The discipline that keeps us honest about animals turns out to be the same discipline that keeps us honest about ourselves.

options.text: To show that people are unreliable witnesses to their own preferences, so behavioral measures should be replaced by neural ones wherever possible.
options.why: The chapter draws no such methodological moral, and §2.4 argues that behavioral and neural methods answer to different levels.

options.text: To show that a difference between two conditions can be caused by something other than the manipulation the researcher introduced.
options.why: That is the confound of §2.5.1. Here the manipulation is position and it worked; what failed was the shoppers' account of why.

options.text: To show that human preferences are shaped by anthropocentrism, since the shoppers treated their own reasoning as the normal case.
options.why: Anthropocentrism is about using the human case as a yardstick for other minds, and the stockings study is about self-explanation.

items.stem: What conclusion did Nisbett and Wilson draw from the stockings result?

options.text: That we often have no direct access to why we did something, and generate a plausible-sounding reason instead.
options.why: Correct. The reasons offered were confident and specific, and the shoppers rejected the position explanation when it was put to them.

options.text: That people prefer objects placed on the right, which is a stable positional bias present across many kinds of consumer choice.
options.why: The position effect is the finding the study produced, and their conclusion was about the shoppers' explanations rather than the bias.

options.text: That people will deny a bias once it has been described to them, even when the description of the bias is plainly correct.
options.why: Denial is part of what was observed, and the conclusion they drew concerned the absence of access rather than the presence of denial.

options.text: That reasoning about one's own choices is unreliable only when the objects being chosen between are genuinely indistinguishable.
options.why: The chapter generalizes well past identical objects, using the study to introduce a routine feature of self-explanation.

items.stem: Someone explains the long human childhood by the learning time it buys. Applying §2.1.8's test, what shows the explanation is unconstrained?

options.text: A short childhood would have been explained just as smoothly, by the years of helplessness it avoids.
options.why: Correct. An explanation that would have accommodated the opposite outcome equally well has not yet told us anything.

options.text: The explanation is not supported by any comparative data from species whose juveniles reach independence at different ages.
options.why: Missing evidence is a different complaint. The test is whether the story would have fitted whatever outcome had turned up.

options.text: A long childhood benefits the individual rather than its offspring, so it is not the sort of trait natural selection acts on.
options.why: Selection acts on whatever raises surviving reproduction, and the section's objection is about the form of the story rather than its content.

options.text: The explanation names a purpose, and §2.2.1 says an evolutionary why is always a claim about the past instead of a purpose.
options.why: That is a genuine warning about the word for, and it is separate from the symmetry test this section actually supplies.

items.stem: §2.1.7 sorts every comparison ahead into three families. What are they?

options.text: Different systems set beside each other, one system across different conditions, and different methods applied to the same system.
options.why: Correct. Species, machines, ages and atypical minds are the first family; the experiment is the second; §2.4 is the third.

options.text: Different species, different machines, and the different developmental stages of one and the same organism as it grows up over a lifetime.
options.why: Those are three cases inside the first family alone, and the division would leave the experiment and §2.4 with nowhere to sit.

options.text: Comparison of origins, comparison of depths, and comparison of the precision with which a given resemblance can be stated.
options.why: Origin, depth and precision are the three questions asked of every comparison, not three kinds of comparison to be asked about.

options.text: Homology, analogy, and coincidence, which between them exhaust the reasons two systems can turn out to be alike.
options.why: Those are the three answers to the origin question in their §2.2.2 vocabulary, rather than families of comparison.

items.stem: §2.1.7 is candid about a mismatch between what the field does and what the book teaches. What is the mismatch?

options.text: The great majority of day-to-day work uses comparison across conditions, and the book gives most of its room to cross-system comparison instead.
options.why: Correct. The section calls that a choice about what a first course should teach rather than a ranking of what matters.

options.text: The great majority of day-to-day work uses cross-system comparison, and the book gives most of its own room to comparison across conditions instead.
options.why: Reversed. Cross-system comparison is the more integrative mode and the less common one, which is why it needs the space.

options.text: The great majority of day-to-day work uses neural methods, and the book gives most of its room to behavioral and computational ones.
options.why: That is a claim about §2.4's three methods rather than about the three families, and the section makes no such comparison.

options.text: The great majority of day-to-day work compares humans with machines, and the book gives most of its room to comparison across species.
options.why: Both comparisons get a section of their own here, and neither is what the section names as the field's day-to-day work.

items.stem: What reason does §2.1.7 give for spending most of the book on cross-system comparison despite its rarity in daily practice?

options.text: Setting a human mind beside an octopus's, an infant's or a machine's exposes things no amount of careful work inside a single system will show.
options.why: Correct. The section calls cross-system comparison the more integrative mode, and that integrative reach is the stated justification.

options.text: Comparison across conditions is a technique better learned in a statistics course, so a first course in this field can safely leave it out altogether.
options.why: The chapter does not leave it out at all: §2.5.1 is the longest subsection in the book and teaches the experiment in detail.

options.text: Cross-system comparison is the only family in which all three of the diagnostic questions from §2.1 can actually be asked.
options.why: The section's whole design is that the same three questions run through all three families, with only the vocabulary changing.

options.text: Cross-system comparison produces findings that are more likely to replicate, since it does not depend on a single laboratory's procedures.
options.why: Replicability is not the argument offered, and §2.5.1's account of confounds applies to cross-system work every bit as much.

items.stem: §2.1.9 says that comparisons of minds are rarely neutral. What reason does it give?

options.text: Claims about who has which capacity have historically tracked claims about who deserves a certain kind of treatment, respect, or rights.
options.why: Correct. Deciding that a creature reasons or suffers has practical consequences, and everyone in the argument knows it.

options.text: Researchers who study animal minds are more likely than other scientists to hold prior commitments about how animals ought to be treated.
options.why: The section makes no claim about who researchers are. Its claim is about what rides on the answers, and it applies to everyone arguing.

options.text: Comparisons between minds cannot be measured objectively, so every conclusion drawn from one ultimately rests on the researcher's values.
options.why: The section does not say the evidence is unmeasurable. It says motives shape which studies get run and which results feel convincing.

options.text: The three diagnostic questions cannot be answered when one of the systems being compared is a human being rather than an animal.
options.why: The questions apply to human minds throughout the chapter, and the section's worry is about motivation rather than about method.

items.stem: §2.1.9 insists the motivational pull runs in both directions. What are the two directions?

options.text: Wanting to raise an animal's moral standing is a reason to read its behavior generously; not wanting to change how animals are used is a reason to read it thinly.
options.why: Correct. Naming both is what stops the warning from becoming an argument for one side of any particular debate.

options.text: Wanting to publish a striking result is a reason to over-read an animal's behavior; wanting to avoid criticism from colleagues is a reason to under-report it.
options.why: Publication incentives are real and are not what this section is about, which is what follows practically from granting a capacity.

options.text: Wanting to protect an animal is a reason to read its behavior generously; wanting to protect a machine from being switched off is a reason to read exactly the same behavior thinly.
options.why: The section's two directions both concern the same subject, and §2.3.4 takes up the machine case with its own version of the point.

options.text: Wanting a simple explanation is a reason to under-attribute; wanting an interesting explanation is a reason to over-attribute a capacity.
options.why: Simplicity and interest are pressures on explanation generally, and this section is specifically about what is morally riding on the answer.

items.stem: A student concludes from §2.1.9 that a researcher with a stake in the outcome is thereby unreliable. What does the section actually claim?

options.text: Neither motive makes anyone wrong; motives shape which studies get run, which results feel convincing, and which get explained away.
options.why: Correct. The claim is about the process rather than about the truth of any conclusion, and a motivated researcher can be perfectly correct.

options.text: A researcher with a stake in the outcome is unreliable on that question, which is why such work needs independent replication before it counts.
options.why: That is the stronger conclusion the section declines to draw, and it would rule out most of the research the chapter goes on to cite.

options.text: Motivated reasoning is unavoidable, so the debates about animal and machine minds are ultimately political rather than empirical ones.
options.why: The section explicitly refuses that reading, and the chapter proceeds to weigh evidence in every one of the debates it raises.

options.text: Researchers should declare their moral commitments before publishing, since a stated commitment can then be corrected for by readers.
options.why: No such remedy is proposed. What the section offers is that thinking clearly is easier when we can see what is riding on the answer.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 says anthropocentrism is rarely announced, and names where it does show up instead. Where?

options.text: In the adjectives, since once the human case is the default every other mind gets described in terms of what it is missing.
options.why: Correct. The lecture's point is that the error is carried by the language of a description rather than by an explicit claim.

options.text: In the choice of species studied, since researchers overwhelmingly work on primates and on other animals closely related to humans.
options.why: Species choice is a real bias and is not the one the lecture names here; the slide is about how findings get written up.

options.text: In the statistics, since a comparison with humans as the baseline condition builds the ranking into the analysis itself.
options.why: The lecture makes no claim about baselines in analysis, and the point it does make is about the vocabulary of description.

options.text: In the funding, since work promising to illuminate the human mind is easier to support than work on any other kind of mind.
options.why: Funding pressure is not mentioned on the slide, and the error the lecture describes is one anybody can commit while writing.

items.stem: A researcher reports that humans sleep in a single long block rather than in several short ones, and explains it as an adaptation for consolidating memory overnight. In a short paragraph, apply §2.1.8's test for unconstrained adaptationism to that explanation, and say what the test establishes and what it leaves open.
items.answer: The test is to ask whether the opposite finding would have been explained just as smoothly. It would have been: several short blocks of sleep would have been described as an adaptation for staying alert to danger through the night, or for spreading rest around the demands of foraging and childcare. Because the story accommodates either outcome, it has not yet told us anything, and that is what makes the explanation unconstrained rather than merely unproven. What the test establishes is that this particular argument carries no evidential weight. What it does not establish is that the claim is false — single-block sleep may well be an adaptation for memory consolidation, and showing it would take evidence the adaptive story does not supply, such as whether the pattern tracks the pressure across species or arose more than once independently.
rubric: Applies the test by producing an equally smooth explanation of the opposite outcome.
Concludes that a story fitting either outcome carries no evidential weight, which is what makes it unconstrained.
Distinguishes the explanation being unconstrained from the underlying claim being false.
Names some kind of independent evidence that would be needed instead.

items.stem: In a few sentences, distinguish anthropomorphism from anthropocentrism, and explain how surface matching relates to both.
items.answer: Anthropomorphism is over-attribution: projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description, as when a dog is taken to look guilty or a chatbot to mean what it says. Anthropocentrism is not over-attribution but mis-calibration: it makes the human case the reference point, so that every other mind gets measured by how near it comes to ours and described in terms of what it lacks. The chapter calls the second subtler and often more damaging, because it shapes which questions get asked in the first place. Surface matching is the theme underneath both. It is the assumption that what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside, and each of the named errors is a special case of taking a handful of measured behaviors as evidence about machinery nobody has looked at.
rubric: Defines anthropomorphism as projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description.
Defines anthropocentrism as treating the human case as reference point or default.
Marks the difference between over-attributing a capacity and ranking other minds against a human standard.
Identifies surface matching as the common theme, and states what it assumes.

items.stem: Lecture 2.1 says one piece of honesty concerning this course should be said out loud. What is it, and how does the lecture characterize it?

options.text: That the comparison a working scientist makes most often is the one getting the least room here — a claim about what to teach rather than a ranking of what matters.
options.why: Correct. The lecture gives the reason: cross-system comparison exposes things no amount of work inside a single system will show.

options.text: That the comparison a working scientist makes most often is the one getting the most room here, which is why the course is a good preparation for research.
options.why: Reversed. The family most used day to day is exactly the one this course spends least time on.

options.text: That the three families overlap so much in practice that the division is a teaching convenience rather than a real distinction.
options.why: The lecture treats the three as genuinely different comparisons, and the honesty concerns how much room each is given.

options.text: That most published comparisons are underpowered, which is why the course teaches the logic of comparison before any particular finding.
options.why: No claim about statistical power is made, and the honesty concerns the course's allocation of attention.

items.stem: Describing the stockings study, lecture 2.1 emphasizes how the shoppers reacted when position was put to them as an explanation. How does it put it?

options.text: They rejected it — and not sheepishly either, but because they simply found the suggestion implausible.
options.why: Correct. The confidence of the after-the-fact reason is what makes the study a case of surface matching about ourselves.

options.text: They accepted it readily once it was pointed out, which shows the bias operates below awareness rather than against it.
options.why: The lecture reports rejection rather than acceptance, and the rejection is what gives the finding its force.

options.text: They were unable to say either way, which shows introspection returns nothing at all about a choice of this kind.
options.why: A blank would be a weaker finding. What the shoppers produced instead were specific reasons about knit and sheerness.

options.text: They asked to repeat the choice with the pairs rearranged, which is how the position effect was originally established.
options.why: No such request is described, and the effect was established by the arrangement rather than by the shoppers' own suggestion.

pools.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
pools.covers: reading §2.2, §2.2.1 · lecture 2.2 slides darwins_premise, three_requirements, selection_edits, no_foresight · lab Part 2

items.stem: What is natural selection?

options.text: What follows when a population shows variation, some of that variation is inherited, and some variants leave more offspring than others.
options.why: Correct. All three are ordinary observations rather than assumptions, and the outcome follows from their holding together.

options.text: A pressure in the environment that pushes a population steadily toward being better suited to the conditions it happens to be living in.
options.why: That is the force picture the chapter explicitly rejects. Selection is closer to bookkeeping: whatever reproduces more becomes more common.

options.text: The process by which an individual organism gradually changes over the course of its own lifetime, in response to the demands its environment makes.
options.why: No individual changes in this process. What changes is which individuals there are, which is why the population is the unit.

options.text: A feature of an organism's environment that makes one variant reproduce more successfully than another, so that variant spreads.
options.why: That is selective pressure, defined in §2.2.3 — one input to selection rather than a name for the whole process.

items.stem: Which term names what follows when a population shows variation, some of that variation is inherited, and some variants leave more offspring than others?

options.text: natural selection
options.why: Correct. The three requirements are ordinary observations, and Darwin worked out the logic without knowing what a gene was.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That is the process producing analogies, in which two lineages arrive at the same solution from different starting points.

options.text: selective pressure
options.why: That is one feature of an environment making a variant reproduce more successfully, rather than the whole process it feeds.

options.text: differential reproduction
options.why: That is the third of the three requirements on its own, and selection is what follows from all three holding at once.

items.stem: What is an adaptation?

options.text: A trait that became common because organisms that had it were more likely to survive and reproduce in the environment they were actually living in.
options.why: Correct. The final clause does the work: an adaptation is a fit to particular conditions rather than a mark of general superiority.

options.text: A trait that improves an organism's general capabilities, so that a lineage carrying it ends up better equipped than its close relatives are.
options.why: That is the improvement reading the section rejects. Adaptation is local fit, and when circumstances change the fit can simply vanish.

options.text: A change that an individual organism makes during the course of its own lifetime in order to cope better with the conditions it happens to be living under.
options.why: That is adjustment within a lifetime. An adaptation is a property of a population that became common across generations.

options.text: A trait shared by two lineages because both faced the same selective pressure and arrived at the same solution to it separately.
options.why: That is an analogy, a claim about why two species resemble each other rather than a claim about what any one trait is.
