items.stem: Which term names a trait that became common because organisms that had it were more likely to survive and reproduce in the environment they were actually living in?

options.text: adaptation
options.why: Correct. The environment clause is what makes it local fit rather than improvement, which is what §2.2.5's anti-ladder argument rests on.

options.text: unconstrained adaptationism
options.why: That is the habit of assuming every trait must be a finely tuned solution, which is an error about explanation rather than a trait.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That is the process producing analogies, two lineages landing on one solution from different starting points.

options.text: selective pressure
options.why: That is the feature of an environment that makes one variant reproduce more successfully than another does.

items.stem: What did Darwin argue in The Descent of Man (1871) about human and animal minds?

options.text: That the difference between the human mind and the minds of other animals is one of degree rather than one of kind.
options.why: Correct. §2.2 treats that claim as the premise the legitimacy of cross-species comparison rests on, and notes it is not unanimous.

options.text: That the difference between the human mind and the minds of other animals is one of kind rather than merely one of degree.
options.why: Reversed. The discontinuity position is the one some later researchers hold, and the Further Reading rather than the chapter argues it.

options.text: That natural selection acts on variation, inheritance and differential reproduction, which was the argument the book set out for the first time.
options.why: Natural selection was laid out in On the Origin of Species in 1859. The 1871 book applied the theory to human beings.

options.text: That the human mind cannot be studied comparatively at all, since introspection is available for one species and for no others.
options.why: Nagel's problem about other minds is raised in §2.2.5, and it is not something Darwin argued in the book named here.

items.stem: Why does §2.2 say Darwin's continuity claim is what makes cross-species comparison legitimate?

options.text: If minds are products of evolution then they have histories, and species related by descent should have related minds.
options.why: Correct. Without that premise a resemblance between a human and a crow would be a superficial coincidence rather than a finding.

options.text: If minds differ only in degree then any two species can be placed on a single scale, which is what makes a comparison meaningful.
options.why: A single scale is precisely the ladder §2.2.5 rejects, and the chapter denies that comparison needs any such ranking.

options.text: If minds are products of evolution then every trait a mind has is an adaptation, and adaptations can be compared across species.
options.why: §2.2.7 says outright that many traits are not adaptations, so the argument the chapter gives cannot run through that claim.

options.text: If human and animal minds are made of the same physical materials, then findings about one can be transferred to the other directly.
options.why: Shared material is an implementational claim and the chapter's argument turns on shared history rather than on shared substance.

items.stem: §2.2.1 gives three requirements and says an outcome follows from them. What are the three, and what follows?

options.text: Variation, inheritance and differential reproduction; from which it follows that variants reproducing more become more common each generation.
options.why: Correct. The chapter stresses that the outcome is guaranteed rather than likely, once all three of the requirements hold together.

options.text: Variation, competition and adaptation; from which it follows that a population steadily becomes better suited to its own environment over time.
options.why: Competition and adaptation are consequences and framings rather than requirements, and "better suited" imports the improvement reading.

options.text: Mutation, inheritance and selective pressure; from which it follows that new variants arise wherever the environment demands them.
options.why: Nothing arises because the environment demands it. Selection edits variation that is already present and never calls it into being.

options.text: Variation, inheritance and survival; from which it follows that the longest-lived individuals come to dominate a population.
options.why: Longevity matters only in so far as it feeds reproduction, and it is surviving offspring rather than lifespan that the third requirement names.

items.stem: §2.2.1 says natural selection is "closer to bookkeeping" than to a force. What is that phrase doing?

options.text: Blocking the picture of selection as something pushing organisms toward being better, when it only records what reproduces more.
options.why: Correct. Whatever reproduces more becomes more common, and nothing in the process is aimed anywhere at all.

options.text: Emphasizing that the effects of selection can be quantified precisely, so that the rate of change in a population can be predicted.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about predicting rates. The metaphor is about what kind of thing selection is, not about measurement.

options.text: Indicating that selection acts on populations rather than on individuals, which is what makes the accounting a population-level matter.
options.why: The population-level point is real and separate, and the bookkeeping metaphor is aimed at the idea of selection as a driving force.

options.text: Signalling that natural selection is a description we impose on the data rather than a process that happens in the world.
options.why: The chapter treats selection as a real process with a guaranteed outcome, not as a way of talking about the data after the fact.

items.stem: A bacterial population becomes resistant within days of an antibiotic being introduced. What does §2.2.1 say happened?

options.text: The drug did not make the bacteria resistant; it killed everything that was not resistant, and the survivors did the rest.
options.why: Correct. Selection edits an existing range of variation and does not create the variation it acts on.

options.text: The drug induced a change in the bacteria that survived it, and that change was then passed on to their descendants.
options.why: That is the inducing picture the section is written to block. The resistant individuals were already present before the drug arrived.

options.text: The drug raised the mutation rate in the population, which produced the resistant variants that then spread through it quickly.
options.why: Nothing about the mechanism requires a raised mutation rate, and the section's point is that the variation was there beforehand.

options.text: The drug applied a selective pressure that the population responded to by developing a resistance mechanism over several generations.
options.why: "Responded by developing" imports foresight into a process the section insists has none, and the resistance was not developed but sorted.

items.stem: Which of these follows from §2.2.1's claim that there is no foresight anywhere in natural selection?

options.text: Selection cannot hold out for a better design if reaching it means passing through a worse one first.
options.why: Correct. It works only on the variation actually present, and only on what pays off now rather than several generations from now.

options.text: Selection cannot produce a trait that is complex, since complexity requires many changes to be coordinated in advance.
options.why: Complex traits are produced routinely, one useful step at a time; what cannot happen is a temporary step down toward a better design.

options.text: Selection cannot preserve a trait once the environment that favored it has changed, so an adaptation is lost as soon as conditions move.
options.why: Traits routinely persist after the conditions that favored them pass, which is exactly why an old adaptation can become a present liability.

options.text: Selection cannot operate at all in an environment that is changing faster than a single generation of the population.
options.why: Rate of change is not what the claim concerns, and the peppered moth case has the environment changing within decades.

items.stem: §2.2.1 contrasts an evolutionary why with the sense in which a hammer is for driving nails. What is the contrast?

options.text: An evolutionary why is a claim about the past, about what happened to work for a creature's ancestors, rather than a statement of purpose.
options.why: Correct. Nobody intended the trait, so there is no purpose to state — only a history of what paid off in a particular environment.

options.text: An evolutionary why is a claim about the future, about what the trait will be useful for as the environment continues to change.
options.why: Selection has no foresight at all, so a claim about future usefulness is exactly what an evolutionary why cannot be.

options.text: An evolutionary why is a claim about the present, about what the trait is doing for the organism carrying it right now.
options.why: Present function is one of Tinbergen's four questions from §2.2.7, and it is not what the word carries in an evolutionary explanation.

options.text: An evolutionary why is a claim about design, since selection produces traits so well fitted that they are indistinguishable from designed ones.
options.why: Fit can be close, and the section's point is that no designer and no intention is involved at any stage of the process.

items.stem: A trait that was an adaptation two hundred years ago may be a liability now, with nothing about the trait having changed. Why, on §2.2.1's account?

options.text: An adaptation is a fit between a creature and a particular set of circumstances, so when the circumstances change the fit can vanish.
options.why: Correct. Adaptation is local fit rather than improvement, which is why it is not movement toward anything and can be lost without changing.

options.text: Traits accumulate deleterious mutations over time, so a trait maintained for many generations becomes less effective than it was.
options.why: Mutation accumulation is a real phenomenon and is not the section's explanation; the chapter's case turns on the environment moving.

options.text: Selection acts more slowly than environments change, so most traits in most populations are always somewhat out of date.
options.why: Lag is a real consequence and the section's claim is stronger and simpler: fit is relative to conditions, so conditions alone can undo it.

options.text: An adaptation is only ever an approximate solution, so a trait that looks well fitted has always had costs that were not being counted.
options.why: The section does not claim adaptations are approximations. It claims the standard they meet is a local one that can move underneath them.

items.stem: What happened to the peppered moth across the industrial period in Britain?

options.text: Pale speckled forms dominated on lichen-crusted bark; coal smoke blackened the bark and dark forms took over the sootiest regions; clean-air laws reversed it.
options.why: Correct. The bark changed and the moths did not: what changed was which form a bird could pick out against it.

options.text: Pale speckled forms dominated until coal smoke darkened the moths themselves, and the population lightened again once the air had been cleaned up by legislation.
options.why: Nothing darkened the moths. Both forms were present throughout, and the soot changed only which of them was easy for a predator to see.

options.text: Dark forms dominated on lichen-crusted bark; coal smoke lightened the bark and pale forms took over, until clean-air laws reversed the pattern.
options.why: The bark and the moths are the wrong way round: lichen-crusted bark is pale, and coal smoke blackened it rather than lightening it.

options.text: Pale and dark forms remained in stable proportions throughout, which is what showed that bird predation was not driving the change at all.
options.why: The proportions shifted dramatically, and Majerus's field study later confirmed bird predation as the mechanism behind the shift.

items.stem: What happened to the bird-predation explanation of the peppered moth after it became a textbook case?

options.text: It was disputed on methodological grounds and then confirmed by a careful seven-year field study by Michael Majerus.
options.why: Correct. The chapter includes the episode because the textbook case survived a serious audit, which many textbook cases do not.

options.text: It was disputed on methodological grounds and then abandoned, with the change now attributed to migration between regions instead.
options.why: The explanation was not abandoned. Majerus's fieldwork was designed to answer the methodological objections and it upheld the account.

options.text: It was accepted without challenge for a century, and the early experiments have never been subjected to independent scrutiny at all.
options.why: The early experiments were challenged directly in the 1990s, which is what made the seven-year replication worth carrying out.

options.text: It was disputed and then confirmed by laboratory work showing that birds prefer moths of one colouration over the other in cages.
options.why: The confirmation came from a long field study rather than from caged preference tests, which is what answered the objections.

items.stem: §2.2.1 notes that Darwin worked out the logic of natural selection without knowing what a gene or DNA was. What does the chapter take from that?

options.text: That the argument does not depend on the details of the mechanism carrying inheritance from one generation to the next.
options.why: Correct. Variation, inheritance and differential reproduction can each be observed without any account of how inheritance works.

options.text: That Darwin's account was necessarily incomplete, and only became a real theory once the mechanism of inheritance was understood.
options.why: The chapter treats the logic as complete on its own terms, and offers Darwin's ignorance of genes as evidence for exactly that.

options.text: That inheritance is the least important of the three requirements, since the argument goes through without any account of it.
options.why: The lab's own knockout shows inheritance is indispensable; what is dispensable is knowing the machinery that implements it.

options.text: That natural selection is a logical truth rather than an empirical claim, so no observation could ever count against it.
options.why: The three requirements are empirical observations about real populations, and each of them could have turned out otherwise.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 illustrates the absence of foresight with a feature of the vertebrate eye. Which, and what does it show?

options.text: The retina's wiring runs across the front of the light-sensitive cells and punches back through the sheet, producing a blind spot no engineer would design.
options.why: Correct. The octopus does it the other way round and has no blind spot; ours is what happens when a process cannot go back and start again.

options.text: The lens focuses an image onto a sheet of light-sensitive cells, which is a solution the octopus lineage arrived at quite independently of the vertebrates.
options.why: That is the analogy case from §2.2.2, about convergence on a good design rather than about being stuck with a poor one.

options.text: The retina performs a great deal of processing before its output leaves the eye, which saves the cortex work it would otherwise have to do.
options.why: Early retinal processing is a feature of the frog example in §2.1.1, and the lecture uses the blind spot rather than efficiency here.

options.text: The eye develops from a genetic switch inherited from a distant ancestor that had no eyes at all, which shows selection reusing whatever happens to be to hand.
options.why: The shared switch is the §2.2.2 caveat about levels, and the lecture's foresight example is the inverted retina and its blind spot.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 asks the room to say carefully what the soot did to the peppered moths. What is the answer it gives?

options.text: It changed which of the moths a bird could see against the bark, since dark and pale forms were both present the whole time.
options.why: Correct. The lecture uses the question to make the same point the antibiotic case makes: selection sorts variation rather than producing it.

options.text: It darkened the moths that were exposed to it, and their descendants inherited the darker colouring they had acquired.
options.why: That is the inducing picture the slide exists to block, and it is the answer the lecture expects and then corrects.

options.text: It killed the lichens the moths depended on for food, so the population shifted toward forms that could feed on bark instead.
options.why: The lichens matter as background rather than as food, and the moths' colouring is about visibility to predators.

options.text: It raised the rate at which new dark variants appeared in the population, which is why the shift happened within a few decades.
options.why: The lecture is explicit that nothing new appeared. The dark form was already there, and the soot only changed how visible it was.

items.stem: In Part 2 of the evolution lab, the mutation rate is set to zero and the run repeated. What happens to the population?

options.text: It improves for a while and then stops, because the only wiring it can ever contain is wiring that was present in the founders.
options.why: Correct. Selection sorted the founding variation and then had nothing further to work on, which is the knockout's whole point.

options.text: Nothing changes at all from the moment the run begins, because without mutation there is no variation for selection to act on.
options.why: The founding population is varied even with mutation at zero, so there is real improvement first — it simply cannot continue.

options.text: It improves steadily throughout the run, though more slowly than a run in which the mutation rate is left at its default value.
options.why: Improvement stops rather than slowing, and the plateau is what shows where the population's wiring actually came from.

options.text: It gets steadily worse, because with no new variation appearing the population cannot keep pace with the food patches as they drift.
options.why: The food drifts in every condition, and the population that emerges from the founders holds its ground once it has been sorted.

items.stem: In the evolution lab, inheritance is switched off so that offspring receive random wiring. What is observed, and what does it show about why inheritance is a requirement in its own right?

options.text: Nothing accumulates, however long the run goes on, even though selection carries on choosing whichever adults stored the most energy — the winning is simply never passed on.
options.why: Correct. That selection was still operating and made no difference is the cleanest statement of why inheritance is not part of selection.

options.text: The population improves more slowly than usual, since a random offspring will occasionally land on wiring as good as its parent's had been.
options.why: Occasional good offspring appear and are not retained, so there is no slow improvement — there is no cumulative change at all.

options.text: The population collapses immediately, because random wiring leaves most vehicles unable to reach any of the food patches in time.
options.why: Some randomly wired vehicles feed perfectly well. What is missing is not survival but the transmission of whatever worked.

options.text: Selection stops operating, because with inheritance off there is no longer any heritable difference for it to choose between.
options.why: Selection carries on choosing throughout the run, which is exactly what makes the absence of any accumulation informative.

items.stem: In the evolution lab, selection is switched off and the identical founding population is run twice over. What is observed across the two runs?

options.text: The population still changes, getting worse at finding food about as often as it gets better, and the two runs end somewhere different despite identical founders.
options.why: Correct. Change with no direction to it is drift, and because neither a shared source nor a shared problem is doing the work it is a source of coincidence.

options.text: The population still changes but not for the better, and the two runs end in much the same place, since identical founders constrain where drift can take them.
options.why: Divergence from identical founders is the observation the experiment is built around, and it is what surprises most students who run it.

options.text: The population stops changing entirely, since with selection switched off there is nothing left to move it in any direction at all.
options.why: Change continues perfectly well without selection; what it loses is not motion but any tendency toward getting better.

options.text: The population changes and gets steadily worse in both of the runs, which converge on much the same poor outcome each time.
options.why: Drift has no direction, so it degrades and improves about equally often rather than driving a population reliably downward.

items.stem: In the evolution lab, a population is evolved to do well and the light regime is then switched from food to poison without resetting. What happens, and what does it show about adaptation?

options.text: The population collapses and the previously most successful individuals are hit hardest, showing that adaptation is a fit to conditions rather than general superiority.
options.why: Correct. The same wiring went from best to worst without changing at all, which is what "local fit" means and what it rules out.

options.text: The population adjusts within a few minutes, showing that a well-adapted population carries enough flexibility to handle a wholesale change of conditions.
options.why: No individual adjusts anything. The wiring a vehicle is born with is the wiring it dies with, and the change costs the best performers most.

options.text: The population is unaffected, showing that an adaptation once established is robust to changes in the environment that produced it.
options.why: The collapse is immediate and severe, and robustness to environmental change is precisely what an adaptation does not confer.

options.text: The population collapses and the least successful individuals are the ones hit hardest, which shows that a poor adaptation is punished under any regime at all.
options.why: It is the ones that had been winning that suffer most, because what made them successful is now what kills them.

items.stem: A news report says that a pest population "developed resistance in response to" a new insecticide. In a short paragraph, say what is wrong with that phrasing, and describe one result from the evolution lab that supports your answer.
items.answer: The phrasing puts the population in the position of responding, which imports both an agent and a direction into a process that has neither. What actually happened is that some individuals were already resistant before the insecticide arrived — variation the population contained for its own reasons — and the insecticide killed the rest. The survivors' descendants are what is left, so the frequency of resistance changed without any individual changing at all. Selection edits an existing range of variation and does not create the variation it acts on. The lab's zero-mutation run makes the same point directly: with no new variation available, the population still improved, because the useful wiring was already present in the founders, and then it stopped improving, because nothing new could appear. Improvement came out of the existing spread and not out of the pressure.
rubric: Identifies that the resistant variants were already present before the insecticide was applied.
States that the insecticide changed which individuals survived rather than changing any individual.
States the general principle that selection edits existing variation and does not create it.
Cites a lab result — the zero-mutation run improving and then stopping — and connects it to that principle.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 opens by asking why it is legitimate to compare a human mind to a crow's at all, and says the question only sounds rhetorical. What is the point?

options.text: For most of the history of thought it was not obvious that it was: if human minds are a different kind of thing, comparing them is a category error and any resemblance found is superficial.
options.why: Correct. Darwin's continuity claim is what removes that objection, and the lecture calls it the license without which there is no comparative psychology.

options.text: For most of the history of thought the comparison was routine, and it was Darwin who first raised doubts about how far it could be pushed.
options.why: The lecture has Darwin supplying the license rather than questioning it, and it presents the earlier default as scepticism.

options.text: The comparison is legitimate because human and animal brains are made of the same cells, which was established well before Darwin wrote.
options.why: Shared material is an implementational fact, and the argument the lecture gives runs through shared history rather than shared substance.

options.text: The comparison is legitimate only for species closely related to humans, which is why the lecture confines itself to primates.
options.why: The lecture goes on to compare humans with crows and octopuses, which are about as distant as living relatives get.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 says something about the three requirements that it calls startling every time. What is it?

options.text: If the three hold, the outcome is not merely likely but guaranteed: whatever reproduces more becomes more common, and enough generations of that make a different population.
options.why: Correct. The lecture also stresses that the three are ordinary observations you could check in an afternoon rather than assumptions or a theory.

options.text: If the three hold, the population will eventually arrive at the best available solution to whatever problem its environment poses.
options.why: Nothing guarantees an optimum: selection has no foresight and works only on the variation that happens to be present.

options.text: If the three hold, the population will change at a rate that can be predicted from the strength of the selective pressure acting on it.
options.why: No claim about rates is made, and what the lecture calls startling is that the direction of change follows with certainty.

options.text: If any two of the three hold, the outcome follows, which is why the knockout experiments in the lab remove more than one at a time.
options.why: The lab removes exactly one at a time, and each knockout shows that the remaining two are not sufficient on their own.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the three things §2.2.1 says natural selection is not — a force, a process with foresight, and a route to general improvement — and give one consequence of each for how an evolutionary explanation should be phrased.
items.answer: Selection is not a force pushing organisms anywhere; it is closer to bookkeeping, in that whatever reproduces more becomes more common. So an explanation should not say that a pressure drove a population toward a trait, only that individuals carrying the trait left more offspring. Selection has no foresight: it cannot plan, cannot aim at a benefit several generations away, and cannot hold out for a better design that would require passing through a worse one. So an evolutionary why is never a statement of purpose in the way a hammer is for driving nails — it is always a claim about what happened to work for a creature's ancestors. And adaptation is local fit rather than improvement: a trait became common because it paid in the environment the organisms were actually living in. So an explanation should always name the conditions, since a trait that was an adaptation two centuries ago may be a liability now with nothing about the trait having changed.
rubric: States that selection is bookkeeping rather than a force, and gives a phrasing consequence.
States that there is no foresight, and draws the consequence that an evolutionary why is a claim about the past rather than a purpose.
States that adaptation is local fit rather than improvement.
Draws the consequence that an explanation has to name the environment the fit was to.

items.stem: In the evolution lab the arena is set to hold as few vehicles as it can and run several times over. Does the best variety always take over?

options.text: No — usually it does, but sometimes a worse one takes over instead, and a population that small can die out altogether.
options.why: Correct. With very few individuals in the arena at a time, whichever ones happen to do well early can take it over regardless of quality — drift competing against selection rather than replacing it.

options.text: Yes — a smaller arena concentrates the competition, so the advantage of the best variety shows up faster than at the default size.
options.why: Selection is indeed sharper per individual, and with so few individuals a run of luck early on can override it entirely.

options.text: No — the worst variety takes over reliably, because a small population cannot sustain the energy cost of chasing the food patches.
options.why: That over-corrects. The best variety wins most of the time; what changes is that the outcome stops being dependable.

options.text: No — the population always dies out before any variety can take over, which is why the smallest setting is used only as a demonstration.
options.why: Extinction happens sometimes and is a genuine result worth recording, rather than the outcome of every run at that setting.
