items.stem: What is a homology?

options.text: A resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor.
options.why: Correct. It is the answer that attributes a similarity to a shared origin rather than to a shared problem.

options.text: A resemblance between two species that arose separately in each lineage under a similar selective pressure.
options.why: That is an analogy, the counterpart claim, and it asserts that the common ancestor did not have the trait at all.

options.text: A resemblance between two species that turns out on inspection to have no meaningful cause behind it whatsoever.
options.why: That is coincidence, the third of §2.1.3's answers, and neither of the two formal names in §2.2.2 covers it.

options.text: A resemblance between two structures within a single organism that were built from the same developmental material.
options.why: Homology as the chapter defines it is a relation between species, not between two parts of one body.

items.stem: Which term names a resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor?

options.text: homology
options.why: Correct. It is a claim about the history of a resemblance rather than a description of how the resemblance looks.

options.text: analogy
options.why: That names a resemblance that arose separately in each lineage, where the common ancestor did not have the trait.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That names the process producing analogies, in which two lineages converge on one solution from different starting points.

options.text: phylogeny
options.why: That names a species' evolutionary history, of which a phylogenetic tree is the map.

items.stem: What is an analogy, in the sense §2.2.2 gives the word?

options.text: A resemblance between two species that arose separately in each lineage under similar pressure, where the common ancestor did not have the trait.
options.why: Correct. It is the answer that attributes a similarity to a shared problem rather than to a shared origin.

options.text: A resemblance between two species that both inherited from a common ancestor that already had the trait in question.
options.why: That is a homology, the counterpart claim, and it is the one that licenses reasoning about the ancestor.

options.text: A comparison drawn between a familiar system and an unfamiliar one, in order to make the unfamiliar one easier to explain to somebody meeting it for the first time.
options.why: That is the everyday sense of the word, and it is not what the term does in evolutionary biology.

options.text: A resemblance whose depth has been established at the algorithmic level but not yet at the implementational one.
options.why: That is a depth claim, and homology and analogy are claims about history rather than about the level a match holds at.

items.stem: Which term names a resemblance that arose separately in each lineage under similar pressure, where the common ancestor did not have the trait?

options.text: analogy
options.why: Correct. Asserting it is precisely asserting that the ancestor lacked the trait, which is why no ancestral inference follows.

options.text: homology
options.why: That names a resemblance both species inherited from a common ancestor that already had it.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That names the process that produces this relation — two lineages converging on one solution — rather than the relation itself.

options.text: adaptation
options.why: That names a trait that became common because organisms with it were more likely to survive and reproduce.

items.stem: What is a common ancestor?

options.text: A species from which two or more later species are descended, and which a branch point on a phylogenetic tree marks.
options.why: Correct. Branch points on a phylogenetic tree mark them, and whether a trait was present in one separates homology from analogy.

options.text: The most recent individual organism from which two living species are each able to trace their own line of descent directly.
options.why: The chapter defines the notion at the level of species rather than at the level of a single individual organism.

options.text: A species that still survives today and closely resembles the form from which its relatives later diverged.
options.why: No living species is the ancestor of another; every living species sits at the end of an equally long lineage.

options.text: A trait that appears in two species because both of them inherited it from the same earlier population.
options.why: That is a homology. The ancestor is the species, not the trait that happens to have been passed down from it.

items.stem: What is convergent evolution?

options.text: The process that produces analogies, in which two lineages converge on the same solution from different starting points.
options.why: Correct. §2.2.4 adds that convergence is also evidence the problem being solved was a real one rather than invented afterward.

options.text: The process by which two related lineages become steadily more similar as they continue to share the same environment.
options.why: Relatedness is what convergence does without. The lineages converge despite having no shared history for the trait in question.

options.text: The process by which a trait inherited from a common ancestor is preserved with very little change across many lineages.
options.why: That describes a conserved homology, which is inheritance rather than independent arrival at the same solution.

options.text: The process by which a single lineage arrives at several different solutions to a problem before settling on one of them.
options.why: Convergence is a relation between two lineages, not a search carried out within one of them over time.

items.stem: What is a phylogeny?

options.text: A species' evolutionary history: which lineages it descends from, and where it branched from its relatives.
options.why: Correct. A phylogenetic tree is the map of it, and the map is what converts a raw resemblance into an inference.

options.text: The developmental history of an individual organism across the course of its own single lifetime.
options.why: That is ontogeny, defined in §2.5.2, and the chapter draws the contrast between the two histories explicitly.

options.text: The complete set of traits that a species carries, arranged by how strongly each one of them has been selected for.
options.why: A phylogeny is a history of descent rather than an inventory of traits or a ranking of how selected they were.

options.text: The process by which two lineages that face the same selective pressure arrive at the same solution to it.
options.why: That is convergent evolution, one of the things a phylogeny is used to detect rather than a name for the history itself.

items.stem: What is a phylogenetic tree?

options.text: A diagram of how species are related by descent, with branch points marking common ancestors.
options.why: Correct. The tree is what says whether inheritance is even available as an explanation for a resemblance.

options.text: A diagram ranking species by complexity, from the simplest at the base to the most complex at the top.
options.why: That is the ladder of intelligence, inherited from the great chain of being, and §2.2.5 rejects it outright.

options.text: A diagram of the traits a single species carries, arranged by the order in which each one appeared.
options.why: A tree relates species to one another; the history of a single species' traits is a different kind of record.

options.text: A diagram of how strongly each species in a group responds to a given selective pressure in its environment.
options.why: Selective pressure appears in §2.2.3 alongside the tree and is not what the tree itself is a diagram of.

items.stem: What is a selective pressure?

options.text: A feature of an organism's environment that makes one variant reproduce more successfully than another, so that the variant spreads.
options.why: Correct. Two lineages facing the same problem are under pressure to develop an adaptation, and few good solutions can put them on one.

options.text: A force acting on a population that drives it in the direction of being better suited to its surroundings over time.
options.why: The chapter rejects the force picture. Nothing pushes; whatever reproduces more simply becomes more common in the population.

options.text: The strength of the competition between individuals of one species for a resource that all of them require in order to be able to reproduce at all.
options.why: Competition can create a pressure and the definition is broader: any environmental feature making one variant reproduce better.

options.text: The rate at which a trait becomes more common in a population once natural selection has begun to act upon it.
options.why: That is a measure of the outcome. The pressure is the feature of the environment producing the difference in reproduction.

items.stem: §2.2.2 is careful about what kind of claim homology and analogy are. What kind is it?

options.text: A claim about the history and cause of a resemblance, so two things can look identical and be either, with appearance settling nothing.
options.why: Correct. What is observed in both cases is a resemblance; the label is an assertion about how the resemblance came to be there.

options.text: A claim about how close a resemblance is, so that a very exact resemblance counts as a homology and a rougher one counts as an analogy instead.
options.why: Exactness is the precision question, and a precise resemblance can perfectly well have arisen twice independently.

options.text: A claim about which Marr level a resemblance holds at, so a shared mechanism is a homology and shared behavior an analogy.
options.why: That is the depth question. Both labels can apply at any level, and neither names a level of description.

options.text: A claim about how the resemblance looks, so careful enough description of two structures will eventually settle which it is.
options.why: The section says this outright and denies it: nothing about how two things look will tell us which of the two they are.

items.stem: Vertebrate and octopus eyes evolved independently, yet the genetic switch that starts an eye developing is shared, inherited from a distant ancestor with no eyes. What does §2.2.2 conclude?

options.text: Both answers are true of different things: the eye is analogous and the switch is homologous, so a claim has to say which structure it is about.
options.why: Correct. That is why an honest claim always specifies what structure, described at what level, is supposed to share an origin.

options.text: The eye must be homologous after all, since a shared developmental switch is what inheriting a structure amounts to.
options.why: A shared switch does not carry the structure with it. The camera eye itself was built twice, from an ancestor that had none.

options.text: The shared switch must have arisen independently as well, since a structure that was built twice over could not have inherited its trigger from anywhere.
options.why: The switch really is inherited, which is exactly what makes the case interesting rather than a straightforward analogy.

options.text: The distinction between homology and analogy breaks down here, so neither label applies to the eye or to the switch.
options.why: Both labels apply cleanly. What the case shows is that they apply to different things, not that they have stopped working.

items.stem: §2.2.2 uses the camera eye for both of its labels. Which grouping is homologous and which analogous?

options.text: Human, mouse, lizard and shark eyes are homologous; human and octopus eyes are analogous.
options.why: Correct. The first four are modifications of one inherited plan; the human and octopus designs were built separately from an eyeless ancestor.

options.text: Human and octopus eyes are homologous; human, mouse, lizard and shark eyes are analogous to one another.
options.why: Reversed. Vertebrates share an ancestor that already had the eye, and the octopus lineage does not.

options.text: All five are homologous, since the physics of forming an image leaves so few options that any camera eye is the same design.
options.why: Few options is exactly the reason the octopus case is an analogy: a shared constraint rather than a shared ancestor.

options.text: All five are analogous, since a camera eye is complex enough that it is unlikely to have been inherited intact by any lineage.
options.why: Camera eyes are inherited routinely within the vertebrates, and the differences among them are modifications of one plan.

items.stem: Two species far apart on a phylogenetic tree share a trait, and every species between them lacks it. What does §2.2.3's procedure license?

options.text: Inheritance is ruled out as an explanation, so what remains is either convergence in the two lineages or coincidence.
options.why: Correct. The tree converts a raw resemblance into an inference by saying whether inheritance is even available as an explanation.

options.text: Inheritance remains the natural first hypothesis, since the intervening species may simply have lost the trait separately.
options.why: Independent loss along every intervening branch is exactly what the pattern makes implausible, which is why inheritance is ruled out.

options.text: Nothing at all is licensed, since a phylogenetic tree records descent and cannot speak to the distribution of any single trait.
options.why: Mapping a trait onto the tree is the whole procedure, and the distribution across tips and branch points is what does the work.

options.text: The trait must be an adaptation in both species, since a trait arising twice independently is necessarily being selected for.
options.why: Convergence is one candidate and coincidence is the other, and §2.2.7 warns against reading every trait as an adaptation.

items.stem: New Caledonian crows manufacture hooked twig tools in the wild, untaught. Running §2.2.3's procedure, what does §2.2.4 conclude about crow and human tool use, and on what grounds?

options.text: Analogous, because the last common ancestor of birds and mammals was a reptile-like vertebrate roughly three hundred million years ago, with nothing suggesting tool manufacture.
options.why: Correct. Inheritance would require the trait to have been lost along every intervening lineage, so convergence is what is left.

options.text: Homologous, because tool use is a capacity general enough that the distant reptile-like vertebrate ancestor may well have possessed some rudimentary version of it already.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about that ancestor suggests tool manufacture, which is what rules inheritance out rather than in.

options.text: Analogous, because crows and humans are both social species and social living is the pressure that produces tool manufacture.
options.why: The verdict is right and the grounds are not: the tree settles it, and no such claim about sociality is made here.

options.text: Coincidental, because manufacturing a hooked twig is a specific enough behavior that two lineages are unlikely to arrive at it separately.
options.why: Specificity is a reason to take convergence seriously rather than to dismiss it, and the chapter treats the case as a genuine analogy.

items.stem: What did Clayton and colleagues show about scrub jays, and why does §2.2.4 include it?

options.text: They remember what they cached and how long ago as well as where, recovering perishable items first — memory for a specific past event, long assumed human-only.
options.why: Correct. It is a second instance of an intelligence feature appearing in a lineage whose brain plan diverged before either group had much brain.

options.text: They remember where they cached food and return to those places far more reliably than any mammal that has so far been tested on the very same caching task.
options.why: Spatial memory alone is unremarkable. What matters is the what and the when, which is what makes the memory look episodic.

options.text: They learn to cache by watching other jays, which shows that the capacity is transmitted socially rather than being built in.
options.why: Social transmission is not what the study established, and the chapter's interest is in what is remembered rather than how caching is acquired.

options.text: They cache food only when another jay is watching, which shows they can represent what a competitor knows about the cache.
options.why: Deception is mentioned in passing as one of the things corvids do; the finding the chapter reports concerns memory for the caching event.

items.stem: Why does §2.2.4 call the octopus the more radical case than the crow?

options.text: Its large nervous system is arranged nothing like ours, with most neurons in the arms, and its lineage separated before anything we would call a brain existed.
options.why: Correct. Godfrey-Smith's suggestion is that meeting one is about as close as we are likely to come to meeting an intelligent alien.

options.text: Its nervous system is larger than a crow's relative to body size, so its convergence with human cognition covers more capacities.
options.why: Relative size is not the chapter's point, and the radical part is the arrangement and the depth of the split rather than the count.

options.text: It is the only invertebrate known to manufacture tools, which makes the convergence with human tool use harder to explain.
options.why: Tool manufacture is the crow's case in this section, and what the octopus contributes is a nervous system organized on another plan.

options.text: It diverged from the vertebrate lineage only after recognizable brains had appeared, so all of its differences from us must have evolved extremely quickly.
options.why: The split came roughly six hundred million years ago, before anything either of us would call a brain had appeared.

items.stem: §2.2.4 says adaptive explanation at the computational level carries a standing vulnerability. What is it, and what is the snake example for?

options.text: The problem may have been invented after the fact to suit the solution, and the snake case shows a finding and its opposite being explained equally smoothly.
options.why: Correct. Quick snake detection reads as anti-venom adaptation; slow detection would have read as freezing being safer once a predator is close.

options.text: The problem may be described at the wrong Marr level, and the snake case shows a computational claim being mistaken for an algorithmic one by researchers who should know better.
options.why: Level confusion is a real hazard elsewhere; the vulnerability here is that the problem gets reverse-engineered from the answer.

options.text: The problem may turn out not to be a problem at all, and the snake case shows a supposed adaptation that later failed to replicate.
options.why: Nothing about replication is at issue. The finding is taken as given, and the objection is to the story built on top of it.

options.text: The problem may be shared with too many species to be informative, and the snake case shows a pressure that nearly all mammals face.
options.why: Breadth is not the objection, and convergence across species is what the section goes on to offer as the remedy rather than the disease.

items.stem: How does §2.2.4 argue that convergence answers the worry about invented problems?

options.text: When two lineages that share no history arrive at the same solution, that is evidence the problem they were both solving was real.
options.why: Correct. The same answer reached twice from different directions is a strong hint the question was not one we made up afterward.

options.text: When two lineages share a history, their common solution can be traced to an ancestor, which shows the problem existed that far back.
options.why: An inherited trait tells us about the ancestor, and it is independent arrival rather than shared history that speaks to the problem.

options.text: When a lineage arrives at a solution more than once, the repeated arrival shows that the trait is under strong selective pressure now.
options.why: The argument concerns two separate lineages rather than one, and it speaks to the reality of the problem rather than to current pressure.

options.text: When two lineages arrive at the same solution, we can conclude that solution is the only workable one available for the problem.
options.why: The chapter says a problem with few good solutions can put two lineages on one, which is weaker than there being only one.

items.stem: Two species both cache food and both recover it. §2.2.4 fences the convergence argument here. How?

options.text: "The same capacity" is an empirical claim with a graded answer, and the way to test it is to find out whether the two break the same way.
options.why: Correct. Capacities identical from outside often prove neighboring but distinct: different cues, different time windows, different failures.

options.text: "The same capacity" is settled by the resemblance itself, provided the behavior has been observed under natural rather than laboratory conditions.
options.why: Natural observation does not upgrade a resemblance into a functional identity, which is the assumption the fence exists to block.

options.text: "The same capacity" cannot be assessed across species at all, since each species' behavior can only be judged against its own Umwelt.
options.why: The Umwelt standard blocks ranking rather than comparison, and the chapter goes on to compare caching across species in detail.

options.text: "The same capacity" is a claim about the implementational level, so it is settled by whether the two species use similar neural machinery.
options.why: Similar machinery is one possible finding; the functional claim is tested by behavior under pressure rather than assumed from anatomy.

items.stem: §2.2.4 describes a live disagreement about multiple realizability. What is the chapter's own position on it?

options.text: It reports both sides — Bechtel and Mundale's mismatched-precision objection, and the reply that the loose description is where the regularities are — and declines to settle it.
options.why: Correct. What the chapter commits to is that sameness of function is always a claim at some level of precision, and that level is a choice.

options.text: It sides with Bechtel and Mundale, on the grounds that matching the level of description makes most of the apparent cases of multiple realization disappear on closer inspection.
options.why: That argument is reported rather than endorsed, and the chapter explicitly says it will not settle the question either way.

options.text: It sides against Bechtel and Mundale, on the grounds that convergent cognition is multiple realizability observed in the wild.
options.why: Convergent cognition is said to look like multiple realizability in the wild, and the section immediately fences that appearance.

options.text: It treats the disagreement as merely verbal, since the two sides are describing the same evidence in two different vocabularies.
options.why: The chapter presents it as a real disagreement about how minds and brains should be described, not as a difference of wording.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 says the phylogenetic tree is a procedure rather than a picture, and gives the reason inheritance can be ruled out for a trait shared by two distant species. What is it?

options.text: Ruling inheritance in would mean believing the trait was independently lost along a dozen intervening lineages.
options.why: Correct. The tree runs in both directions, and the implausibility of repeated loss is what leaves convergence or coincidence.

options.text: Ruling inheritance in would require a common ancestor older than the fossil record can reach, which makes any claim about the trait untestable.
options.why: The lecture's argument turns on the pattern of trait presence across the tree rather than on how far the fossil record extends.

options.text: Ruling inheritance in would contradict the claim that every living species has been evolving for exactly the same span of time.
options.why: That claim is the anti-ladder argument from a later slide, and it says nothing about whether a particular trait was inherited.

options.text: Ruling inheritance in would require the two species to be more closely related than their branch points on the tree indicate.
options.why: Relatedness is read off the tree rather than adjusted to fit a trait, and the argument is about repeated loss along the branches.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 calls a story that would have accommodated the opposite result "a shape you can pour any outcome into." What does that phrase mark?

options.text: That the explanation has told us nothing yet, since its fitting the finding is no evidence when it would have fitted the reverse just as well.
options.why: Correct. The lecture uses the snake case both ways round before offering convergence as the way out of the difficulty.

options.text: That the explanation is false, since a story capable of accommodating any outcome must be inconsistent with the actual finding.
options.why: The story may well be true. What it lacks is evidential force, and the lecture is careful to make that the complaint.

options.text: That the explanation belongs at the algorithmic level rather than at the computational one, which is where adaptive stories are properly told.
options.why: Adaptive stories are computational-level claims throughout the chapter, and the objection is to their symmetry rather than their level.

options.text: That the explanation needs a larger sample before it can be assessed, since a single finding cannot discriminate between accounts.
options.why: Sample size is not the issue. Any number of confirmations would leave a story that fits either outcome exactly where it started.

items.stem: In Part 3 of the evolution lab, populations W, X and Y all approach the light. After pressing Reveal wiring and then Reveal tree, what did you find, and what does it make the W–Y resemblance?

options.text: Y is wired the opposite way from W, and descends from a founder pool that fled light — so Y arrived at light-approach independently, and the resemblance is an analogy.
options.why: Correct. The tree supplies exactly what behavior alone could not, which is why the lab makes students commit to a guess before either reveal.

options.text: Y is wired the same way as W and descends from the same founder pool, so all three inherited light-approach and the resemblance is a homology.
options.why: That is the guess most students commit to on behavior alone, and both reveals contradict it: the wiring differs and the founder pools differ.

options.text: Y is wired the opposite way from W and descends from the same founder pool, so the shared behavior is a coincidence rather than a response to anything.
options.why: Both lineages were under selection to reach the light, so the repeated arrival was driven rather than accidental.

options.text: Y is wired the same way as W but descends from a different founder pool, so the shared wiring is what was inherited and the behavior followed from it.
options.why: The wiring is exactly what turns out to differ, which is what makes the shared behavior a case of two routes to one job.

items.stem: Two bird species on opposite sides of a mountain range both build hanging nests. In a short paragraph, say what would have to be established before the resemblance could be called a homology, and what would have to be established before it could be called an analogy.
items.answer: Neither label can be read off the nests, however carefully they are described, because both are claims about history rather than descriptions of a resemblance. Calling it a homology requires showing that the two species sit close enough on the phylogenetic tree that a common ancestor is available, and that the ancestor itself built hanging nests — which is inferred from the trait being present across the intervening lineages rather than absent from them. Calling it an analogy requires the opposite pattern: the two species far enough apart that the species between them do not build hanging nests, which makes inheritance implausible because it would require repeated independent loss. In that case the resemblance is left to convergence or to coincidence, and separating those two would mean showing that some shared feature of the two environments made hanging nests pay.
rubric: States that homology and analogy are claims about history, so appearance cannot settle which applies.
Says what would support homology: closeness on the tree plus the trait present in the intervening lineages and the ancestor.
Says what would support analogy: distance on the tree plus the trait absent from intervening lineages, making inheritance implausible.
Notes that ruling inheritance out leaves convergence and coincidence, which need separating in their turn.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why §2.2.4 treats convergence as evidence, and say precisely which worry it answers.
items.answer: The worry is about adaptive explanation at the computational level. When we say a capacity is there because it solved some problem for a creature's ancestors, we usually identified the problem after seeing the capacity, and the snake case shows how cheap that is: fast detection reads as an anti-venom adaptation, and slow detection would have read just as smoothly as freezing being safer once a predator is close. A story that accommodates either outcome is not yet evidence. Convergence answers exactly that worry, and nothing else. When two lineages that share no relevant history arrive independently at the same solution, the problem they were both solving has to have been real rather than reconstructed from the answer, because it constrained two separate attempts. It is a claim about the problem, not about either lineage, and it still leaves open whether the two capacities are really the same one.
rubric: States the worry as the problem being invented after the fact to fit the capacity.
Uses the snake case, or an equivalent, to show the same story fitting either outcome.
Explains that independent arrival in two lineages is what makes the problem's reality more than a reconstruction.
Notes a limit: convergence speaks to the problem, and does not establish that the two capacities are identical.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 is emphatic that homology and analogy cannot be settled by looking. How does it put the point?

options.text: You are not looking at two eyes and saying those look homologous — the words are claims about history, so two things can look identical and be either, and looking harder settles nothing.
options.why: Correct. The lecture then asks what to do instead, which is what introduces the tree as a procedure on the following slide.

options.text: You are not looking at two eyes at all, since homology and analogy apply to genes rather than to the structures those genes build.
options.why: The lecture applies both terms to eyes directly, and it applies homology to the developmental switch as a separate claim about a different thing.

options.text: You are looking at two eyes, and a sufficiently detailed description of both will eventually reveal which of the two relations holds.
options.why: That is exactly the position the lecture denies: appearance underdetermines history however finely it is described.

options.text: You are looking at two eyes, and whichever is the more complex of the two is the one the common ancestor is likely to have had.
options.why: No such rule is offered, and complexity says nothing about whether a structure was inherited or built twice over.

items.stem: Running the tree procedure on crow and human tool use, lecture 2.2 gives the reason inheritance is implausible in one clause. What is it?

options.text: Every one of the lineages in between would have had to lose the trait independently.
options.why: Correct. The last common ancestor was a reptile-like vertebrate about three hundred million years back with nothing suggesting tool manufacture.

options.text: Every lineage in between would have had to acquire it separately as well, which multiplies the coincidences required.
options.why: Independent acquisition in the intervening lineages is not claimed; what makes inheritance implausible is the repeated loss it would require.

options.text: The common ancestor lived before the dinosaurs, and no behavior can be reconstructed for an animal that old with any confidence.
options.why: The lecture does reconstruct enough about it to say nothing suggests tool manufacture, and the clause it gives concerns repeated loss.

options.text: Birds and mammals diverged before brains had evolved, so neither lineage could have inherited a cognitive trait from that ancestor.
options.why: The six-hundred-million-year figure and the pre-brain split belong to the octopus case rather than to birds and mammals.

items.stem: In Part 3 of the evolution lab, pressing Reveal wiring gives each population's connection pattern and its sign. Which set of four is what the panel shows?

options.text: W contralateral excitatory, X contralateral excitatory, Y ipsilateral inhibitory, Z ipsilateral excitatory.
options.why: Correct. Y's inhibitory sign is the load-bearing cell: it is what makes Y behaviorally like W and X while built the opposite way.

options.text: W contralateral excitatory, X contralateral excitatory, Y ipsilateral excitatory, Z ipsilateral inhibitory.
options.why: Y and Z have had their signs exchanged. Y is the population that reaches the light by an unexpected route, and Z is the one that flees it.

options.text: W contralateral excitatory, X ipsilateral inhibitory, Y contralateral excitatory, Z ipsilateral excitatory.
options.why: W and X are the sister lineages and are wired alike; it is Y that departs from them, which is the whole point of the reveal.

options.text: W ipsilateral excitatory, X ipsilateral excitatory, Y contralateral inhibitory, Z contralateral excitatory.
options.why: Every pattern here is inverted. Approaching a light on this wiring calls for crossed excitatory connections, which is what W and X have.

pools.title: No Ladder, Anthropodenial, and Just-So Stories
pools.covers: reading §2.2.5, §2.2.6, §2.2.7, §2.2.8 · lecture 2.2 slides no_ladder, anthropomorphism_anthropodenial, just_so_stories, the_spine · lab Part 4

items.stem: What does Morgan's Canon hold?

options.text: That a behavior should not be explained by a higher mental process if a simpler process accounts for it.
options.why: Correct. C. Lloyd Morgan stated it in 1894, and §2.2.6 stresses that it is a rule about explanation rather than about animals.

options.text: That an animal should not be denied a capacity it plainly has merely because granting it feels unscientific.
options.why: That is the warning behind anthropodenial, which Morgan's Canon has to be applied carefully in order to avoid.

options.text: That a behavior observed in a laboratory should be confirmed in natural conditions before it is taken as genuine.
options.why: That is closer to the methodological commitments of ethology than to the canon, which is about competing explanations.

options.text: That the simplest available explanation of a behavior is the one most likely to be true of the animal in question.
options.why: The canon is a rule about what we are entitled to claim rather than a general bet on which explanation is true.

items.stem: Which principle holds that a behavior should not be explained by a higher mental process if a simpler process accounts for it?

options.text: Morgan's Canon
options.why: Correct. The working rule that follows from it, developed by Shettleworth among others, is to eliminate plain associative learning first.

options.text: anthropodenial
options.why: That is de Waal's name for refusing an animal a capacity it plainly has, which is the error Morgan's Canon can produce if applied as a policy.

options.text: unconstrained adaptationism
options.why: That is the habit of treating every trait as a finely tuned solution, which is an error rather than a principle of caution.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That is using methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether the answers they give agree with one another.

items.stem: What is ethology?

options.text: The study of animal behavior as a biological trait with an evolutionary history, usually observed under natural conditions.
options.why: Correct. Cognitive ethology, which Griffin's argument founded, is the branch treating animal awareness as a legitimate object of study.

options.text: The study of the moral obligations we owe to animals, given what is known about their capacities for thought and suffering.
options.why: That is the moral question §2.1.9 and §2.2.8 say hangs over the science, and the chapter explicitly declines to settle it.

options.text: The study of animal behavior under controlled laboratory conditions, where the variables acting on the animal can be manipulated.
options.why: Ethology's characteristic setting is natural conditions, which is part of what distinguishes it from laboratory comparative psychology.

options.text: The study of how a behavior develops over the course of an individual animal's own lifetime from birth to maturity.
options.why: That is development, one of Tinbergen's four questions rather than the name of the field the four questions belong to.

items.stem: §2.2.5 rejects the picture of a single ladder of intelligence. What reason does it give?

options.text: Every living species is equally the product of the same span of evolutionary time, and each is adapted to its own circumstances.
options.why: Correct. The ranking habit is anthropocentrism, inherited from the medieval great chain, and the chapter says it is hard to shake.

options.text: Intelligence has too many components for species to be ordered on one scale, though each component can be ranked separately.
options.why: The objection is not that the scale needs splitting. It is that there is no direction along which lineages could be ordered at all.

options.text: Ranking species requires measuring them on a task, and no task can be devised that is equally fair to every species tested on it.
options.why: Task fairness is a real difficulty and the argument here is about evolutionary standing rather than about measurement.

options.text: Species alive today descend from ancestors of very different ages, so the more recently evolved ones have had less time to develop.
options.why: Every living lineage is exactly as old as every other, which is the fact the section uses against the ladder rather than for it.

items.stem: What does §2.2.5 offer in place of ranking, and what is its example?

options.text: Judge a capacity against the world the animal actually senses and acts on — von Uexküll's Umwelt — as with a tick's world of butyric acid, warmth and touch.
options.why: Correct. The standard is local fit made into a method, which is what §2.2.1's account of adaptation had already prepared.

options.text: Judge a capacity against the range of tasks the species is able to perform, as with a tick's extremely small repertoire of possible behaviors and responses.
options.why: Counting behaviors reintroduces a ranking under another name, and the Umwelt is about the world as sensed rather than acts performed.

options.text: Judge a capacity against the capacities of the species most closely related to it, as with a tick against other arachnids.
options.why: Nearest-relative comparison is a useful control in some designs and it is not the standard this section proposes.

options.text: Judge a capacity against the problem it evolved to solve, as with a tick's ability to wait on a branch for a passing mammal.
options.why: That is close, and the section's standard is the animal's perceptual and behavioral world as a whole rather than one problem.

items.stem: §2.2.5 says asking whether a tick is smarter than a crow is "not a hard question." What is it instead, and why?

options.text: A badly formed one, because the two animals live in different worlds and there is no scale on which both could be placed.
options.why: Correct. Once a capacity is judged against the animal's own Umwelt, the comparison the question demands has nothing to range over.

options.text: An empirical one that has not yet been answered, because no task has been devised that both a tick and a crow can attempt.
options.why: The section's claim is stronger than that: no such task would settle it, because the ranking the question presupposes is not there.

options.text: A moral one rather than a scientific one, because ranking animals by intelligence has historically been used to justify how they are treated.
options.why: The moral stakes are real and are taken up in §2.2.8, and here the objection to the question is that it is malformed.

options.text: A question about Umwelten rather than about intelligence, so it can be answered by comparing the two animals' sensory worlds directly.
options.why: Comparing sensory worlds describes the two animals without ranking them, which is not an answer to the question as asked.

items.stem: §2.2.5 names two assumptions that comparing minds across species rests on, each with serious opposition. What are they?

options.text: That another mind can be understood from the outside at all, and Darwin's claim that the difference is one of degree rather than kind.
options.why: Correct. Nagel's bat is the opposition to the first, and the discontinuity position is the opposition to the second; neither is settled here.

options.text: That every species has been evolving for the same span of time, and that each is adapted to the circumstances it lives in.
options.why: Those are the section's own commitments rather than its open assumptions, and it argues for them rather than flagging opposition.

options.text: That behavior can be measured reliably in animals, and that laboratory results generalize to how those animals behave in natural conditions.
options.why: Both are genuine methodological worries elsewhere in the field, and neither is one of the two assumptions this section names.

options.text: That minds are products of evolution, and that a capacity can be judged against the world the animal actually senses and acts on.
options.why: The first is the premise §2.2 established rather than an open assumption, and the second is the corrective this section supplies.

items.stem: What did Nagel argue in 1974, and what does §2.2.5 use the argument for?

options.text: That we could know everything about how a bat's echolocation works and still not know what it is like to be a bat, so aspects of another mind may be closed to us in principle.
options.why: Correct. The section uses it as opposition to the first of the two assumptions, and §2.3 meets the same problem with an artificial mind.

options.text: That a bat's echolocation cannot be understood by a species that lacks it, so cross-species comparison of perception is unreliable.
options.why: The argument concedes that the mechanism can be fully understood; what it denies is access to what having it is like.

options.text: That the question of what it is like to be a bat is meaningless, since experience cannot be measured by any available method.
options.why: Nagel's point is the reverse: the question is meaningful and may be unanswerable from the outside, which is what makes it a problem.

options.text: That bats and humans differ in kind rather than in degree, which is why Darwin's continuity claim should be treated as unproven.
options.why: The discontinuity position is the second of the section's two assumptions under challenge, and it is not what Nagel argued.

items.stem: §2.2.6 pairs anthropomorphism with its opposite. What is the opposite, and what do the two have in common?

options.text: Anthropodenial, refusing an animal a capacity it plainly has because granting it feels unscientific; both come from deciding in advance what the answer should be.
options.why: Correct. The section treats them as symmetric errors with one cause rather than as a real danger and a curiosity.

options.text: Anthropocentrism, measuring every other mind by how near it comes to a human one; both of them come from using ourselves as the reference case throughout.
options.why: Anthropocentrism is a distinct error from §2.1.8, and the opposite number of anthropomorphism is under-attribution rather than ranking.

options.text: Surface matching, reading a behavioral resemblance as evidence about machinery; both come from checking too few dimensions of a similarity.
options.why: Surface matching is the theme under all the named errors rather than the specific opposite of over-attributing a capacity.

options.text: Adultomorphism, reading adult concepts into infant minds; both come from projecting the observer's own way of thinking onto a subject.
options.why: Adultomorphism appears in §2.5.2 as anthropomorphism in different clothes, and it is not the opposite error this section pairs.

items.stem: Clever Hans could reliably tap out the answer to a question like "what is three plus five." What did Pfungst establish about how?

options.text: Hans was reading tiny unintentional changes in the posture and breathing of whoever in the room knew the answer.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is careful to call that a real and impressive ability, and equally careful to say it is not arithmetic.

options.text: Hans had memorized the responses to the questions he was most often asked, which covered nearly every question put to him.
options.why: Memorization would fail on a novel question, and Hans succeeded on questions his owner had not rehearsed with him.

options.text: Hans's owner was signalling the answers deliberately, which is why the effect disappeared once observers were watching closely.
options.why: The chapter and the lecture both note the owner was not cheating; the cues were unintentional and he believed in the horse.

options.text: Hans was responding to the rhythm of the question rather than its content, which correlated with the size of the correct answer.
options.why: Nothing about rhythm is involved. The cue was postural and it came from whoever knew the answer, not from the question's form.

items.stem: §2.2.6 names three habits that keep the field honest. Which pairs the working rule with Griffin's reminder correctly?

options.text: Eliminate plain associative learning before reaching for anything richer; and refusing to study animal awareness at all is not caution but avoidance.
options.why: Correct. The first follows from Morgan's Canon, and the second founded cognitive ethology as a branch of ethology.

options.text: Eliminate any explanation that cannot be tested in natural conditions; and refusing to study animal awareness is a reasonable caution.
options.why: Griffin's reminder runs the other way, and the working rule concerns associative learning rather than the setting of a study.

options.text: Prefer the richer explanation whenever an animal's behavior is flexible; and study animal awareness only once simpler accounts have failed.
options.why: Preferring the richer explanation inverts Morgan's Canon, which the section offers as the guard against over-attribution.

options.text: Eliminate plain associative learning before reaching for anything richer; and study animal awareness only under properly natural conditions in the field.
options.why: The first half is right and the second is not Griffin's point, which was about whether to study awareness rather than where.

items.stem: §2.2.6 turns Morgan's Canon around at the end. What is the turn?

options.text: It is a rule about explanation rather than about animals, so it applies to human self-explanation with equal force.
options.why: Correct. The stockings shoppers are the case: we are frequently the Clever Hans in our own experiments and introspections.

options.text: It is a rule about animals rather than about explanation, so applying it to humans would be a category mistake.
options.why: The section says explicitly that it is not really a rule about animals, and the whole closing move depends on that.

options.text: It is a rule about laboratory work rather than about field work, so an ethologist observing in natural conditions is not bound by it.
options.why: Nothing about the canon is restricted to a setting, and the section applies it to introspection, which is neither.

options.text: It is a rule about simplicity rather than about mental processes, so it applies to any theory in any science whatsoever.
options.why: Generalizing that far loses what the turn actually claims, which is that our own accounts of our own behavior are over-rich.

items.stem: §2.2.7 states a plain counter-fact against treating every trait as an adaptation. What is it?

options.text: Many traits are not adaptations at all: they can be byproducts, constraints of development, or leftovers that never cost enough to remove.
options.why: Correct. That is why an adaptive story cannot be the default explanation for whatever a researcher happens to find.

options.text: Many traits are adaptations to environments that no longer exist at all, so their present function cannot be read off their current usefulness to the organism.
options.why: Mismatch to a past environment is a real phenomenon and is a claim about which adaptation a trait is rather than about whether it is one.

options.text: Many traits vary so much within a species that no single adaptive explanation could apply to all of the individuals carrying them.
options.why: Within-species variation is what selection acts on and it is not the counter-fact the section offers here.

options.text: Many traits appear in more than one lineage, so an adaptive story for one species cannot be transferred to any of the others.
options.why: Convergence across lineages is offered in §2.2.4 as evidence for a real problem rather than as a problem for adaptive explanation.

items.stem: Gould and Lewontin's 1979 image is the decorated space where a cathedral dome's arches meet. What is the point of the image?

options.text: Those spaces are a byproduct of putting a dome on arches, so someone studying only the paintings would badly misread what the spaces are for.
options.why: Correct. The structure came first for structural reasons, and the decoration found a use for it afterwards.

options.text: Those spaces were designed in order to be decorated, so someone studying only the structure of the arches would badly misread why the builders ever included them.
options.why: Reversed. The argument depends on the spaces being unavoidable given the dome, and on the decoration arriving later.

options.text: Those spaces vary between cathedrals, so a single explanation of why they are there could not cover every building that has them.
options.why: Variation between buildings is not the point. The argument is about mistaking a byproduct for something built on purpose.

options.text: Those spaces are decorated because decoration is what cathedrals are for, so their purpose can be read directly from their use.
options.why: That is exactly the inference the image is designed to block, and the chapter calls it a badly misread purpose.

items.stem: Kipling's tales explain how the leopard got his spots and the camel his hump, and each fits its animal perfectly. Why does §2.2.7 say the perfect fit is the problem?

options.text: Each story was written to fit, so fitting the animal is no evidence at all that the story is the right one.
options.why: Correct. The same shape of objection is what §2.1.8's symmetry test formalizes for an adaptive explanation of any real trait.

options.text: Each story is fictional, so no conclusions about real adaptation can be drawn from any of them however well they fit.
options.why: The fictional status is what makes the case vivid; the objection generalizes to serious adaptive stories about real traits.

options.text: Each story explains only one trait, so a full account would need many more stories than Kipling ever actually wrote.
options.why: Coverage is not the complaint. A story that fitted every trait would be exactly as unconstrained as one that fits a single trait.

options.text: Each story attributes the trait to something the animal did, when a trait's history is a matter of which ancestors reproduced.
options.why: Kipling's mechanism is beside the point; the objection is that a story built backwards from the answer cannot support it.

items.stem: §2.2.7 goes out of its way to distinguish Tinbergen's four questions from §2.1.3's three sources of similarity. What is the distinction?

options.text: Tinbergen's four are ways of explaining a single trait; the three sources are ways of diagnosing a resemblance between two systems.
options.why: Correct. What they share is the warning that different kinds of question have different answers, and collapsing them is how a story feels like evidence.

options.text: Tinbergen's four apply to behavior and the three sources apply to anatomy, so the two sets cover different kinds of trait.
options.why: Both sets are used on behavior throughout the chapter, and the difference is what each is a question about rather than what it is asked of.

options.text: Tinbergen's four are answered by observation and the three sources are answered by the phylogenetic tree, so they need different evidence.
options.why: The tree answers the origin question and that is one of the three; the sets differ in their subject rather than in their evidence.

options.text: Tinbergen's four are a modern refinement of the three sources, which is why he proposed them more than a century after Darwin.
options.why: The two sets are not versions of one another. Tinbergen's four are about a trait and the three sources are about a resemblance.

items.stem: Which set of four questions did Tinbergen propose in 1963 as a full account of any behavior?

options.text: What causes it right now, how it develops over a lifetime, what it is good for, and how it evolved.
options.why: Correct. Keeping them separate is the corrective §2.2.7 offers against collapsing several questions into one adaptive story.

options.text: Where it came from, how deep it goes, how precisely it can be stated, and what it licenses us to conclude from it.
options.why: Those are §2.1's diagnostic questions about a resemblance, and the chapter distinguishes them from Tinbergen's set explicitly.

options.text: What problem it solves, by what procedure, in what physical stuff, and what else in the world solves the same problem.
options.why: The first three are Marr's levels and the fourth is the comparative move, which is a different apparatus altogether.

options.text: Whether it is inherited, whether it is learned, whether it is a byproduct, and whether it has any function at all.
options.why: Those are candidate answers of various kinds rather than the four distinct questions Tinbergen proposed.

items.stem: §2.2.8 announces the structure of everything after Module 2. What is it, and on what argument does it rest?

options.text: Each module takes up a step in the evolution of the human mind and brain, on the argument that we understand what a capacity is for by understanding the problem it solved.
options.why: Correct. And the way to see the problem clearly is to look at who else solved it, which is why the spine is a comparative one.

options.text: Each module takes up one of Marr's three levels of analysis in turn, on the argument that a complete explanation of any capacity needs all three of them together.
options.why: Module 3 gives each level a section, and the course-wide ordering the section announces is evolutionary rather than by level.

options.text: Each module takes up one discipline within brain and cognitive science, on the argument that the field is defined by its methods.
options.why: The disciplines are Module 0's material, and this section commits the course to an evolutionary rather than a disciplinary ordering.

options.text: Each module takes up a different species in turn, on the argument that comparison across species is by some distance the field's oldest form of comparison.
options.why: Comparison across species is the organizing spine, and what each module takes up is a step in an evolutionary history rather than an animal.

items.stem: §2.2.8 raises an objection to the course's own structure. What is the objection, and how is it answered?

options.text: Walking forward from the first cells to human cognition looks like the rejected ladder; the answer is that the human lineage is followed because human cognition is what this book sets out to explain, not because it is best or last.
options.why: Correct. Evolution has no destination, and no lineage is further along than any other, so the ordering is a choice about the subject.

options.text: Walking forward in time understates how much of the brain is shared across species; the answer given is that later modules return to that shared machinery in considerable detail.
options.why: That is not the objection raised, and the section's worry is about the impression of progress rather than about coverage.

options.text: Following one lineage means neglecting convergent cases; the answer is that convergence is covered separately in each module's AI parallel.
options.why: The AI parallel is the second thread announced in §2.3.6, and it is not offered as an answer to the ladder objection.

options.text: Starting before neurons existed makes the early modules speculative; the answer is that the earliest steps are supported by comparative evidence from living species.
options.why: Speculation about early steps is not what the section defends against, and the objection it raises is about direction rather than evidence.

items.stem: §2.2.8 makes its denial of the ladder concrete with a hypothetical. What is it?

options.text: A course built around octopus cognition could follow a different path through the same tree and be no less complete.
options.why: Correct. Every species alive today sits at the end of a lineage exactly as long as ours, and none stopped when our lineage branched away.

options.text: A course built around octopus cognition would be shorter, since the octopus lineage diverged before most of the steps we cover.
options.why: Length is not the point, and an equally long lineage means an equally long path, whichever tip of the tree is chosen.

options.text: A course built around octopus cognition would need a different set of Marr levels, since the octopus nervous system is arranged differently.
options.why: Marr's levels are questions rather than a description of any one nervous system, and they apply unchanged to an octopus.

options.text: A course built around octopus cognition is not possible, since far less is known about octopus cognition than about our own.
options.why: The hypothetical is about what the tree permits rather than about the state of the literature, and the section treats it as available.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 says the ladder is not a modern scientific idea that turned out wrong. What does it say the ladder is?

options.text: An inherited picture — the medieval great chain of being with the theology removed and the ordering kept.
options.why: Correct. Hodos and Campbell argued in 1969 that keeping the ordering left comparative psychology without a real theory for a long time.

options.text: A misreading of the phylogenetic tree, which appears to run upward when it is drawn with humans at the top of the page.
options.why: Drawing conventions can encourage the error and the lecture traces the ladder to a much older picture of nature.

options.text: A consequence of studying species in the order they were discovered, which happened to run from simpler organisms to complex ones.
options.why: No such history is given, and the lecture's account is about an inherited hierarchy rather than about the order of discovery.

options.text: A shorthand adopted by comparative psychologists for communicating results, which was never intended to be taken literally at all.
options.why: The lecture treats it as a picture people genuinely hold, which is why it says the habit is hard to shake once named.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 says the tick is "a finished, superbly adapted solution to the problem of being a tick." What does it give as the evidence?

options.text: Within an Umwelt of butyric acid, warmth and touch, a tick can wait years on a branch for those three signals in the right order.
options.why: Correct. The lecture's point is that the tick is superb within its own world rather than an early draft of something else.

options.text: Ticks are found on every continent and on a very wide range of different host species, which shows how broadly the design actually works.
options.why: Distribution is not what the lecture cites, and the argument is about fit to a specific sensory world rather than about range.

options.text: Ticks have changed very little over evolutionary time, which shows that the design was well fitted from very early on.
options.why: Morphological conservatism is not mentioned, and the lecture is explicit that every lineage has been evolving for the same span.

options.text: Ticks can detect a mammal at a distance greater than most arthropods manage, which shows their sensory system is unusually good.
options.why: No such comparison is drawn. The Umwelt standard judges a capacity against the animal's own world rather than against other species.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 gives an example of anthropodenial. Which is it?

options.text: Watching a chimpanzee reconcile after a fight and insisting that we must not call it reconciliation.
options.why: Correct. Refusing a capacity the animal plainly has, because granting it feels unrigorous, is the mirror image of Clever Hans.

options.text: Watching a horse tap out the answer to an arithmetic question and concluding that the horse understands arithmetic.
options.why: That is anthropomorphism, and Clever Hans is the classic case of it rather than of the opposite error.

options.text: Watching a dog lower its head on your return and concluding from the posture that the dog is feeling guilty about something.
options.why: That is the chapter's own example of anthropomorphism, the over-attribution error rather than the under-attribution one.

options.text: Watching a scrub jay recover perishable caches first and concluding that the jay remembers a specific past event.
options.why: The chapter treats that inference as well supported by Clayton's work rather than as an instance of either error.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 asks whether the curved triangular spaces in a cathedral were built in order to be decorated. What answer does it give, and what is the moral?

options.text: No — they are what is left over when a dome is put on arches, and someone studying only the paintings would conclude backwards.
options.why: Correct. Biology is full of the same shape: byproducts, developmental constraints, and leftovers that never cost enough to remove.

options.text: No — they were structurally necessary and were later filled in, so the paintings are what a builder would study to date the building.
options.why: Dating is not the moral, and the lecture's point is about mistaking a byproduct for something that was built on purpose.

options.text: Yes — later builders found them excellent for paintings, so the decoration became the reason later cathedrals included them at all.
options.why: The lecture grants that builders found a use for them and denies that the use explains why the spaces are there.

options.text: Yes — the spaces are decorated in every great cathedral, and a feature that consistent is unlikely to be an accident of construction.
options.why: Consistency follows from every dome-on-arches producing them, which is exactly why it is no evidence about purpose.

items.stem: The lab asks which of two populations evolved in different worlds is better adapted, and which is better. Why are these different questions?

options.text: Better adapted needs a world named before it means anything, and each population is fitted to its own; better has no answer, because there is no world-independent scale.
options.why: Correct. It is the ladder of intelligence in miniature, with a world standing in for a species' circumstances.

options.text: Better adapted is measured by the energy gathered and better by how long individuals survive, so the two questions are asked using quite different measurements.
options.why: Both would still be measured within some world, and the lab's point is that the second question lacks a scale rather than a measure.

options.text: Better adapted refers to the population now and better refers to what it would become given more generations of selection.
options.why: Selection is not aimed anywhere, so no amount of further running produces a population that is better in a world-independent sense.

options.text: Better adapted applies to a whole population and better applies to individuals within it, so the two are asked at different levels.
options.why: The level is the same in both. What differs is that one question specifies a world and the other quietly assumes a universal one.

items.stem: In the lab you wrote the best adaptive story you could for why one inherited trait had become common in your run, and were then told the trait does nothing at all. What test does the lab then ask you to apply to your own story?

options.text: Whether you would have written an equally good story had your run happened to fix a different variant of the same trait instead.
options.why: Correct. It fixed by riding along with the wiring that was actually winning, so the fault lies in the question rather than in the reasoning — Gould and Lewontin's point made on your own answer.

options.text: Whether your reasoning contained a mistake, since a good adaptive story about a trait that does nothing at all has to have gone wrong somewhere inside it.
options.why: The lab is explicit that the reasoning can be perfectly good. What fails is the presupposition built into what was asked.

options.text: Whether your run was long enough for the frequency to have stabilized, since a short run cannot support an explanation of any kind.
options.why: Run length is not the issue, and the trait really did become common; what is unwarranted is the adaptive reading of that fact.

options.text: Whether a second population would have fixed the same variant, since one population cannot show whether a trait was favored at all.
options.why: A control population would help with other questions, and the lab's lesson is about a story built backwards from an outcome.

items.stem: A student says the course's module order shows that evolution was working toward human cognition. In a short paragraph, answer them using §2.2.5 and §2.2.8.
items.answer: The order is a choice about what is being explained, not a claim about direction. Evolution has no destination, and no lineage is further along than any other: every species alive today sits at the end of a lineage exactly as long as ours, and none of them stopped evolving when our lineage branched away. Crows, octopuses and the bacteria in a puddle have all had the same span. The course follows the human lineage because human cognition is what it is trying to explain, and because we understand what a capacity is for by understanding the problem it solved — which means looking at who else solved it and how. A course built around octopus cognition could follow a different path through the same tree and be no less complete. What would make the ordering a ladder is treating the last step as the best one, and that is exactly what the chapter refuses.
rubric: States that evolution has no destination and no lineage is further along than another.
Gives the concrete version: every living species sits at the end of an equally long lineage.
Says why the human lineage is followed — it is what the course is trying to explain.
Uses the octopus-course hypothetical, or an equivalent, to show the path is a choice rather than a ranking.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why §2.2.6 treats anthropomorphism and anthropodenial as the same error rather than as opposite dangers, and say what that implies about how Morgan's Canon should be applied.
items.answer: The two look like opposite sins — crediting an animal with more mind than it has, and refusing it a capacity it plainly has — but the section says they share a cause: in both cases somebody decided in advance what the answer ought to be and then read the evidence to reach it. What differs is only the direction of the prior commitment. That matters for Morgan's Canon because the canon is a guard against one of the two and can be turned into the other if it is applied as a policy rather than as a test. Refusing an animal a capacity it has earned is its own error, so the canon licenses declining to explain a behavior richly when a simpler account covers it — not a standing preference for the thinnest possible description. And because it is a rule about explanation rather than about animals, the same discipline applies to our accounts of ourselves.
rubric: States that anthropomorphism is over-attribution and anthropodenial is under-attribution.
Identifies the shared cause: deciding in advance what the answer should be.
Says that Morgan's Canon can itself produce anthropodenial if applied as a standing preference rather than a test.
Notes that the canon is a rule about explanation, so it applies to human self-explanation as well.

items.stem: Lecture 2.2 says it wants to raise an objection to itself rather than let the room raise it in week nine. What is the objection?

options.text: Having spent a whole slide saying there is no ladder, the lecture then announces a course that walks forward from the first cells to human cognition, in order, ending with us.
options.why: Correct. The answer given is that evolution has no destination and the human lineage is followed because human cognition is what the course explains.

options.text: Having spent a whole slide on the tick's Umwelt, the lecture then judges every species by how much of a nervous system it has.
options.why: Nervous-system size is never used as a standard, and the objection raised is about the course's own ordering.

options.text: Having argued that adaptive stories are cheap, the lecture then offers an adaptive story for every capacity the course covers.
options.why: Just-so stories are the previous slide's material, and the objection this slide raises concerns the shape of the course.

options.text: Having argued that comparison across species is legitimate, the lecture then spends most of the course on a single species.
options.why: The course does centre on human cognition and the objection actually raised is that walking forward in time looks like a ranking.

items.stem: A colleague explains a bird's elaborate song entirely as an adaptation for attracting mates. In a few sentences, name two routes other than adaptation by which a trait can come to exist, and say how Tinbergen's four questions would improve the explanation.
items.answer: §2.2.7 lists three non-adaptive routes and any two will do: a trait can be a byproduct of some other structure, in the way a spandrel is a byproduct of putting a dome on arches; it can be a constraint of development, something that had to come out this way given how the organism is built; or it can be a leftover that never cost enough to be removed. So mate attraction is one candidate among several rather than the default. Tinbergen's four questions improve the explanation by keeping apart four things the single story runs together: what causes the song right now, how it develops over the bird's lifetime, what it is good for, and how it evolved. The colleague's account answers the third and quietly implies the fourth. Separating them makes it visible that the developmental and causal questions have not been addressed at all, and collapsing the four is precisely how a plausible story starts to feel like evidence.
rubric: Names two non-adaptive routes from byproduct, developmental constraint, or leftover.
States that an adaptive explanation is one candidate rather than the default.
Lists Tinbergen's four questions, or at least three of them accurately.
Explains that keeping the four apart is what stops a plausible story from feeling like evidence.
