items.stem: What is behavioral equivalence?

options.text: A match between two systems in what they do, judged from outside: the same inputs produce the same outputs, and an observer watching only those could not tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. The claim says nothing whatever about what is happening inside either system, which is why reading it as evidence about mechanism is surface matching.

options.text: A match between two systems in how they reach those outputs, through the same operations carried out on the same kinds of intermediate representation as each other.
options.why: That is mechanistic equivalence, a much stronger claim and, as the chapter says, a much harder one to establish.

options.text: A match between the behavior of one system in two different conditions, which is what an experiment sets out to produce.
options.why: That is a comparison across conditions from the second family, not a relation between two different systems.

options.text: A use of an artificial system as a simplified stand-in for a natural one, chosen because the artificial one is easier to study.
options.why: That is engineering convenience, which is not a similarity claim at all but a claim about a model's usefulness.

items.stem: Which term names a match between two systems in what they do, judged from outside, with the same inputs producing the same outputs?

options.text: behavioral equivalence
options.why: Correct. It is a match at the computational level only, and the Turing test is its cleanest statement as a criterion.

options.text: mechanistic equivalence
options.why: That names a match in how the outputs are reached, through the same operations on the same kinds of intermediate representation.

options.text: engineering convenience
options.why: That names the use of an artificial system as a tractable stand-in, which is a claim about usefulness rather than similarity.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That names using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether the answers agree with one another.

items.stem: What is mechanistic equivalence?

options.text: A match between two systems in how they arrive at their outputs, through the same operations on the same kinds of intermediate representation.
options.why: Correct. It is a much stronger claim than behavioral equivalence and, the chapter adds, much harder to establish.

options.text: A match between two systems in the physical materials they happen to be built from, so that both of them are realized in the same kind of stuff.
options.why: Shared material is an implementational claim, and mechanistic equivalence is about operations and representations rather than substance.

options.text: A match between two systems in what they do as judged from outside, without any commitment about what goes on inside either one.
options.why: That is behavioral equivalence, which the chapter says is the weaker of the two and is what the Turing test tests for.

options.text: A match between a natural system and a model of it, close enough that the model can stand in for the natural one in research.
options.why: That is engineering convenience, which the chapter is careful to quarantine as a different kind of claim altogether.

items.stem: Which term names a match between two systems in how they arrive at their outputs, through the same operations on the same kinds of intermediate representation?

options.text: mechanistic equivalence
options.why: Correct. Establishing it takes evidence from inside the system, which is why it is so much harder than the behavioral claim.

options.text: behavioral equivalence
options.why: That names a match in what two systems do as judged from outside, with no commitment about the inside of either.

options.text: multiple realizability
options.why: That is Module 1's idea that one functional state can be realized in many different physical arrangements.

options.text: homology
options.why: That names a resemblance two species inherited from a common ancestor, which is a claim about history rather than about depth.

items.stem: What is engineering convenience?

options.text: The use of an artificial system as a simplified stand-in for a natural one, chosen because it is easier to study.
options.why: Correct. It is not a claim about similarity at all but a claim about usefulness, the way a wind tunnel is a model of the sky.

options.text: The use of an artificial system that matches a natural one behaviorally, chosen because building it is cheaper than studying the original.
options.why: Cost is not the criterion, and engineering convenience carries no commitment that the model matches the original in what it does.

options.text: The use of the simplest possible artificial system that can reproduce a behavior, so that the mechanism can be read off directly.
options.why: Reading the mechanism off would be a mechanistic-equivalence claim, and the whole point of the third mode is that it makes none.

options.text: The practice of designing an artificial system so that it can be tested against a natural one under identical conditions.
options.why: Matched testing belongs to establishing behavioral equivalence, and this third mode is a reason for building rather than a comparison.

items.stem: Which term names the use of an artificial system as a simplified stand-in for a natural one, chosen because it is easier to study?

options.text: engineering convenience
options.why: Correct. Treating it as though it were a similarity claim is, the chapter says, a large share of the confused writing about artificial intelligence.

options.text: behavioral equivalence
options.why: That names two systems doing the same things as judged from outside, which is a similarity claim rather than a research decision.

options.text: synthetic method
options.why: That names studying a mind by building a system that does the thing, which is the practice engineering convenience licenses.

options.text: reverse inference
options.why: That names the move from a brain region being active during a task to the task having involved the process that region does.

items.stem: What is the Turing test?

options.text: If a person conversing with a hidden partner cannot reliably tell whether that partner is a person or a machine, the machine passes.
options.why: Correct. Turing set aside the question of whether machines can think, which he thought too vague, and replaced it with something runnable.

options.text: If a machine can produce an output no person could have produced, it has demonstrated a capacity people do not have.
options.why: Exceeding human performance is not the criterion. The test turns on being indistinguishable from a person, not on outperforming one.

options.text: If a machine's internal operations match a person's own closely enough, then the machine can be said to be thinking in the way that the person does.
options.why: That would be a mechanistic-equivalence criterion, and the test's logic is deliberately behavioral rather than mechanistic.

options.text: If a machine can pass on its own knowledge to another machine, it has demonstrated the kind of understanding people have.
options.why: Nothing about transmission appears in Turing's proposal, which concerns a conversation between a person and a hidden partner.

items.stem: What is the Chinese Room Argument?

options.text: A person following a rulebook turns incoming Chinese characters into outgoing ones, so the room answers fluently while understanding nothing — and Searle says the same holds for any program.
options.why: Correct. His claim is that behavior of the right kind is not sufficient to demonstrate understanding, however fluent the output.

options.text: A person translating Chinese by hand is slower than a machine, so any system fluent enough to keep up must be doing more than looking rules up.
options.why: Speed plays no part in the argument, and the conclusion drawn is the opposite of the one this option reaches.

options.text: A machine trained only on Chinese text cannot learn what the words refer to, so a system trained on form alone has no route to meaning.
options.why: That is Bender and Koller's argument, reported in §2.3.3, rather than Searle's thought experiment about a rulebook in a room.

options.text: A person standing outside a room cannot tell whether the answers came from a person or from a machine, so the room passes a version of the Turing test and understands Chinese.
options.why: That describes the setup Searle is objecting to, and the argument is about what passing it fails to establish.

items.stem: §2.3.1 says behavioral and mechanistic equivalence should look familiar. Why?

options.text: They are §2.1.4's depth question given formal names for the case where one of the systems is artificial.
options.why: Correct. Behavioral equivalence is a match at the computational level only; mechanistic equivalence runs down to the algorithm and sometimes further.

options.text: They are §2.1.3's origin question given formal names, since a designed system and an evolved one cannot share an ancestor.
options.why: Homology and analogy are the origin question's formal names. These two say nothing about where a resemblance came from.

options.text: They are §2.1.5's precision question given formal names, since each names a degree of exactness with which a match can be stated.
options.why: Precision is a separate axis, and §2.3.1 goes on to complicate these two using precision rather than identifying them with it.

options.text: They are Marr's three levels renamed, with behavioral equivalence at the top and mechanistic equivalence covering the lower two.
options.why: The pair maps onto the levels and is not a renaming of them, and the third mode is not a level at all.

items.stem: §2.3.1 says the two equivalences are not really distinct categories. What is its point, and what does it draw from it?

options.text: They are one question asked at two grains, so a coarse behavioral match nearly always comes apart at a finer one — and those fine-grained differences are what let us infer what is inside without opening the system up.
options.why: Correct. What looks like a nuisance is the engine of comparison, and §2.3.3 turns it into an operational test.

options.text: They are one question asked at two different grains, so a coarse behavioral match ought to be reported as provisional until some finer measurement has confirmed it, which is rarely done in practice.
options.why: Reporting practice is not what the section draws. Its point is that divergence under finer measurement is itself the source of evidence.

options.text: They are two names for the same claim, so any system that is behaviorally equivalent to a mind is thereby mechanistically equivalent to it.
options.why: That inference is exactly what §2.3.2's zombie argument blocks, and the section keeps the two claims distinct in strength.

options.text: They are two grains of one question, so the finer grain is always the more scientifically useful one to work at.
options.why: The section says how much equivalence is enough depends on what it is for, which makes neither grain always preferable.

items.stem: §2.3.1 closes by saying how much equivalence is enough depends on what it is for. What are the two cases it distinguishes?

options.text: Whether a machine can do a person's job is practical, and behavioral equivalence at that grain may answer it; whether it solves the problem the same way is scientific, and behavioral equivalence cannot.
options.why: Correct. Confusing the two is how a system that is genuinely useful comes to be described as though it were genuinely a mind.

options.text: Whether a machine can do a person's job is the scientific question, and it needs mechanistic equivalence; whether the machine seems humanlike is the practical one, and behavioral equivalence answers that.
options.why: The two are swapped: doing the job is the practical question, and behavioral equivalence at that grain can be a complete answer to it.

options.text: Whether a machine is safe to deploy is practical; whether it is conscious is scientific, and neither kind of equivalence has any bearing on either.
options.why: Safety and consciousness are not the pair the section draws, and it says explicitly what behavioral equivalence can and cannot answer.

options.text: Whether a machine matches a person on average is practical; whether it matches on every individual case is scientific, so the difference is one of coverage.
options.why: Coverage is a precision matter, and the distinction the section makes turns on the purpose the comparison is being put to.

items.stem: §2.3.1 says one confusion accounts for a large share of the confused writing about artificial intelligence. Which?

options.text: Treating engineering convenience as though it were a similarity claim, when it is a claim concerning a model's usefulness and nothing more.
options.why: Correct. The related confusion, between the practical and the scientific question, is how a useful system gets described as a mind.

options.text: Treating behavioral equivalence as though it were weaker than it is, so that genuinely matched performance gets dismissed as superficial.
options.why: The chapter's worry runs the other way: behavioral matches get read as evidence about machinery they cannot support.

options.text: Treating mechanistic equivalence as unattainable, so that no artificial system is ever compared with a natural one at the level of operations.
options.why: The chapter treats mechanistic equivalence as hard rather than unattainable, and §2.4.1 describes researchers pursuing it directly.

options.text: Treating a model's failures as uninformative, so that only the behaviors a model reproduces successfully get reported in the literature.
options.why: That is a real hazard which §2.3.5 addresses, and it is not what the section names here as the source of the confusion.

items.stem: According to §2.3.1, what would establish behavioral equivalence, and what would establish mechanistic equivalence?

options.text: The same outputs for the same inputs including where each fails and how each degrades under pressure; and evidence from inside the system.
options.why: Correct. Failure and degradation belong to the behavioral test, which is why §2.3.3 can sharpen it without opening either system up.

options.text: The same outputs for the same inputs on a representative sample; and the same outputs across every input that could ever be presented.
options.why: Both halves are behavioral, and exhaustive testing would still say nothing about the operations either system runs.

options.text: Agreement between independent judges that the two systems are indistinguishable; and agreement between independent laboratories about the mechanism.
options.why: Judges and laboratories are not the criteria given, and the second confuses replication with evidence about internal operations.

options.text: The same outputs for the same inputs; and the same physical materials arranged in the same way inside each of the two systems.
options.why: Shared material is an implementational claim, and mechanistic equivalence concerns operations and representations rather than substance.

items.stem: §2.3 opens by saying the machine-mind question gets no clear yes or no, and diagnosing why the argument never ends. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: People asking whether a machine really thinks are usually asking three different questions at once without noticing, and most disagreements are about which is being asked.
options.why: Correct. Every subsection of §2.3 is an unpacking of that claim, beginning with the three modes of equivalence.

options.text: People asking whether a machine really thinks disagree about the evidence, and the evidence available is not yet good enough to settle the matter one way or the other.
options.why: The section locates the trouble in the question rather than in the evidence, which is why naming the three modes is the remedy offered.

options.text: People asking whether a machine really thinks are asking a moral question in scientific language, so no amount of evidence could settle it.
options.why: The moral stakes are raised in §2.3.4 and §2.3.6, and the diagnosis here is that three distinct questions are being run together.

options.text: People asking whether a machine really thinks are applying a human standard to a non-human system, which is anthropocentrism.
options.why: Anthropocentrism is a real hazard in this comparison and the specific diagnosis the section gives is about three conflated questions.

items.stem: What does §2.3.2 say about the logic of the Turing test?

options.text: It is deliberately behavioral — what the machine does is all that matters — and whether behavioral equivalence is all that matters is highly controversial.
options.why: Correct. The test is the cleanest statement of behavioral equivalence as a criterion, which is exactly what the Chinese Room attacks.

options.text: It is deliberately mechanistic, since a machine could only sustain a long conversation by running operations rather like the ones a person runs.
options.why: The test makes no claim about operations at all, and its behavioral character is what makes the Chinese Room objection possible.

options.text: It is deliberately statistical, since a single conversation could not distinguish a machine from a person with any reliability.
options.why: Reliability appears in the criterion, and the logic the section names is behavioral rather than a matter of sampling.

options.text: It is deliberately provisional, since Turing expected it to be replaced once the mechanisms of human thinking were understood.
options.why: No such expectation is reported. Turing's move was to replace a question he thought too vague with one that could be run.

items.stem: §2.3.2 recalls Module 1's philosophical zombie. What work does it do in the argument?

options.text: If a perfect behavioral match is even conceivably compatible with the absence of a mind, then behavioral equivalence cannot by itself establish mechanistic equivalence.
options.why: Correct. The section notes that whether such a being is genuinely possible is contested, and that its role in the argument is clear regardless.

options.text: If a perfect behavioral match is possible without a mind being present, then no machine could ever be said to have a mind on the strength of any evidence at all.
options.why: That is far stronger than the section's conclusion, which is about what a behavioral match on its own can establish.

options.text: If a being behaviorally identical to a person is impossible, then behavioral equivalence is sufficient to establish that a mind is present.
options.why: The zombie's conceivability is what does the work; the section does not argue from its impossibility in the other direction.

options.text: If a machine can be built that is behaviorally identical to a person, then the Turing test has been passed and the question is settled.
options.why: That is the position the zombie is raised against, and the section treats the settling as exactly what does not follow.

items.stem: §2.3.2 diagnoses the whole Turing–Searle exchange with a term from §2.1.8. Which, and what does the diagnosis say?

options.text: Surface matching: both sides are arguing about whether a behavioral match tells us about the machinery underneath.
options.why: Correct. The section teaches the two arguments as a visible instance of a general error rather than for their own sake.

options.text: Anthropomorphism: both sides are projecting human qualities onto a system that has not earned the description at all.
options.why: Over-attribution is one thing at stake in the debate, and the error the section names concerns depth rather than attribution.

options.text: Unconstrained adaptationism: both sides can explain any outcome of the test, so neither position is constrained by the evidence.
options.why: That error belongs to adaptive explanation in biology, and neither Turing nor Searle is offering an evolutionary story.

options.text: Anthropocentrism: both sides treat the human case as the standard a machine has to be measured against before it counts.
options.why: The human case is the comparison in question here, and the error the section names is about reading machinery off behavior.

items.stem: Which pairing of proposals and dates does §2.3.2 give?

options.text: Turing proposed the test in 1950; Searle published the Chinese Room objection in 1980.
options.why: Correct. Searle's claim is that behavior of the right kind is not sufficient to demonstrate understanding in any program.

options.text: Turing proposed the test in 1950; Searle published the Chinese Room objection in 1994 as a reply to early neural networks.
options.why: The year is wrong. Searle's paper appeared in 1980, three decades after Turing's proposal.

options.text: Turing proposed the test in 1936; Searle published the Chinese Room objection in 1980 shortly after the cognitive revolution.
options.why: The 1936 work is Turing's on computability. The test itself was proposed in 1950.

options.text: Turing proposed the test in 1950 and Searle replied within the decade, which is why the two are usually discussed together as a pair.
options.why: Thirty years separate them, and the chapter gives both dates so that the gap is visible.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 restates the Module 1 argument for taking the machine-mind question seriously. What is the argument, and what does the lecture say it does and does not do?

options.text: A mind looks like a property of how a system is organized rather than of what it is made of; that removes an objection without establishing anything positive.
options.why: Correct. Which is why the honest answer to whether a machine could have a mind is neither yes nor no.

options.text: A mind looks like a property of what a system is made of rather than of how it is organized; that rules a machine out altogether unless it is built from the very same materials.
options.why: Reversed. Organization rather than substance is what the argument turns on, and it is what keeps the question open.

options.text: A machine that passes the Turing test has a mind; that establishes the positive case and leaves only the question of which machines pass.
options.why: The lecture treats passing as a behavioral criterion whose sufficiency is exactly what is in dispute, not as an established result.

options.text: A mind is whatever a mature science of the brain turns out to describe; that postpones the question rather than answering it either way.
options.why: No such deferral is offered. The lecture gives the organization argument and is explicit about what it removes and what it leaves.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 is emphatic about how much behavioral equivalence says about the inside of a system. What is its answer?

options.text: Nothing — and the slide stresses that the word means nothing rather than not much.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes reading a behavioral match as evidence about machinery an instance of surface matching.

options.text: Very little, though enough to narrow the range of algorithms the system could plausibly be running internally.
options.why: Narrowing the range is what fine-grained behavioral differences do, and the coarse claim itself carries no such content.

options.text: Enough to establish the computational level, which in turn constrains what the algorithmic level could look like.
options.why: Behavioral equivalence is a match at the computational level, and the lecture denies that it constrains the level below.

options.text: As much as any external measurement could, since the inside of a system is only ever reached through its behavior.
options.why: The chapter and lecture both allow evidence from inside a system, which is what would establish mechanistic equivalence.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 warns against leaving the Turing–Searle slide with a particular conclusion. Which, and what does it offer instead?

options.text: That one of the two won the argument; instead it asks what the whole exchange is, and answers that both sides are reading machinery off a behavioral match.
options.why: Correct. The lecture presents the debate as a famous instance of surface matching with very smart people on both sides.

options.text: That the argument is unresolved; instead it holds that Searle's objection is decisive against any purely behavioral criterion for understanding.
options.why: The lecture declines to award the argument to Searle, and it treats his conclusion as an objection rather than a proof.

options.text: That the argument matters; instead it treats both positions as historical curiosities that the modern evidence has left behind.
options.why: The lecture treats the exchange as live and instructive, which is why it spends a slide diagnosing the shape of it.

options.text: That the test is a good one; instead it proposes replacing the Turing test with a behavioral criterion based on failure patterns.
options.why: Failure patterns arrive on the next slide as a way of testing precision, and they are not offered as a replacement criterion for a test.

items.stem: In Part 3 of the evolution lab, populations W, X and Y all reach the light. What does pressing Reveal wiring show, and how is that stated in the reading's vocabulary?

options.text: W and X are contralateral and excitatory while Y is ipsilateral and inhibitory, so Y is behaviorally equivalent to them without being mechanistically equivalent.
options.why: Correct. Watching all three do the same job said nothing about how any of them was built, which is behavior underdetermining mechanism.

options.text: All three turn out to be wired contralateral and excitatory, so Y is mechanistically equivalent to W and X as well as behaviorally equivalent.
options.why: Y departs from the other two on both pattern and sign, which is precisely what the reveal is built to show.

options.text: Y is wired ipsilateral and inhibitory, so it is neither behaviorally nor mechanistically equivalent to W and X after all.
options.why: All three reach the light, which is a behavioral match; the reveal shows only that the match does not reach down to the wiring.

options.text: W and X differ from each other in sign while Y matches W, so it is X that is behaviorally equivalent without being mechanistically equivalent.
options.why: W and X are sister lineages and are wired alike; Y is the one that departs from both of them.

items.stem: A company reports that its model "matches human performance on medical triage." In a short paragraph, say which mode of equivalence that report is about, what it licenses, and what it would take to say the model triages the way a clinician does.
items.answer: The report is a behavioral-equivalence claim, and a coarse one: the same outputs for the same inputs, judged from outside, on a particular task. That licenses an answer to the practical question — whether the machine can do the job at that grain — and it licenses nothing at all about how the outputs are reached. The scientific question, whether the model solves the problem the way a clinician does, is a mechanistic-equivalence claim and behavioral equivalence cannot answer it however good the match is. Establishing it would take evidence from inside the system: the same operations over the same kinds of intermediate representation. Short of that, the behavioral route is to look harder — whether the two fail on the same cases in the same direction, whether both degrade the same way under time pressure or noisy notes — since a coarse match will nearly always come apart at a finer grain. Confusing the practical answer for the scientific one is how a genuinely useful system comes to be described as though it were genuinely a mind.
rubric: Identifies the claim as behavioral equivalence, and notes that it is judged from outside.
Says what it licenses: the practical question of whether the machine can do the job at that grain, and nothing about how.
States that mechanistic equivalence would require evidence from inside the system — the same operations over the same kinds of representation.
Notes that finer behavioral measurement, such as shared failures or degradation, is the available route short of that.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why §2.3.2 presents the Turing test and the Chinese Room as an instance of surface matching rather than as two free-standing philosophical positions.
items.answer: Surface matching is the assumption that what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside. Turing's proposal takes a behavioral match to be all that matters, so it treats the outside as settling the question. Searle's objection takes a behavioral match to be compatible with understanding nothing, so it treats the outside as settling the question in the other direction. Both are arguing about what a behavioral match tells us about the machinery underneath, which means the whole exchange runs on the relationship §2.1.8 already named. Presenting them that way is what makes the pair useful to the chapter: it is a visible, well-argued example of a general error, with very capable people on both sides, rather than a curiosity from the philosophy of mind.
rubric: Defines surface matching as reading inner workings off outward behavior.
Says how the Turing test instantiates it — a behavioral match taken as sufficient.
Says how the Chinese Room instantiates it — the same behavioral match argued to settle the question negatively.
Explains what the chapter gains by the framing: a named general error illustrated by a famous case rather than a stand-alone debate.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 explains why engineering convenience "gets its own row" on the three-modes figure. What is the reason?

options.text: It is different in kind from the other two: it makes no claim about similarity at all, only about a model's usefulness, which is why it causes so much trouble.
options.why: Correct. The wind tunnel is a workable model of the sky without anybody claiming the sky is a wind tunnel.

options.text: It is the weakest of the three claims, so it is set apart to show that a researcher should reach for it only when the other two fail.
options.why: The lecture is explicit that it is not a weaker version of the other two but a different kind of claim altogether.

options.text: It is the strongest of the three claims, since a model useful enough to stand in for a brain must resemble the brain closely.
options.why: Usefulness carries no commitment about resemblance, which is precisely the confusion the separate row is drawn to prevent.

options.text: It applies only to artificial systems, whereas behavioral and mechanistic equivalence can hold between any two systems at all.
options.why: All three modes concern a machine set beside a mind, and what separates the third is the kind of claim rather than its scope.

items.stem: In the evolution lab you spent an hour calling a few dozen moving dots evolution. In a short paragraph, say which of the three modes of equivalence best describes the simulation and why, then say what running it let you learn that reading about evolution could not, and one thing it would be wrong to conclude from it.
items.answer: Engineering convenience is the best fit. Nobody is claiming the dots are alive or that this is what evolution is; the simulation was chosen because it is simple enough to take apart, which is a claim about usefulness rather than about similarity. What running it gave me was the knockouts. Setting mutation to zero, switching inheritance off and switching selection off, one at a time from the identical founding population, showed which of the three requirements each outcome depended on — and no real population can be edited that way, so reading about variation, inheritance and differential reproduction could not have delivered it. What it would be wrong to conclude is anything about real biology's numbers or machinery: how fast evolution runs, what a genome looks like, or that a real heritable trait is as simple as a handful of connection strengths. A case can also be made for behavioral equivalence at a coarse grain, since the population really does change in the way selection makes populations change; what cannot be defended is mechanistic equivalence.
rubric: Names engineering convenience, and says why: the claim being made is about usefulness rather than similarity.
Says what the simulation licensed — removing an ingredient and watching what stops, which a real population does not permit.
Names something the simulation does not license, such as real timescales, real genetics, or the complexity of real traits.
Rules out mechanistic equivalence, or acknowledges that a coarse behavioral-equivalence reading is arguable while mechanistic equivalence is not.

items.stem: Returning to the person and the image model who agree on 95% of photographs, §2.3.3 says what would settle the interpretation. What is it?

options.text: What happens when both of the systems are pushed hard enough that they start making mistakes.
options.why: Correct. Not more agreement, not better accuracy, and not more images — the failures are where the informative evidence sits.

options.text: Whether the level of agreement holds up when a much larger and more varied set of photographs is used.
options.why: More images is exactly what the section rules out. A larger sample at the same grain reproduces the same ambiguity at greater cost.

options.text: Whether the model's accuracy can be raised above the person's, which would show it is not simply copying human answers.
options.why: Better accuracy is one of the things the section says does not settle it, and outperforming a person is not evidence about mechanism.

options.text: Whether an independent laboratory can reproduce the agreement figure using its own model and its own set of judges.
options.why: Replication confirms the number and leaves every competing explanation of the number exactly where it was.

items.stem: §2.3.3 states the principle behind the failure test in one line. Which is it?

options.text: Agreement on the easy cases is cheap; agreement on the failures is more informative.
options.why: Correct. Both systems are usually right, so agreeing when the item is easy costs nothing at all and carries no evidence with it.

options.text: Agreement on the easy cases is informative; agreement on the failures is contaminated by noise in the measurement.
options.why: Reversed. Noise is what makes the easy agreement uninformative, and the failures are where a real similarity would show.

options.text: Agreement on the hard cases is cheap; agreement across the whole distribution is what a comparison should be reporting.
options.why: The hard cases are precisely the expensive ones, and reporting the whole distribution restates the ambiguity rather than resolving it.

options.text: Agreement on any case is cheap; only a shared mechanism established from inside the system counts as evidence of similarity.
options.why: The section's whole point is that a behavioral test can be sharpened until it is informative without opening either system up.

items.stem: Which set of questions does §2.3.3 give as the operational form of the failure test?

options.text: Do they fail on the same items, in the same proportions and the same direction; does noise degrade them along the same curve; does each generalize to a new category the same way?
options.why: Correct. Every one of these is a behavioral measurement, which is what makes the test runnable without evidence from inside either system.

options.text: Do they reach the same accuracy on the same benchmark; do they improve at the same rate as more training data is added; do the two of them use similar amounts of computation?
options.why: Accuracy, learning rate and cost are all coarse performance figures, and none of them concerns the pattern of failures at all.

options.text: Do they use the same internal representations; do those representations change in the same way with experience; are they built from similar components?
options.why: Those would establish mechanistic equivalence directly, and the test exists precisely because that evidence is usually unavailable.

options.text: Do they agree on more items than chance would produce; do they agree on the hardest items; do independent judges rate their outputs alike?
options.why: Agreement counts of every kind are what the section has just ruled insufficient, however the items are selected.

items.stem: Applying the failure test to current language models, what verdict does §2.3.3 report?

options.text: Behaviorally close to people on many tasks, mechanistically uncertain, and diverging under pressure in ways no person would.
options.why: Correct. They fail at problems a child handles, succeed at problems most adults cannot, and can be pushed into confident nonsense by a rephrasing.

options.text: Behaviorally close to people on many tasks and mechanistically close as well, since the divergences are small enough to be treated as noise.
options.why: The divergences are not small: the section describes them as the kind no person would produce, and it calls the mechanism uncertain.

options.text: Behaviorally distant from people on most tasks, which settles the question of whether such systems understand anything at all.
options.why: The section reports close behavioral performance on many tasks, and it explicitly declines to settle the understanding question.

options.text: Behaviorally close and mechanistically equivalent on tasks involving language, though not on tasks involving perception or action.
options.why: No such split by domain is drawn, and mechanistic equivalence is reported as uncertain rather than established anywhere.

items.stem: §2.3.3 examines the dismissal that a language model is "just predicting the next word." What does it say the dismissal assumes?

options.text: That we know what real thinking is at the mechanistic level and that prediction is not it — while an influential family of theories holds the brain is itself largely a prediction engine.
options.why: Correct. The section's claim is that the dismissal is unearned, which is a different claim from saying that such systems do think.

options.text: That prediction is a simple operation, whereas the evidence shows that next-word prediction requires internal representations every bit as rich as any a person could be said to use.
options.why: The section makes no claim about the richness of what the models represent, and its objection concerns what the dismissal takes for granted.

options.text: That language models are trained on text alone, whereas people learn from a much wider range of experience than text can supply.
options.why: That is Bender and Koller's argument, reported alongside as one side of the disagreement rather than as the dismissal's assumption.

options.text: That behavior is evidence about mechanism, which is surface matching and would be an error whichever way the verdict came out.
options.why: Surface matching is diagnosed in §2.3.2; here the objection is that the dismissal presupposes knowledge of human mechanism that we lack.

items.stem: §2.3.3 calls the unearned dismissal "the machine version of the Clever Hans mistake made about ourselves." What is the parallel?

options.text: We credit ourselves with a rich process we cannot describe, and deny the machine one we can describe.
options.why: Correct. A fairer position holds humans and machines to the same standard, which is what the section asks for.

options.text: We credit the machine with a rich process it does not have, and deny ourselves one that we demonstrably do have.
options.why: That reverses the direction. The dismissal under discussion is generous to us and stingy toward the machine.

options.text: We attribute a machine's success to a trick, exactly as Pfungst attributed Clever Hans's success to reading body language.
options.why: Pfungst was right about Hans, and the parallel here concerns our account of ourselves rather than our account of the machine.

options.text: We respond to cues we have not noticed and then supply a dignified account, exactly as the horse did in front of the commission.
options.why: The horse was reading cues; the humans were supplying the dignified account. The parallel here is with the humans in that room.

items.stem: Which two positions does §2.3.3 cite in the disagreement about whether language models understand anything?

options.text: Mitchell and Krakauer have surveyed the disagreement; Bender and Koller have argued that a system trained on form alone has no route to meaning.
options.why: Correct. The chapter reports both without settling between them, which is why no item may key a verdict either way.

options.text: Mitchell and Krakauer have argued that such systems understand; Bender and Koller have argued that they do not, and the chapter sides with the second.
options.why: The chapter takes no side, and Mitchell and Krakauer are cited for surveying the disagreement rather than for a position within it.

options.text: Bechtel and Mundale have argued that the systems are multiply realized; Clayton and Emery have argued that behavioral evidence suffices.
options.why: Bechtel and Mundale appear in §2.2.4 on multiple realizability, and Clayton and Emery on corvid cognition.

options.text: Turing argued that behavior settles the question; Searle argued that it does not, and the modern disagreement is a continuation of theirs.
options.why: That pair is §2.3.2's material, and §2.3.3 names two contemporary contributions rather than restating the classic exchange.

items.stem: §2.3.4 gives the uncomfortable half of what to do with a strong intuition about machines. What does it say?

options.text: Reasoning backward from the answer we want is not reasoning, and if no possible observation would change our minds, then whatever we are doing is not science.
options.why: Correct. The section pairs this with a motive: granting that a machine understands may be inconvenient or frightening in ways unrelated to evidence.

options.text: Strong intuitions about machines are always the product of unfamiliarity, and they weaken as a person works with the systems in question.
options.why: No such empirical claim is made, and the section is careful to let a firmly held belief off the hook in its second half.

options.text: Strong intuitions have no place in science at all, and any researcher who finds they have one should recuse themselves from the question entirely and leave it to somebody else.
options.why: The section explicitly declines that conclusion, arguing that a firm prior is not by itself irrational.

options.text: Reasoning from a strong intuition is legitimate only when the intuition is shared widely, since agreement is what makes a starting point defensible.
options.why: Popularity is not the criterion offered. What separates the reasonable version is whether one can say what would change it.

items.stem: §2.3.4 also lets the intuition partly off the hook. On what two grounds?

options.text: Holding a belief firmly enough that it takes a great deal to move is not irrational, since a surprising claim should need stronger evidence; and when an argument reaches somewhere we know cannot be right, we may suspect the argument.
options.why: Correct. Both moves are respectable, which is why the section refuses to treat a strong prior as simple stubbornness.

options.text: Intuitions about minds are formed by a lifetime's experience of other minds, and experience of that kind is a legitimate form of evidence in its own right, so a conviction built on it deserves the same weight as a measurement would.
options.why: No appeal to experience is made. The two grounds concern the rationality of a firm prior and the entitlement to doubt an argument.

options.text: Intuitions cannot be argued away, so the practical course is to set them aside and judge the evidence as though one did not hold them.
options.why: Setting the intuition aside is not what the section recommends; it supplies a criterion for telling a good one from a bad one.

options.text: Intuitions about machines are usually correct, since our long practice at recognizing minds gives us a reliable detector for them.
options.why: No such reliability is claimed, and the section's whole concern is that this particular intuition may be motivated rather than reliable.

items.stem: What does §2.3.4 offer as the criterion separating a reasonable strong intuition from an unreasonable one?

options.text: Whether we can say, in advance, what observation would change our minds about it.
options.why: Correct. If we can answer, the intuition is doing scientific work; if there is no answer at all, this is not for us a scientific question.

options.text: Whether the intuition is held by most of the people qualified to judge the question at issue.
options.why: Consensus is not the criterion. A widely held conviction can be exactly as unfalsifiable as a lonely one.

options.text: Whether the intuition can be traced to a specific piece of evidence that the person encountered earlier.
options.why: Provenance is not what the section asks about; the test is prospective rather than a matter of where the belief came from.

options.text: Whether the intuition is held about machines specifically rather than about minds in general.
options.why: The scope of the intuition is not the issue, and the criterion the section gives applies to any strongly held conviction.

items.stem: §2.3.4 notes a motive that has nothing to do with evidence, and a fact about when the feeling arrives. What are they?

options.text: Granting that a machine understands may be inconvenient or frightening; and the feeling arrives before any argument does, which is what makes the Chinese Room feel compelling.
options.why: Correct. The argument gives a shape to something already believed rather than producing the belief in the first place.

options.text: Granting that a machine understands would require rewriting a great deal of the philosophy of mind; and the feeling arrives only once the Chinese Room argument has actually been encountered.
options.why: The section says the feeling comes first, which is why it can lend the argument its force rather than the other way round.

options.text: Denying that a machine understands protects a research programme; and the feeling arrives as a conclusion from the evidence about failures.
options.why: Neither is what the section reports. The motive it names is about what would follow morally, and the feeling is pre-argumentative.

options.text: Granting that a machine understands may be inconvenient; and the feeling is what the Chinese Room argument was designed to produce in a reader.
options.why: The section has the influence running the other way: the argument feels compelling because the feeling was there beforehand.

items.stem: §2.3.5 rehabilitates engineering convenience as a research method. What is its reframing?

options.text: An artificial system need not be a candidate mind to be scientifically useful; it can be a hypothesis, and building one is a way of finding out what a capacity requires.
options.why: Correct. The section is short and dense — three claims in 135 words, all of them core — and it hands the method to §2.4.

options.text: An artificial system that is not a candidate mind can still be useful for teaching, while producing few scientific findings of its own.
options.why: The section claims real findings, not illustration: what a model has to be given is a claim about the natural system.

options.text: An artificial system becomes scientifically useful after it has been shown to be behaviorally equivalent to the natural one it stands in for.
options.why: Behavioral equivalence is not required. Engineering convenience is explicitly not a similarity claim of any kind.

options.text: An artificial system is a hypothesis about the machinery, so building one that works establishes that the natural system operates in much the same way as it does.
options.why: Building one that works shows what the capacity requires rather than showing that the natural system meets the requirement that way.

items.stem: §2.3.5 says the failures of an artificial system are as informative as its successes. Why?

options.text: If a model has to be given something extra before it can handle a new situation, that requirement is a claim about what the natural system needs as well.
options.why: Correct. §2.4.3 restates the same point from the other side, when behavior and a model disagree.

options.text: If a model fails in the places where people fail, the shared pattern of failure is evidence that the two of them are solving the problem in the same way.
options.why: Shared failure is §2.3.3's test for similarity between two systems, which is a different use of failure from this one.

options.text: If a model fails, the failure shows that the modeller's assumptions about the natural system were mistaken from the start.
options.why: The failure locates a missing ingredient rather than condemning the whole set of assumptions the model was built on.

options.text: If a model fails on a task people find easy, that shows the task is harder than it looks and should be studied in its own right.
options.why: Task difficulty is a side observation; the section's claim is about what the model had to be given in order to succeed.

items.stem: §2.3.6 announces the course's second organizing thread. What is it, and what are two of the pairings named?

options.text: Alongside the evolutionary walk, an artificial system built to solve a version of the same problem — simple nervous systems with the robot vacuum, learning from reward with the chess and Go systems.
options.why: Correct. Pattern recognition with layered networks, planning and search in Module 12, and language models in Module 13 complete the list.

options.text: Alongside the evolutionary walk, a philosophical debate about each capacity in turn — simple nervous systems paired with the Chinese Room, and learning from reward paired with the Turing test.
options.why: The second thread is a series of artificial systems rather than arguments, and the classic debates are confined to §2.3.

options.text: Alongside the evolutionary walk, a comparison across ages for each capacity — simple nervous systems with infancy, learning from reward with adolescence.
options.why: Development is one of the comparisons in §2.5 rather than the second organizing thread of the course as a whole.

options.text: Alongside the evolutionary walk, a method for each capacity — simple nervous systems with behavioral methods, learning from reward with neural ones.
options.why: The three methods are §2.4's material, and the announced parallel pairs each evolutionary step with a designed system.

items.stem: What does §2.3.6 say each natural-and-artificial pairing is for?

options.text: Each is an instance of the three questions: why do the two resemble each other given that one was designed and one evolved, how deep does the resemblance run, and how precisely can it be stated.
options.why: Correct. The answers come out differently every time, and the differences are what is revealing about both systems.

options.text: Each shows that the artificial system solves the problem in the way the natural one does, which is what makes the comparison instructive.
options.why: The answers differ every time, and the section makes no such standing claim about how any pairing turns out.

options.text: Each provides a working model that can substitute for the natural system when the natural one is difficult to study directly.
options.why: That is engineering convenience, one possible reading of a pairing rather than what the pairings are said to be for.

options.text: Each demonstrates a capacity that evolution produced and that engineering has now reproduced, which traces the progress of the field across the decades and up to the present.
options.why: No progress narrative is offered, and several pairings involve systems that solve their version of the problem quite differently.

items.stem: §2.3.6 closes on a moral point it distinguishes explicitly from §2.3.4's. What is the difference?

options.text: §2.3.4's worry is that moral stakes bend our judgment about what a machine is; this one is about what would follow if the judgment came out a particular way.
options.why: Correct. If a machine were mechanistically equivalent to a mind in whatever respects we claim should matter, questions would follow about what we owe it.

options.text: §2.3.4's worry is about what we might owe a machine; this one is that the moral stakes involved bend our judgment about what a machine actually is.
options.why: The two are swapped. The earlier worry is about distorted judgment and this one is about the consequences of a verdict.

options.text: §2.3.4's worry concerns researchers and this one concerns the public, so the two describe the same distortion in two different audiences.
options.why: Both worries apply to anyone arguing, and what separates them is their direction rather than who holds them.

options.text: §2.3.4's worry is about animals and this one is about machines, so the two are the same point applied to two different comparisons.
options.why: Both §2.3.4 and §2.3.6 concern machines; §2.1.9 and §2.2.8 are where the same shape is worked for animals.

items.stem: What does §2.3.6 say about how close current systems are to the bar at which what we owe a machine becomes a serious question?

options.text: Most researchers think current systems are nowhere near it, and the question of what would have to be true first is not a foolish one to ask now.
options.why: Correct. The section gives a reason for asking early rather than late, without claiming the bar is close to being met.

options.text: Most researchers think current systems have already crossed it, which is why the question is being asked now rather than later.
options.why: The section says the opposite about where current systems stand, while still defending the value of asking the question.

options.text: Most researchers regard the question as unanswerable in principle, so it is generally left to philosophers rather than pursued within the field itself.
options.why: The section treats the question as a serious one worth asking now, and does not hand it off to another discipline.

options.text: Most researchers think the bar cannot be specified in advance, so asking what would have to be true first is premature.
options.why: Asking what would have to be true first is exactly what the section defends, and it calls doing so far from foolish.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 explains why agreement on failures carries evidence that agreement on easy cases does not. What is the explanation?

options.text: Both systems are usually right, so agreeing when the item is easy costs nothing, whereas there are a thousand ways to be wrong and landing on the same one is not free.
options.why: Correct. Two systems producing the same wrong answer, at the same rate, in the same circumstances, is not something independence supplies.

options.text: Failures are a good deal rarer than successes, so a match on them is statistically much less likely to have occurred by chance alone than a match on the successes would be.
options.why: Rarity alone would not do it; what matters is the number of available wrong answers rather than how often failure occurs.

options.text: Failures are more carefully measured than successes, since researchers examine the items a system gets wrong far more closely.
options.why: No claim about measurement practice is made. The argument turns on how many different ways there are to be wrong.

options.text: Failures reveal the training data a system was given, which is what determines whether it inherited its answers from people.
options.why: Inherited labels are one candidate explanation of surplus agreement, and the lecture's argument here is about the space of wrong answers.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 points out that students have met the break-the-same-way rule before. Where, and what does the repetition show?

options.text: In the species comparison, on whether two species that both cache and recover food are really doing the same thing — which shows the course is teaching a method rather than a list of topics.
options.why: Correct. Crows in the species comparison, machines here, and the same rule doing the work in both places.

options.text: In Module 1's Braitenberg lab, on whether two vehicles that are wired differently produce the same behavior — which shows that the method was introduced in a laboratory before the reading ever named it.
options.why: The Braitenberg lab returns later in the lecture as the synthetic method, and the rule was spent on caching in the species comparison.

options.text: In the frog and human vision comparison, on whether the two visual systems fail in the same circumstances — which shows the rule applies at every level.
options.why: The frog comparison illustrates decomposition and comparison together, and the failure rule was introduced with caching in §2.2.4.

options.text: In the stockings study, on whether shoppers and researchers explain the same choice the same way — which shows the rule applies to people too.
options.why: The stockings study makes the surface-matching point about self-explanation rather than illustrating the failure test.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 says the "just predicting the next word" dismissal is one where people get lazy, "including people who agree with me." What is its own position?

options.text: That "prediction is obviously not thinking" is a claim somebody has to argue for, and the people waving it around usually have not.
options.why: Correct. The lecture is explicit that it is not telling the room the prediction theories are settled, only that the dismissal is unearned.

options.text: That prediction is thinking after all, since an influential family of theories holds that the brain is itself largely a prediction engine.
options.why: The lecture states those theories exist and immediately says it is not telling the room that the matter is settled.

options.text: That language models think, since they are behaviorally very close to people on a great many different tasks.
options.why: The lecture gives the mixed verdict deliberately and declines to draw that conclusion from behavioral closeness.

options.text: That the dismissal is correct but poorly argued, so the conclusion survives even though the reasoning offered for it does not.
options.why: The lecture does not endorse the conclusion. Its position is that a fairer standard applies equally to humans and machines.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 asks the room what a machine would have to do before they granted it understood something, and says what follows from each kind of answer. What does it say?

options.text: If they can answer, the intuition is doing scientific work and a high bar is fine; if nothing they can imagine would count, then for them this is not a scientific question.
options.why: Correct. The lecture adds that learning the latter about oneself is worth knowing and is not a criticism.

options.text: If they can answer, the intuition is unfounded and should be abandoned; if they cannot, it is a genuine insight that argument cannot reach.
options.why: Reversed. Being able to name what would change one's mind is what makes the intuition respectable rather than what defeats it.

options.text: If they can answer, the machine can be tested against whatever criterion they named; if they cannot, the question should be referred to philosophers instead of scientists.
options.why: Testing is the point of an answerable criterion, and the lecture's conclusion about the unanswerable case is about the person rather than the discipline.

options.text: If they can answer, they have described the Turing test in their own words; if they cannot, they have discovered why Searle's objection is compelling.
options.why: Neither classic argument is where the exercise lands, and the lecture pushes for specificity about failures rather than about conversation.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 tells the room they have already used the synthetic method, in the Braitenberg lab, and asks them to hold two halves of the experience together. Which two?

options.text: They built it, so they know exactly what is inside and can see every wire; and it still pulled the description afraid out of them.
options.why: Correct. The lecture says that tells us something about vehicles and something about the people watching them.

options.text: They built it, so they know exactly what is inside; and it behaved in ways they had not predicted from the wiring diagram.
options.why: Unpredictability is not what the lecture asks them to hold. The second half is about the description the behavior elicited.

options.text: They did not build it, so the wiring was hidden; and describing it as afraid was therefore a reasonable inference at the time.
options.why: Students did build it in Lab 1, and the wiring was fully visible, which is precisely what makes the pull of the description striking.

options.text: They built it, so they know it has no mental states; and the description afraid was therefore a mistake that better training would prevent.
options.why: The lecture treats the pull as a finding about observers rather than as an error to be trained away.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 closes by naming the toolkit the course has assembled in its first three weeks. What is it?

options.text: Marr's three levels for taking one system apart, and three questions for setting any two things beside each other.
options.why: Correct. The lecture's framing is that everything from Module 3 onward is a matter of using that toolkit rather than adding to it.

options.text: Marr's three levels, the three families of comparison, and the three modes of equivalence between a mind and a machine.
options.why: The families and the modes are contents of the toolkit's second half rather than separate instruments alongside the levels.

options.text: The comparative method, converging operations, and the synthetic method, which are the three ways of studying a mind.
options.why: Two of those are §2.4's methods and one is the chapter's overall method, which is not how the lecture states the closing summary.

options.text: Homology and analogy for comparing species, and behavioral and mechanistic equivalence for comparing minds with machines.
options.why: Those are two domain vocabularies for the same underlying questions, and the lecture names the general apparatus rather than the names.

items.stem: A laboratory wants to know whether its model recognizes speech the way people do. It has already shown that the model and human listeners reach the same accuracy on a standard benchmark. In a short paragraph, say why that is not enough, and describe two further measurements §2.3.3 would recommend.
items.answer: Matched accuracy is agreement on the easy cases, and agreement on the easy cases is cheap: both systems are usually right, so they will mostly say the same thing whether or not anything connects them. What settles the interpretation is what happens when both are pushed to make mistakes, because there are a great many ways to be wrong and landing on the same one is not something independence supplies for free. Two measurements follow directly. First, look at the errors themselves: do the model and the listeners misrecognize the same words, in the same proportions, in the same direction — the same wrong answers rather than merely wrong ones. Second, degrade the input: add noise and ask whether the two fall off along the same curve, or whether one collapses while the other sags. A third, if the laboratory wants it, is generalization: present a new accent or a new speaker and see whether both extend in the same way.
rubric: Explains that matched accuracy is agreement on easy cases and carries little evidence, because both systems are usually right.
States the general test: what happens when both systems are pushed to make mistakes.
Gives one concrete measurement about the pattern of errors — same items, proportions, or direction.
Gives a second concrete measurement — degradation under noise, or generalization to a new category.

items.stem: Two people both say they are certain no machine will ever understand anything. One can describe an experiment that would change their mind; the other says nothing could. In a few sentences, say what §2.3.4 concludes about each, and why the difference matters more than how strongly each belief is held.
items.answer: Strength of conviction does not separate them, and §2.3.4 says so directly: holding a belief firmly enough that it takes a great deal of evidence to shift is not by itself irrational, since a more surprising claim should require stronger evidence. What separates them is whether they can say in advance what would change it. The first person's intuition is doing scientific work — they have set a bar, it may be a high one, and high bars are perfectly acceptable, because their position is now answerable to something outside itself. The second person has learned something about themselves rather than about machines: if no possible observation would move them, then whatever they are doing is not science, and the section says that is worth knowing and is not a criticism. The difference matters because only the first position can be wrong, and a position that cannot be wrong cannot be evidence for anything either.
rubric: States that how strongly the belief is held does not distinguish the two cases.
Notes that a firm prior is not by itself irrational, since a surprising claim should need stronger evidence.
Identifies the criterion as whether one can say in advance what would change the belief.
Concludes that the unfalsifiable version is not science, and that only the falsifiable position can be evidence for anything.

pools.covers: reading §2.4, §2.4.1, §2.4.2, §2.4.3, §2.4.4 · lecture 2.3 slides three_ways, converging_operations, disagreement_as_data, reverse_inference

items.stem: What is the synthetic method?

options.text: Studying a mind by building a system that does the thing and seeing what building it requires — understanding by building.
options.why: Correct. Its failures are as informative as its successes, since whatever a model has to be given is a claim about the natural system too.

options.text: Studying a mind by combining behavioral and neural measurements of the same task into a single unified account of it.
options.why: Combining methods is converging operations, which is the strategy of §2.4.2 rather than the third way of studying a mind.

options.text: Studying a mind by synthesizing the results of many separately published experiments into a single estimate of the true size of an effect.
options.why: That is meta-analysis, a technique for pooling findings rather than one of the three methods this section inventories.

options.text: Studying a mind by building an artificial system and then testing whether people can tell it apart from a person.
options.why: That is the Turing test as a criterion, and the synthetic method is about what building teaches rather than about passing a test.

items.stem: Which term names studying a mind by building a system that does the thing and seeing what building it requires?

options.text: synthetic method
options.why: Correct. Braitenberg's vehicles are the chapter's historical example, and object-recognition networks used as cortical hypotheses the modern one.

options.text: engineering convenience
options.why: That names the use of an artificial system as a tractable stand-in, which is the reason for building rather than the method of studying.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That names using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether the answers they give agree.

options.text: comparative method
options.why: That names setting systems or situations side by side and asking what their similarities and differences reveal.

items.stem: What is converging operations?

options.text: Using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether they agree, since no one technique's flaws could produce that agreement.
options.why: Correct. The load-bearing word is unrelated: it is the independence of the blind spots rather than the number of methods that does the work.

options.text: Using several different methods on the same question and then reporting whichever result the majority of them turns out to support most strongly.
options.why: Nothing is decided by majority. The strategy turns on whether the methods could have agreed by any single technique's error.

options.text: Using one method repeatedly under a range of different conditions until the results converge on a stable and reproducible estimate of the effect.
options.why: Repetition of one method reproduces that method's blind spot every time, which is exactly what the strategy is designed to escape.

options.text: Using several methods in sequence, each chosen to test the specific hypothesis that the previous method left open.
options.why: Sequential refinement is good practice and different: convergence turns on independent weaknesses rather than on order of use.

items.stem: Which term names the strategy of using several methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether they agree?

options.text: converging operations
options.why: Correct. Face recognition is the chapter's worked case: inversion, the fusiform response, and prosopagnosia all pointing one way.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That names the process that produces analogies, two lineages arriving at one solution from different starting points.

options.text: reverse inference
options.why: That names going from a region being active during a task to the task having involved the process that region does.

options.text: synthetic method
options.why: That names studying a mind by building a system that does the thing and seeing what building it requires.

items.stem: What is reverse inference?

options.text: Going from "this brain region was active during the task" to "therefore the task involved the process that region does."
options.why: Correct. It is tempting and often wrong, because brain regions are not dedicated to single processes.

options.text: Going from "this process was involved in the task" to "therefore the region that does it should have been active."
options.why: That is the forward prediction, which is ordinary hypothesis testing rather than the characteristic error of the family.

options.text: Going from a behavioral result to a claim about the algorithm, without checking whether the algorithm could produce the behavior.
options.why: Checking that an algorithm produces the behavior is what models are for in §2.4.1, and this is not the named error.

options.text: Going from a model's success at a task to the claim that the brain solves the task the same way the model does.
options.why: That is a brain-and-model confusion of the kind §2.4.3 discusses, and it is not what the term names.

items.stem: Which term names the move from a brain region having been active during a task to the conclusion that the task involved the process that region does?

options.text: reverse inference
options.why: Correct. How much an activation licenses depends on how selectively that region responds, which varies from region to region.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That names using methods whose weaknesses are unrelated and asking whether the answers they give agree with each other.

options.text: surface matching
options.why: That names assuming what a system does on the outside tells us how it works on the inside, the error under §2.1.8's other three.

options.text: surface matching
options.why: That names assuming what a system does on the outside reveals how it works inside, which is the same shape of error one level up.

items.stem: What changes when the chapter moves from §2.2 and §2.3 to comparison across methods?

options.text: There is one mind on the table and what gets compared is the ways we have of looking at it — whether two independent measurements tell the same story.
options.why: Correct. It is no longer why two things resemble each other, and what to make of disagreement becomes the section's main business.

options.text: There are still two systems on the table, but both are now artificial, so the comparison is between two models rather than a model and a mind.
options.why: Only one system is on the table, and what is being set side by side is a pair of methods rather than a pair of systems.

options.text: There is a single mind on the table and what gets compared is its behavior under two conditions the researcher chose.
options.why: That is comparison across conditions, the second family, which the chapter reaches in §2.5.1 rather than here.

options.text: There are two minds on the table and what gets compared is how each one of them is measured, so the method and the system are varying together throughout.
options.why: Holding the system fixed is what makes the family work; varying both would leave a disagreement impossible to interpret.

items.stem: What are the three ways of studying a mind, on §2.4.1's inventory?

options.text: Watch what it does, look at the brain directly, and build a system that does the thing.
options.why: Correct. The three arrived in stages, from a period when only behavior was respectable, through the cognitive revolution, to a turn toward the brain.

options.text: Watch what it does, ask what it reports about itself, and look at the brain directly.
options.why: Introspective report is not one of the three, and §2.1.8's stockings study is the chapter's warning about relying on it.

options.text: Compare it across species, compare it across ages, and compare it with an artificial system built to do the same job.
options.why: Those are three cases of comparison across systems, which is a family of comparison rather than a set of methods.

options.text: Measure its behavior, model its behavior, and measure how confident it is in each of the answers it produces.
options.why: Confidence reports are one behavioral measure among many, and the third method the section names is building rather than measuring.

items.stem: How does §2.4.1 map the behavioral and neural methods onto Marr's levels?

options.text: Behavioral methods speak mostly to the algorithmic level, constraining the procedure without revealing the hardware; neural methods to the implementational.
options.why: Correct. The mapping is what makes §2.4.3's taxonomy of disagreements a levels story rather than a list of methods failing.

options.text: Behavioral methods speak mostly to the computational level, since they show what problem is being solved by the system; neural methods speak to the algorithmic level instead.
options.why: Behavior constrains the procedure being run, which is the algorithmic level, and the neural methods reach the level below that.

options.text: Behavioral methods speak mostly to the implementational level, since reaction times are a property of the hardware; neural methods to the algorithmic.
options.why: The two are swapped, and reaction times are treated as evidence about the procedure rather than about the physical machinery.

options.text: Behavioral and neural methods both speak to the computational level, since both are ways of finding out what problem a system solves.
options.why: Both bear on the computational level indirectly and the section assigns each of them to a different level below it.

items.stem: What role does §2.4.1 give models that neither of the other two methods can fill?

options.text: They are often the only way to check that a proposed algorithm actually produces the behavior it is supposed to explain.
options.why: Correct. It is very easy to describe an algorithm in words that turns out not to work once it is made to run.

options.text: They are the only way to establish what problem a system is solving, since the other two methods measure rather than explain.
options.why: Computational-level claims come from many sources, and the role the section gives models is a check on a proposed procedure.

options.text: They are the only way to observe a process directly, since behavior and brain measurements are both indirect indicators of it.
options.why: A model's internal workings are the modeller's rather than the mind's, so building one observes nothing about the natural system.

options.text: They are the only way to compare two species without having to test both of them, which is what makes them efficient.
options.why: Efficiency is not the claim, and the section's point concerns whether a described algorithm actually does what it is said to.

items.stem: §2.4.1 makes a quiet observation about how nearly all behavioral measurement works. What is it?

options.text: It works by comparing a person under one set of circumstances to the same person under another.
options.why: Correct. That places almost the whole of the first method inside §2.5.1's family, which is the one the field uses most.

options.text: It works by comparing one person's performance to the average performance of a large group of other people.
options.why: Group norms are one use of behavioral data, and the section's observation is about within-person comparison across circumstances.

options.text: It works by measuring how long a task takes, since reaction time is the only behavioral quantity that can be compared across studies.
options.why: Errors, error types and the effect of context are all named alongside timing as things a behavioral measure records.

options.text: It works by asking people to report what they were doing, which is why behavioral methods depend on introspective access.
options.why: Behavioral methods measure what people do rather than what they say about it, which is what makes them robust to §2.1.8's warning.

items.stem: §2.4.2 says every method has a characteristic blind spot. What does it add about those blind spots?

options.text: They are different from one another, and none is a flaw to be fixed — each is a boundary on what that kind of measurement is able to see.
options.why: Correct. That both halves hold is what makes converging operations work: unrelated boundaries cannot all produce one artifact.

options.text: They are much the same across the different methods, which is why agreement between any two methods is weaker evidence than it first appears to be.
options.why: If the blind spots were the same, agreement would indeed be weak — and the section's claim is that they differ, which is what rescues it.

options.text: They are flaws that better instruments will eventually remove, so the strategy is a stopgap until measurement improves.
options.why: The section is explicit that these are not flaws waiting to be fixed but limits on what each kind of measurement can see at all.

options.text: They are worst in behavioral methods and least severe in neural ones, which is why the field has turned toward the brain.
options.why: No ranking is offered. Each of the three is given its own blind spot, and the section treats none as the weakest.

items.stem: Which set of blind spots does §2.4.2 assign to the three methods?
