options.text: Behavior shows that something changed but not what changed inside; a brain measure shows where or when but not what the activity accomplished; a model shows assumptions suffice but not that a mind uses them.
options.why: Correct. The three are unrelated to one another, which is precisely what makes their agreement hard to explain by any one technique's error.

options.text: Behavior is slow to collect; brain measurement is expensive; and models take a long time to build, so each method is limited by its cost.
options.why: Practical costs are real and are not blind spots. A blind spot is something the method cannot see however much of it is done.

options.text: Behavior varies a great deal between people; brain structure varies a great deal between people; and models are fitted to a single dataset, so all three of the methods are limited in the end by exactly the same kind of variability.
options.why: Variability is a shared limitation rather than three unrelated ones, and shared limitations are exactly what convergence cannot overcome.

options.text: Behavior cannot reach unconscious processes; brain measurement cannot reach conscious ones; and models can reach neither directly.
options.why: No such division is drawn, and blindsight in §2.4.3 turns on behavior reaching something awareness does not.

items.stem: §2.4.2 runs face recognition through three methods. What are the three findings, and what do they converge on?

options.text: Inversion costs more for faces than houses; a temporal patch responds far more to faces; damage there can produce prosopagnosia — so face recognition is not object recognition applied to faces.
options.why: Correct. Three methods with almost nothing in common, and the chapter adds the honest hedge that exactly what is going on is still debated.

options.text: Faces are recognized rather faster than other objects; a patch of temporal cortex responds strongly to faces; and damage in that region impairs the whole of visual recognition — so faces must be processed first.
options.why: Damage in that region spares vision and object recognition, which is what makes the case a selective loss rather than a general one.

options.text: Inversion costs more for faces than for houses; face recognition improves through childhood; and models recognize faces well — so face recognition is learned.
options.why: Development and model performance are not the three legs used here, and the conclusion drawn concerns specialness rather than learning.

options.text: Inversion costs more for faces; a patch of temporal cortex responds to faces; models trained on faces develop similar responses — so the cortex works like the model.
options.why: The third leg in the chapter is damage rather than modelling, and the conclusion is about faces being special rather than about the model.

items.stem: What does §2.4.3 say follows when two methods disagree?

options.text: The disagreement is itself a finding, and which particular pair of methods is at odds tells us what kind of finding we have.
options.why: Correct. That second half is what turns disagreement from an embarrassment into a three-way taxonomy grounded in Marr's levels.

options.text: One of the two methods must be unreliable, and a disagreement between brain and behavior is a signal to repeat both measurements with better instruments.
options.why: Neither method need be unreliable. What has failed is an assumption about what one of them was measuring.

options.text: The finding should be set aside until a third method can be brought in to decide between the first two.
options.why: A third method is useful and the section treats the disagreement itself as the finding rather than as a tie to be broken.

options.text: The two methods are measuring at different levels, so the disagreement is only apparent and dissolves once the levels are named.
options.why: Naming levels is how the section unifies the taxonomy, and the disagreements are real rather than dissolved by it.

items.stem: How does §2.4.3 say a brain-and-behavior disagreement almost always begins?

options.text: As a failed prediction: a neural measure supports a claim, the claim predicts what damage should do, and what people then do is something else.
options.why: Correct. Blindsight is the section's worked case, and the contradiction is what shows processing and awareness to be separable.

options.text: As a measurement error: one of the two techniques was applied incorrectly, and the disagreement disappears once the procedure is repeated.
options.why: Repeating the procedure is not what the section describes, and the disagreements it discusses survive careful measurement.

options.text: As a disagreement between laboratories: two groups using different equipment obtain results that cannot both be right about the same structure.
options.why: The disagreement is between two kinds of method rather than between two groups, and both results are typically sound.

options.text: As a theoretical dispute: two competing accounts of what a structure does make opposite predictions, and the data turn out to support neither of the two.
options.why: The section's shape is a single prediction from a brain measure being contradicted by an observed behavior.

items.stem: Patients with damage to primary visual cortex report seeing nothing in the corresponding field, say guessing is pointless, and then guess far better than chance. What does §2.4.3 draw from that?

options.text: Visual processing and visual awareness are separable, and some visual information reaches behavior by a route that bypasses the damaged structure.
options.why: Correct. The anatomy predicted nothing would get through, and the contradiction between prediction and behavior is the finding.

options.text: The patients retain some conscious vision in the affected field after all, and their own reports understate what they are actually able to see there.
options.why: The section takes the reports as accurate rather than as understatements, which is what makes the above-chance guessing informative.

options.text: Primary visual cortex is not in fact where signals from the eye first arrive, so the anatomical claim behind the prediction was wrong.
options.why: The anatomical claim stands. What fails is the assumption that behavior depends on that route alone.

options.text: Guessing recruits a different cognitive process from seeing, so the two tasks were never measuring the same capacity to begin with.
options.why: The point is that visual information is guiding the guess, which is what makes processing without awareness the conclusion.

items.stem: §2.4.3 gives different lessons for a behavior-model disagreement and a brain-model disagreement. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Behavior and model: the gap specifies what the model is missing. Brain and model: the task can be solved more than one way, and the brain's solution needs its own explanation.
options.why: Correct. The first is why building a model is worth doing even when the model turns out to be wrong.

options.text: Behavior and model: the task can be solved in more than one way. Brain and model: the gap specifies what the model is missing, and that missing part should then be added to it.
options.why: The two are swapped. A model outperforming by a route the brain does not take is what shows a problem admits several solutions.

options.text: Behavior and model: the model should be discarded. Brain and model: the model should be retrained on neural data until the two agree.
options.why: Neither remedy is what the section proposes, and it treats a wrong model as informative rather than as something to throw away.

options.text: Behavior and model: the behavior was mismeasured. Brain and model: the brain measure lacks the resolution to settle the comparison.
options.why: Both readings blame the measurement, where the section locates the lesson in the model and in the task's space of solutions.

items.stem: §2.4.3 unifies its three disagreements using Marr. What is the unification, and what follows?

options.text: Each is a collision between levels, and evidence about one level constrains the others without determining them — so two methods aimed at different levels can both be right and still disagree.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes the taxonomy principled rather than a list, and it is why disagreement is informative rather than awkward.

options.text: Each is a case of two methods aimed at the very same level producing different answers, which means that one of the two of them must be measuring something badly, and the task is to work out which.
options.why: The methods are aimed at different levels, which is exactly why both can be right while refusing to agree with each other.

options.text: Each shows that one of Marr's levels is more fundamental than the others, so a complete account should be built from that level upward.
options.why: No level is given priority, and §2.4.4 closes by saying a complete account needs all three of them together.

options.text: Each shows that Marr's levels cannot be applied to real measurements, since a method never speaks to exactly one level of description.
options.why: The mapping is treated as workable and approximate, and it is what makes the three disagreements interpretable at all.

items.stem: Why does §2.4.4 say reverse inference is so often wrong?

options.text: Brain regions are not dedicated to single processes, so a region active during fear is also active during many other things.
options.why: Correct. Its activation is therefore weak evidence that fear was the critical ingredient, however the finding is reported.

options.text: Brain imaging measures blood flow rather than neural activity, so the signal is an indirect indicator of what a region is doing.
options.why: The indirectness of the measure is a real limitation and is not the reason the section gives for the inference failing.

options.text: Brain regions vary in location between individuals, so a region identified in one person may not correspond in another.
options.why: Anatomical variability is a methodological problem, and the section's objection concerns what a region does rather than where it is.

options.text: Brain activity during a task includes the demands of the task instructions, so activation reflects the procedure rather than the process.
options.why: Task demands are a genuine confound and the section's stated reason is that regions serve many processes rather than one.

items.stem: §2.4.4 says reverse inference is the chapter's central problem in a new setting. How so, and what determines how much an activation licenses?

options.text: An activation is a relationship between two measurements, and a relationship never interprets itself; how much it licenses depends on how selectively that region responds.
options.why: Correct. It is the sentence from §2.1.2 applied to an imaging result, and the answer is empirical rather than general.

options.text: An activation is a relationship between two measurements, and a relationship never interprets itself; how much it licenses depends on how large the activation is relative to baseline.
options.why: Effect size does not settle interpretation. What matters is whether the region responds to that process rather than to many.

options.text: An activation is a measurement of one thing rather than a relationship, which is why the chapter's earlier problem does not apply to it directly.
options.why: The section says the opposite: activity in a region during a task is exactly the kind of relationship §2.1.2 described.

options.text: An activation is a relationship between two measurements; how much it licenses depends on whether the study in question was pre-registered before any of the data were collected.
options.why: Pre-registration guards against a different problem, and the section's answer turns on the selectivity of the region itself.

items.stem: How does §2.4.4 close the section on the three methods?

options.text: They are not competing accounts of the same thing but attempts on different levels of one explanation, and a complete account needs all of them.
options.why: Correct. That is why the modules ahead take each level in turn, and why Module 3 gives each of Marr's three a lecture of its own.

options.text: They are competing accounts, and the field has been steadily settling on neural methods as the most informative of the three.
options.why: No such verdict is offered anywhere in the section, which treats the three as complementary rather than as rivals to be ranked.

options.text: They are three ways of measuring the same level, so a disagreement between them always indicates that one has been misapplied.
options.why: Aiming at different levels is exactly what §2.4.3 uses to explain how two methods can both be right and still disagree.

options.text: They are historically successive, so the earlier methods are now of interest mainly for understanding how the field arrived where it currently is.
options.why: The stages are reported as history, and all three are treated as live methods that a complete account requires together.

items.stem: Introducing the behavioral method, lecture 2.3 connects it back to the first lecture of the module. What is the connection?

options.text: Almost all behavioral measurement compares a person in one set of circumstances to the same person in another — the second family, which the field uses most and the course teaches least.
options.why: Correct. The lecture points out that this is where that family actually lives, having flagged the asymmetry on day one.

options.text: Almost all behavioral measurement compares one species to another, which is the first family of comparison and the one the course emphasizes.
options.why: Cross-system comparison is the first family, and the point being made is that behavioral work sits in the second.

options.text: Almost all behavioral measurement compares two different methods applied to one and the same person, which is the third family and the whole subject of this section.
options.why: The third family is what the whole section is about, and the observation here concerns what the behavioral method itself consists of.

options.text: Almost all behavioral measurement compares what a person does with what they say they did, which is the surface-matching warning from day one.
options.why: Self-report is not what the lecture identifies here, and the connection drawn is to the families of comparison.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 calls one role of models "a real service." Which, and why?

options.text: Checking that a proposed algorithm actually produces the behavior it is meant to explain, since it is easy to describe one in words that fails once it is made to run.
options.why: Correct. The lecture treats that as a service the other two methods cannot perform at all.

options.text: Producing predictions rather faster than an experiment can, because a simulation can be run many more times over than any study could realistically be repeated.
options.why: Speed is not the service the lecture names, and it says nothing about the number of runs a model permits.

options.text: Replacing animal experiments where a manipulation would be unethical, because a model can be lesioned in ways a brain cannot.
options.why: Lesioning models is a real practice and is not what the lecture identifies as the service models uniquely provide.

options.text: Establishing what problem a system is solving, because a model has to be given an explicit objective before it can be built at all.
options.why: Making an objective explicit is a genuine benefit of modelling and it is not the check the lecture singles out.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 names the three legs of the face-recognition case as "an upside-down photograph, a scanner, and a brain injury," and adds an honest hedge. What is the hedge?

options.text: Converging operations got us to a conclusion; it did not get us to a mechanism, and exactly what is going on is still very much argued about.
options.why: Correct. The conclusion is that face recognition is not simply object recognition applied to faces, which stops well short of a mechanism.

options.text: Converging operations got us to a mechanism; what remains disputed is whether the mechanism is present from birth or acquired through experience.
options.why: No mechanism has been reached, and the developmental question is not the hedge the lecture offers here.

options.text: Converging operations works only when all three methods are applied by the same laboratory, which was not the case for these three findings.
options.why: Independence between the methods is what makes the strategy work, and nothing about a single laboratory is required or claimed.

options.text: Converging operations was not really achieved here, since two of the three findings concern the temporal lobe and are therefore not independent.
options.why: The lecture treats the three as having almost nothing in common, which is what makes their agreement hard to attribute to one technique.

items.stem: Presenting blindsight, lecture 2.3 is careful about how the patients' reports should be taken. What does it say?

options.text: They are not being coy; they are reporting accurately when they say they see nothing over there.
options.why: Correct. Taking the report at face value is what makes the above-chance guessing a contradiction worth explaining.

options.text: They are describing a faint residual percept that is hard to put into words, which is what the guessing then reveals.
options.why: A residual percept would dissolve the contradiction, and the lecture presents the report of seeing nothing as accurate.

options.text: They are reporting what they expect to see given what they know about their injury, rather than what they actually experience.
options.why: Expectation effects are a real hazard elsewhere and are not what the lecture proposes about these reports.

options.text: They are unable to describe the experience because the damage also affects the language areas adjacent to visual cortex.
options.why: No claim about language areas is made, and the damage under discussion is confined to primary visual cortex.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 says each family of comparison has a characteristic error, and names all three. What are they?

options.text: The ladder across species, surface matching across the natural and artificial divide, and reverse inference across methods.
options.why: Correct. Naming them together is what makes the three families feel like one method rather than three separate topics.

options.text: Anthropomorphism across species, the Turing test across the natural and artificial divide, and confounding across methods.
options.why: The Turing test is a criterion rather than an error, and confounding belongs to comparison across conditions.

options.text: The ladder across species, the Chinese Room across the natural and artificial divide, and blindsight across methods.
options.why: The Chinese Room is an argument and blindsight a finding; neither is a characteristic error of its family.

options.text: Just-so stories across species, engineering convenience across the natural and artificial divide, and converging operations across methods.
options.why: Engineering convenience and converging operations are both legitimate practices rather than errors of any kind.

items.stem: A researcher proposes to strengthen a finding by running the same behavioral task in four more laboratories. In a short paragraph, say why §2.4.2 would not count that as converging operations, and what would.
items.answer: Converging operations does not turn on the number of measurements but on the independence of their weaknesses. Every method has a characteristic blind spot, and the strategy works because unrelated blind spots cannot all produce one and the same agreement — no single technique's flaws could have generated it. Running the same behavioral task four more times reproduces that method's blind spot four more times: a behavioral measure shows that something changed without showing what changed inside, and repeating it in another building does not change what it is able to see. What the researcher has bought is replication, which is valuable for a different reason. Converging operations would mean adding methods whose limits are unrelated to the behavioral one — a brain measure, which shows where or when something happened without showing what the activity accomplished, or a model, which shows whether a set of assumptions suffices without showing that any mind uses them — and asking whether all of them point the same way.
rubric: States that the strategy turns on the weaknesses being unrelated rather than on the number of measurements.
Explains that repeating one method reproduces its blind spot rather than escaping it.
Distinguishes replication, which the proposal achieves, from convergence.
Names at least one other method with a different blind spot that would count, and says what its blind spot is.

items.stem: A model of reading reproduces adult word-recognition times closely but breaks on unfamiliar names. In a few sentences, say which of §2.4.3's three disagreements this is, what the lesson is, and why the section says building a model is worth doing even when the model turns out to be wrong.
items.answer: This is a behavior-and-model disagreement, which is the case where the synthetic method is doing its real work. The lesson is usually about the model rather than about the behavior: a model that reproduces most of a phenomenon and then breaks on one particular case is telling us precisely what it is missing, and the gap between what the model does and what people do is a specification of the missing part. Here it says that whatever handles unfamiliar names is something the model has not been given, which is a claim about the natural system too. That is why a wrong model is worth building — the failure is a finding rather than a wasted effort. In Marr's terms the collision is about what the algorithm actually is, and evidence at that level constrains the implementation without determining it.
rubric: Identifies it as a behavior-and-model disagreement.
States that the lesson is about the model, and that the gap specifies what the model is missing.
Explains why a wrong model is still worth building — its failure is informative about the natural system.
Locates the disagreement at Marr's algorithmic level, or otherwise says which level the collision is about.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 says reverse inference is tempting for a particular reason, and adds a qualification about how far it is ever safe. What are they?

options.text: It feels like reading the answer off the machine; and how much an activation licenses depends on the region — some are quite selective and the inference is reasonable, most are not.
options.why: Correct. The lecture ends the module by noting this is the same sentence from the first lecture, in a lab coat.

options.text: It is the only inference imaging permits; and it is safe whenever the activation is large relative to the baseline condition used.
options.why: Imaging supports forward predictions too, and effect size is not what determines how much an activation licenses.

options.text: It is endorsed by most imaging researchers; and it is safe whenever the study was designed to test that specific region in advance.
options.why: The lecture says the move is often wrong rather than endorsed, and prior specification does not make a region any more selective.

options.text: It follows directly from the mapping of methods onto Marr's levels; and it is safe whenever behavioral evidence points the same way.
options.why: Converging evidence helps and the lecture's qualification concerns the selectivity of the particular region rather than agreement between methods.

items.stem: What is a confound?

options.text: Something other than the change we introduced that varied along with it and would produce the same result on its own.
options.why: Correct. A confound leaves the observed difference real and our explanation of it wrong, which is the wrong-why error in this family.

options.text: A difference between conditions that turns out to have been produced by random variation rather than by anything systematic.
options.why: That is chance, the third source of a difference, and it is answered by statistical inference rather than by design.

options.text: A variable the researcher manipulates deliberately in order to see what effect it has on the measure of interest.
options.why: That is the manipulation itself. A confound is whatever else moved alongside it without anybody intending it to.

options.text: A condition matched to the experimental one in every respect except the thing being tested, so the manipulation stands alone.
options.why: That is a control condition, which is the design that answers a confound rather than a name for the problem.

items.stem: Which term names something other than the manipulation that varied along with it and would produce the same result on its own?

options.text: confound
options.why: Correct. §2.6 calls it the wrong-why error in the setting of comparison across conditions.

options.text: control condition
options.why: That names a condition matched to the experimental one in every respect except the thing being tested.

options.text: naturalistic study
options.why: That names a study in which a relationship is observed as it occurs rather than produced by a manipulation.

options.text: chance
options.why: That names the random variation always present between two measurements, which is the third source of a difference rather than the second.

items.stem: What is an experiment, as §2.5.1 defines it?

options.text: A study in which, rather than observing variation as it occurs, we introduce it: variables are chosen, manipulated, and the effects observed.
options.why: Correct. It is the only design that can promise more than a naturalistic study with respect to confounds.

options.text: A study carried out under laboratory conditions, where the surroundings can be held constant across all of the conditions compared.
options.why: A laboratory helps and is not what defines the design. What defines it is that the researcher introduces the variation.

options.text: A study in which a large enough sample is collected that statistical inference can rule out chance as an explanation.
options.why: Sample size bears on chance rather than on confounds, and an observational study of any size is still not an experiment.

options.text: A study comparing two groups that already differ in the respect of interest, treating that difference as though it had been introduced.
options.why: That is a naturalistic study, which is precisely the design an experiment is contrasted with here.

items.stem: Which design introduces the variation itself, choosing variables and manipulating them explicitly rather than observing variation as it occurs?

options.text: experiment
options.why: Correct. It is the only design that can promise more than a naturalistic study where confounds are concerned.

options.text: naturalistic study
options.why: That is the design in which a relationship is observed as it occurs, with subjects who cannot be assigned to conditions.

options.text: converging operations
options.why: That is a strategy for combining methods whose weaknesses are unrelated, not a design for comparing conditions.

options.text: control condition
options.why: That is one condition inside an experiment rather than a name for the design as a whole.

items.stem: What is a naturalistic study?

options.text: A study in which a relationship is observed as it occurs in the everyday world rather than produced by a manipulation; also called observational.
options.why: Correct. Because subjects cannot be assigned to conditions, every respect in which the compared groups differ is a potential confound.

options.text: A study of animal behavior conducted in the field rather than in a laboratory, so that the behavior observed is unconstrained.
options.why: Field observation of animals is ethology's characteristic setting, and this term names a design rather than a location or a subject.

options.text: A study in which the manipulation is introduced so gently that the participants are unaware anything has been changed.
options.why: Concealing a manipulation is still manipulating; what defines this design is that no manipulation is introduced at all.

options.text: A study in which the researcher records everything that happens without deciding in advance which variables to measure.
options.why: Naturalistic studies look for a relationship between specified variables; what they lack is assignment, not a plan.

items.stem: What is a control condition?

options.text: A condition matched to the experimental one in every respect except the thing being tested, so the manipulation is the only possible cause of a difference.
options.why: Correct. And the honest limit is that it controls only for the confounds somebody actually thought of.

options.text: A condition in which nothing at all is done to the participants, so that their untouched performance can serve as a baseline.
options.why: Doing nothing rarely matches the experimental condition; matching is what the design requires, not absence of treatment.

options.text: A condition run before the experimental one, so that any change over time can be measured against the earlier result.
options.why: Order is itself a potential confound, and the definition turns on matching rather than on when a condition is run.

options.text: A condition run by an independent laboratory, so that the result can be checked against a group with no stake in it.
options.why: Independent checking is replication, which is valuable for a different reason and is not what this term names.

items.stem: What makes comparison across conditions different from the comparisons in §2.2, §2.3 and §2.4?

options.text: It takes a single system, uses the same method, and measures it twice under circumstances that differ in one respect the researcher chose.
options.why: Correct. Earlier comparisons set different systems side by side, or different methods; here both are held fixed and the circumstances vary.

options.text: It takes two systems that are as similar as possible, so that any difference between them can be attributed to the one respect in which they differ.
options.why: Matching two systems is a different design. Here there is one system, measured under two sets of circumstances.

options.text: It takes a single system and applies two different methods to it, asking whether the two measurements tell the same story.
options.why: That is comparison across methods, which §2.4 has just finished, and it holds the circumstances fixed rather than the method.

options.text: It takes a single system and follows it over time, so that changes can be attributed to development rather than to any manipulation.
options.why: That is comparison across ages, taken up in §2.5.2, and it does not involve a chosen difference in circumstances.

items.stem: §2.5.1 says one thing makes a condition contrast informative. What is it?

options.text: The theory predicted a different pattern in each of the two before any of the data arrived.
options.why: Correct. That is what separates an experiment from a fishing expedition, and it is easy to overlook in an account of the design.

options.text: The two conditions were run in a randomized order, so that fatigue and practice could not favor either of them.
options.why: Order effects are a confound worth controlling, and controlling them does not by itself make a contrast informative.

options.text: The difference between the two conditions reached the conventional threshold for statistical significance.
options.why: Statistical inference addresses chance, and a difference can be reliable while telling us nothing anybody predicted.

options.text: The same participants were tested in both conditions, so that individual differences could not explain the result.
options.why: Within-subject designs remove one class of confound, which is again a matter of design rather than of prediction.

items.stem: In the visual search illustration, what pattern does §2.5.1 report, and what claim about attention does it support?

options.text: A red circle among blue circles takes about the same time at five items or fifty; a red circle among red squares and blue circles gets steadily slower — so some properties register across the whole display at once and combinations are checked one at a time.
options.why: Correct. One system, one method, two conditions, and a difference the theory predicted in advance.

options.text: Both searches get steadily slower as the display fills, though the second one slows faster — so all search is serial and combinations simply take longer per item.
options.why: The first search is flat in set size, which is the whole contrast, and a uniformly serial account cannot produce that flatness.

options.text: Both searches take about the same time regardless of set size — so attention registers the entire display at once whatever is being searched for.
options.why: Only the feature search is flat. The conjunction search slows with set size, which is what the contrast is built to show.

options.text: A red circle among blue circles gets steadily slower, while a red circle among red squares and blue circles is flat — so combinations are easier to detect than single properties.
options.why: The two are reversed, and the conclusion inverts the claim about attention the finding actually supports.

items.stem: §2.5.1 lists three places a difference between conditions can come from. What are they?

options.text: The change we deliberately introduced, a confound that varied alongside it, or plain random chance.
options.why: Correct. It is §2.1.6's three-way shape again, with candidate answers adapted to a comparison across conditions.

options.text: The change we introduced, a difference between the two groups of participants taking part, or measurement error somewhere in the instrument.
options.why: Group differences and instrument error are both kinds of confound rather than two separate categories alongside it.

options.text: The change we introduced, a shared origin between the conditions, or convergence between them under a common pressure.
options.why: Shared origin and convergence answer the origin question for comparisons across systems, and neither applies to one system measured twice.

options.text: The change we introduced, the order in which the conditions were run, or the expectations of the person running the study.
options.why: Both of the last two are examples of confounds rather than a complete list of where a difference can come from.

items.stem: In the visual search study, the harder condition is also run second, when people are tired. What does §2.5.1 say about the result in that case?

options.text: The difference between the conditions is real, and our explanation of that difference is wrong.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes a confound the wrong-why error rather than a reason to doubt the measurement itself.

options.text: The difference is an artifact and would disappear if the study were repeated with a properly rested sample of participants.
options.why: The difference is genuine. What fails is the attribution of it to the feature structure rather than to fatigue.

options.text: The difference is real and our explanation of it is correct, since fatigue would have affected both conditions equally.
options.why: Fatigue falls on only one of the two conditions here, which is precisely what makes it a candidate explanation of the difference.

options.text: The difference cannot be interpreted until the study has been replicated by another laboratory using the same materials.
options.why: Replication with the same design would reproduce the confound faithfully, which is why the remedy is a matter of design.

items.stem: Why does §2.5.1 say every respect in which two compared groups differ is a potential confound in a naturalistic study?

options.text: Subjects cannot be randomly assigned, so the groups already differ and the difference of interest is treated as though it had been introduced.
options.why: Correct. Nobody can be assigned to be bilingual, to have had a particular childhood, or to have sustained a particular brain injury.

options.text: Naturalistic studies are usually smaller than experiments, so chance differences between the groups are harder to rule out.
options.why: Sample size is about chance, and the problem being described here concerns systematic differences rather than random ones.

options.text: Naturalistic studies measure variables that are harder to define precisely, so the groups may not differ in the way the researcher assumes.
options.why: Definitional slippage is a real hazard elsewhere; the point here is that the groups differ in many ways nobody chose.

options.text: Naturalistic studies observe behavior in the everyday world, where more variables are present than could be recorded in a laboratory.
options.why: Setting is not the issue. An observational study run in a laboratory would have exactly the same assignment problem.

items.stem: What three techniques does §2.5.1 offer for handling confounds in a naturalistic study, and what limit do all three share?

options.text: Match the groups on measurable variables, measure a suspected confound and see whether the difference survives, and follow the same people over time — each controlling only for confounds someone thought of.
options.why: Correct. None of them can rule out a cause nobody has imagined, which is what an experiment is able to promise more about.

options.text: Increase the sample size, repeat the study in a second population, and report the effect with a confidence interval — and each addresses chance rather than confounding.
options.why: All three are sound practice for a different problem, and none of them is among the techniques the section names.

options.text: Randomly assign subjects to groups, use a control condition, and conceal the hypothesis from the experimenter — and each requires a manipulation.
options.why: Random assignment is precisely what a naturalistic study cannot do, which is what creates the problem in the first place.

options.text: Match the groups on measurable variables, use a control condition, and follow the same people over time — and each requires the confounds to be measurable.
options.why: A control condition belongs to an experiment, and the shared limit the section names concerns confounds nobody thought of.

items.stem: §2.5.1 states an honest limit on the control condition. What is it, and what practical consequence does the section draw?

options.text: We can only control for confounds we have thought of, which is why results are believed after others have tried and failed to break them rather than on first appearance.
options.why: Correct. The limit is what makes an experimental literature a social process rather than a sequence of decisive single studies.

options.text: We can only control for confounds we can measure, which is why experimental results are reported with the measured covariates listed alongside them.
options.why: Measurability is the limit on the naturalistic techniques; the limit on a control condition is what anybody happened to think of.

options.text: We can only control for one confound at a time, which is why an experiment usually needs several control conditions to be convincing.
options.why: A well-matched control handles everything it matches at once, and the limit named concerns unimagined confounds rather than a count.

options.text: We can only control for confounds present in the laboratory, which is why experimental results have to be checked in natural settings.
options.why: Ecological validity is a separate worry, and the limit stated is about the researcher's imagination rather than the setting.

items.stem: What role does §2.5.1 give statistical inference?

options.text: Estimating how often and by how much two conditions would differ if they were in reality the same, so what is observed can be compared against that.
options.why: Correct. Twenty flips of a fair coin twice over will rarely give ten and ten each time, and knowledge of probability is the protection against reading that as real.

options.text: Establishing that a difference between two conditions was caused by the manipulation rather than by anything else that varied alongside it.
options.why: Confounds are answered by design rather than by statistics, which is a distinction the section is careful to keep.

options.text: Measuring how large a difference between two conditions is, so that results from different studies can be compared with one another.
options.why: Effect size is worth reporting and the role the section gives inference is specifically about what chance alone would produce.

options.text: Determining how many participants a study needs before it can be expected to detect a difference of the predicted size.
options.why: Power analysis uses the same machinery for a planning question, and it is not the role the section describes.

items.stem: What is the first of the two limitations §2.5.1 closes with?

options.text: A condition contrast shows only that a manipulation moved a measure in the predicted direction, not how the system works inside.
options.why: Correct. That is why a single result usually does not rule out every explanation but one, and why comparison across systems or methods helps.

options.text: A condition contrast shows only that a difference exists, not whether the difference is large enough to matter in any practical setting.
options.why: Practical significance is a real question and the limitation named concerns the inside of the system rather than the size of the effect.

options.text: A condition contrast shows only what happens under the specific manipulation used, not what a stronger version of it would do.
options.why: Dose is one thing a contrast leaves open, and the limitation stated is about mechanism rather than about the strength of a manipulation.

options.text: A condition contrast shows only an average across participants, not what happened to any individual person in the study.
options.why: Averaging is a genuine limitation of many designs, and the one the section names is about how the system works internally.

items.stem: What is the second limitation §2.5.1 closes with, and what example does it give?

options.text: A contrast is run within a single kind of system, so the finding is limited to it — and much of what textbooks report about the human mind was measured in undergraduates at wealthy universities in a few countries.
options.why: Correct. The section calls that a claim about who was available to study as much as it is a claim about minds.

options.text: A contrast is run at a single point in time, so the finding is limited to that period — and much of what textbooks report was measured before the 1990s.
options.why: The limitation named concerns the kind of system studied rather than when the study was run.

options.text: A contrast is run by a single laboratory, so the finding is limited to its procedures — and much of what textbooks report has never been replicated elsewhere.
options.why: Replication is a different concern, and the section's point is about the population a finding was drawn from.

options.text: A contrast is run on a single task, so the finding is limited to that task — and much of what textbooks report rests on reaction-time measures alone.
options.why: Task specificity is real, and the example the section gives is about who was studied rather than about what they were asked to do.

items.stem: §2.5 gives three remaining comparisons only a few paragraphs each. What does it say about what that space means?

options.text: It is not a judgment about importance, and for comparison across conditions it is the reverse of one.
options.why: Correct. §2.1.7 made the same admission about the chapter's allocation, and §2.5 restates it before spending the sections.

options.text: It reflects how much is settled in each area, since the three remaining comparisons rest on findings that are less contested.
options.why: No such claim is made, and §2.5.2 presents three competing accounts precisely because the area is not settled.

options.text: It reflects how much of each is assumed knowledge, since students will have met experiments and development in earlier courses.
options.why: Nothing is assumed: §2.5.1 teaches the experiment from the beginning and is the longest subsection in the chapter.

options.text: It is a judgment about importance, since the two spine comparisons are the ones that run through every module that follows.
options.why: The spine comparisons do run through the course, and the section explicitly denies that the allocation ranks importance.

items.stem: The evolution lab gives the full log of two runs that reached different outcomes, where the person running them changed the mutation rate on purpose. Reading that log, what else differed between the two runs?

options.text: The two runs held different numbers of vehicles and were started from different seeds, so their founding populations were not the same either.
options.why: Correct. Either one alone is a complete answer; the seed is the harder case, because two runs can differ with no setting on the panel differing at all.

options.text: Nothing else differed, so the two runs are a clean comparison and the outcome can be attributed to the mutation rate directly.
options.why: The log records a second difference, and finding it is the point of the question; a clean comparison is what would have to be built.

options.text: The two runs used different light regimes, so one population was feeding while the other was being poisoned throughout the whole run.
options.why: The regime is the same in both; the poison switch belongs to Part 2's fifth experiment rather than to this pair of runs.

options.text: The two runs were stopped after different numbers of births, so one population simply had longer to sort its founding variation than the other.
options.why: The log records how far each run went, and the differences it actually shows are in the arena's size and in the seed.

items.stem: A study reports that children who take music lessons score higher on a reasoning test than children with no lessons. In a few sentences, say what kind of study this is, name two plausible confounds, and say what the available techniques achieve and where they stop.
items.answer: It is a naturalistic study: nobody assigned these children to take lessons, so two groups that already differ are being compared as though the difference had been introduced. That makes every other respect in which the groups differ a potential confound, and there are always many. Two plausible ones are family income, since lessons cost money and money buys other things that bear on test scores, and the disposition of the parents, since families who arrange lessons may differ in how much else they arrange. Both of these can be partly handled: the groups can be matched on income, the suspected confound can be measured directly and the difference checked to see whether it survives, and the same children can be followed over time so each serves as their own comparison. What none of that can do is rule out a cause nobody has imagined, which is the limit these techniques share and the reason an experiment can promise more.
rubric: Identifies the design as a naturalistic or observational study, and says why: no random assignment.
Names two plausible confounds specific to this case.
Gives at least two of the three techniques — matching, measuring the suspected confound, or following the same people over time.
States the shared limit: each controls only for confounds someone thought of.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what a control condition is for, and why §2.5.1 says experimental results are believed only after other people have tried and failed to break them.
items.answer: A control condition is matched to the experimental condition in every respect except the thing being tested, so that if the matching is done well the manipulation is the only thing that could have caused the difference observed. In the visual search case the control matches the number of items, their size and how long they are shown, which is what licenses attributing the difference to the feature structure rather than to one display simply being busier. The honest limit is that we can only control for confounds we have thought of. Nothing in the design guarantees that the list of matched respects is complete, and a confound nobody imagined will pass through a perfectly executed control. That is why a result is believed after other people, who will have thought of different things, have tried to break it and failed — the confidence comes from the accumulated attempts rather than from any single study, however well built.
rubric: Defines a control condition as matched in every respect except the thing being tested.
Says what the matching licenses: attributing the difference to the manipulation.
States the limit — only confounds someone thought of can be controlled for.
Connects that limit to why belief follows repeated failed attempts to break a result rather than the first report of it.

pools.title: Across Ages, Atypical Minds, and the Close

items.stem: What is ontogeny?

options.text: The developmental history of an individual across its own lifetime, as against the evolutionary history of its lineage.
options.why: Correct. Watching a capacity come into being over an ontogeny is itself evidence about how that capacity is built.

options.text: The evolutionary history of a species, showing which lineages it descends from and where it branched from its relatives.
options.why: That is phylogeny, and §2.5.2 opens by drawing the contrast between the two kinds of history explicitly.

options.text: The study of how a capacity varies between individuals of the same age within a single population.
options.why: Individual variation at one age is a different comparison, and ontogeny is a history running across a lifetime.

options.text: The sequence in which the parts of the nervous system mature, from the earliest structures to the latest ones.
options.why: Neural maturation is one thing an ontogeny includes, and the term covers the whole developmental history rather than that alone.

items.stem: Which term names the developmental history of an individual across its own lifetime, as distinct from the evolutionary history of its lineage?

options.text: ontogeny
options.why: Correct. Where §2.2 asked where a capacity came from across millions of years, §2.5.2 asks across a single lifetime.

options.text: phylogeny
options.why: That names the evolutionary history of a species, of which a phylogenetic tree is the map.

options.text: adaptation
options.why: That names a trait that became common because organisms with it were more likely to survive and reproduce.

options.text: convergent evolution
options.why: That names two lineages arriving at one solution from different starting points, which produces analogies.

items.stem: What is the nativist account of an observed capacity?

options.text: That it is best explained by innate, genetic properties, so development starts from rich, structured, built-in foundations.
options.why: Correct. Its weakness, which the chapter states alongside it, is that a bias to attend to something is not the same as knowledge about it.

options.text: That it is best explained by learning and experience, some of which can occur before birth.
options.why: That is the empiricist account, whose own weakness is that prenatal learning cannot explain why a fetus attends to voices at all.

options.text: That it is best explained by a modest built-in bias combined with a powerful general learning capacity.
options.why: That is the constructivist account, which treats the other two as halves of one story.

options.text: That it is best explained by the specific environment an individual happens to develop in rather than by any general capacity.
options.why: Environmental specificity is part of the empiricist and constructivist stories rather than a fourth account of its own.

items.stem: Which account explains an observed capacity by learning and experience, locating that learning before birth in the case of newborn speech preferences?

options.text: empiricist
options.why: Correct. Its weakness is that prenatal learning explains which voice and which language are preferred without explaining why a fetus attends to voices at all.

options.text: nativist
options.why: That account explains the capacity by innate, genetic properties, with development starting from rich built-in foundations.

options.text: constructivist
options.why: That account treats the other two as halves of one story, combining a modest built-in bias with a general learning capacity.

options.text: naturalistic
options.why: That is a study design in which a relationship is observed as it occurs rather than produced by a manipulation.

items.stem: What is the constructivist account?

options.text: That a modest built-in bias and a general learning capacity together produce an outcome neither would produce alone.
options.why: Correct. Its weakness is that, stated loosely, it can accommodate any result, so the job is to name the biases and mechanisms and test them.

options.text: That an observed capacity is constructed entirely from experience, with no built-in contribution of any kind required.
options.why: That would be a strong form of the empiricist account, and the constructivist position keeps a built-in bias in the story.

options.text: That an observed capacity is constructed by the child's own active exploration rather than by anything given to it passively.
options.why: Activity is a theme in developmental psychology and is not what this account is defined by in the chapter.

options.text: That an observed capacity is built from innate foundations which experience then refines without adding anything new to them.
options.why: Refinement of rich innate structure is closer to the nativist picture, and the constructivist claim is that neither half suffices alone.

items.stem: What does the chapter say the nature versus nurture debate really turns on?

options.text: Not whether a capacity is innate or learned, but what exactly is claimed to be innate: content, an architecture, or a bias.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's argument is that the question as usually posed does not survive contact with the evidence.

options.text: Not whether a capacity is innate or learned, but how much of the variation between individuals is attributable to each.
options.why: Partitioning variance is one way the debate has been run elsewhere, and it is not the reframing this chapter offers.

options.text: Whether a capacity is innate or learned, since the evidence from newborns is now good enough to settle that question directly.
options.why: The chapter says the question as usually posed does not survive the evidence, and it does not treat newborn work as settling it.

options.text: Whether a capacity appears before or after birth, since anything present at birth must have been built in rather than learned.
options.why: Prenatal learning is exactly what defeats that inference, and it is the empiricist's strongest evidence in this section.

items.stem: §2.5.2 lists what developmental comparison is used for. Which of these is on the list?

options.text: Separating gains in an ability from gains in the machinery for displaying it, since a child who fails may instead lack memory or attention.
options.why: Correct. Alongside it: when a capacity first appears, what order capacities appear in, and what waits on experience.

options.text: Establishing which capacities are unique to humans, by finding the age at which a human child first outperforms an adult of another species.
options.why: Cross-species comparison is §2.2's business, and nothing in this section proposes ranking children against other animals.

options.text: Measuring how much individual variation there is in a capacity, by testing many children of the same age on the same task.
options.why: Variation within an age is a different comparison, and the uses listed here all run across ages rather than within one.

options.text: Determining whether a capacity is an adaptation, by checking whether it appears reliably in every child regardless of environment.
options.why: Reliability of appearance bears on the nature-versus-nurture question, and adaptation is not what this list is about.

items.stem: Infants cannot report anything. How does §2.5.2 say researchers establish newborn preferences?

options.text: By measuring looking time, sucking vigor, head turning and heart rate — an infant will adjust its sucking to hear its mother.
options.why: Correct. A preference expressed by a means the researcher can measure is what stands in for a report that cannot be given.

options.text: By recording brain activity during presentation of each sound, since electrical measures are the only route into a preverbal mind.
options.why: Neural measures are used in developmental work and are not the ones the section names; the measures here are all behavioral.

options.text: By waiting until the children are old enough to report, and then asking them which sounds they remember preferring as infants.
options.why: Retrospective report is not available for infancy, and the section's point is that a measurable behavior can serve instead.

options.text: By asking parents to record which sounds their infant appears to respond to, since a parent observes far more hours than a laboratory can.
options.why: Parental report is a real method in some designs and is not what the section describes for these findings.

items.stem: What did Vouloumanos and Werker find, and what does the nativist take from it?

options.text: Infants only hours old prefer speech to carefully matched non-speech sounds, which is difficult to attribute to anything learned after birth.
options.why: Correct. The weakness the chapter states alongside it is that the preference might track acoustic properties rather than speechness — a confound.

options.text: Infants only hours old prefer their mother's voice to another woman's, which is difficult to attribute to anything other than a built-in template.
options.why: That is DeCasper and Fifer's finding, and the mother's voice is the empiricist's best case rather than the nativist's.

options.text: Infants prefer speech to non-speech from about six months, which is the age at which language-specific perception is established.
options.why: The finding concerns infants who are hours old, which is what makes learning after birth an implausible explanation of it.

options.text: Infants only hours old prefer the rhythms of their mother's language, which cannot have been learned before birth.
options.why: That is Mehler and colleagues' finding, and the chapter treats it as evidence that it was learned before birth.

items.stem: Why does §2.5.2 call Mehler and colleagues' rhythm finding the decisive case for the empiricist?

options.text: Newborns prefer their mother's language's rhythms over a rhythmically different one, and which language that is depends on where the child developed.
options.why: Correct. A preference that looks innate turns out to be the product of months of listening in utero.

options.text: Newborns prefer the rhythms of their mother's language, which shows that rhythm perception matures earlier than any other aspect of hearing.
options.why: Maturation order is not the argument. What makes the case decisive is that the specific language cannot have been anticipated.

options.text: Newborns prefer their mother's voice over another woman's, which shows they recognize a specific individual heard before birth.
options.why: That is DeCasper and Fifer's result, which the section reports separately and treats as supporting but less decisive.

options.text: Newborns cry with the melodic contour of the language heard in the womb, which shows prenatal learning affects production as well as perception.
options.why: That finding is reported alongside, and the decisive case turns on a preference that could not have been built in.

items.stem: §2.5.2 presents each of the three accounts with a weakness. Which pairing of account and weakness is correct?

options.text: Nativist: a bias to attend is not knowledge. Empiricist: prenatal learning leaves unexplained why a fetus attends to voices. Constructivist: stated loosely it accommodates anything.
options.why: Correct. Presenting all three with their weaknesses is what stops the section being a case for one of them.

options.text: Nativist: it cannot explain individual differences. Empiricist: it cannot explain learning before birth. Constructivist: it cannot be tested at any age.
options.why: Prenatal learning is the empiricist's strongest evidence rather than a difficulty, and the constructivist's problem is looseness rather than untestability.

options.text: Nativist: stated loosely, it can accommodate anything. Empiricist: a bias to attend is not knowledge. Constructivist: it does not explain why a fetus attends to voices.
options.why: The three weaknesses have been rotated between the accounts they belong to.

options.text: Nativist: it relies on findings from infants too young to test reliably. Empiricist: it relies on findings that have not replicated. Constructivist: it relies on unmeasured biases.
options.why: None of these is the weakness the chapter names, and it treats all three sets of findings as sound.

items.stem: §2.5.2 says what the comparison in the newborn case actually did. What is its point?

options.text: Nobody watched a mind before and after learning; a preference was observed at an age, and the inference ran backwards to what could have produced it.
options.why: Correct. That is the general shape of developmental evidence, and nature versus nurture is only its most famous instance.

options.text: Nobody measured the preference directly; it was inferred from sucking and looking, which are indirect indicators of what an infant prefers.
options.why: The measures are indirect and that is a separate point; the observation here is about the direction the inference runs.

options.text: Nobody compared newborns with older infants, so the design cannot establish that the preference changes across development at all.
options.why: Change across development is not what these studies claim; they use a single age and reason backwards from it.

options.text: Nobody controlled for the acoustic properties of the stimuli, which is the confound the nativist account is vulnerable to.
options.why: That confound is named as the nativist's weakness, and the point here concerns the logic of developmental inference generally.

items.stem: Which three misuses does §2.5.2 say cluster around developmental comparison?

options.text: The recapitulation fallacy, confusing competence with performance, and adultomorphism.
options.why: Correct. The last of these the chapter calls anthropomorphism wearing different clothes.

options.text: The recapitulation fallacy, confusing correlation with causation, and anthropocentrism.
options.why: Correlation and causation is a general worry rather than one specific to development, and the third named misuse is adultomorphism.

options.text: Confusing competence with performance, over-reliance on parental report, and testing children too young for the task.
options.why: Only the first is on the chapter's list, and the other two are practical problems rather than the named misuses.

options.text: The recapitulation fallacy, confusing competence with performance, and the assumption that development is complete at adulthood.
options.why: The first two are right and the third is not; the chapter's third misuse is reading adult concepts into infant minds.

items.stem: A four-year-old fails a task that a six-year-old passes, and a researcher concludes the ability is absent at four. Which of §2.5.2's misuses is that, and what is the alternative?

options.text: Confusing competence with performance: the child may hold the capacity while lacking what the task happens to demand.
options.why: Correct. Competence asks whether the capacity is there at all, and performance asks how well and under what conditions it can be shown.

options.text: The recapitulation fallacy: treating a lifetime's development as a replay of the evolutionary history of the species.
options.why: That misuse concerns reading ontogeny as a rerun of phylogeny, which is a different error from misreading a failure.

options.text: Adultomorphism: reading adult concepts into an infant mind, which is anthropomorphism wearing a different set of clothes.
options.why: Adultomorphism over-attributes rather than under-attributes, so it is the opposite direction from the error described here.

options.text: Anthropocentrism: treating the older child as the reference case against which the younger one is described as deficient.
options.why: That framing is a real hazard which §2.5.3 takes up, and the specific misuse named for this case is competence versus performance.

items.stem: What does §2.5.3 say comparison across typical and atypical minds buys that no other comparison provides?

options.text: If a capacity can be lost while everything around it remains, that is evidence it is a real component rather than an incidental consequence.
options.why: Correct. Prosopagnosia is the chapter's case, with face recognition failing while vision and object recognition stay intact.

options.text: If a capacity is absent from birth, that is evidence it depends on experience rather than on any built-in contribution.
options.why: Absence from birth is developmental evidence of the kind §2.5.2 handles, and it is not what selective loss establishes.

options.text: If a capacity is impaired along with several others, that is evidence the impaired capacities share a common underlying resource.
options.why: Co-occurring impairment is harder to interpret, and the inference the section describes turns on loss while everything else remains.

options.text: If a capacity can be trained back after injury, that is evidence the system is more plastic than a typical developmental account allows.
options.why: Recovery and plasticity are important elsewhere, and the evidence this section describes comes from the selectivity of the loss.

items.stem: Which pair of cases does §2.5.3 give as running on the logic of selective loss?

options.text: Prosopagnosia, where face recognition fails while vision remains; and language, where some lose fluent production while comprehension survives, and others the reverse.
options.why: Correct. The reversed pattern in the language case is what makes the two capacities separable rather than one being a prerequisite of the other.

options.text: Prosopagnosia, where all visual recognition fails together; and language, where production and comprehension are always lost together.
options.why: Losses that always co-occur are exactly what cannot support the inference, and both cases here are selective rather than global.

options.text: Blindsight, where vision is lost while guessing survives; and prosopagnosia, where face recognition fails while vision remains intact.
options.why: Blindsight is §2.4.3's case, used there for a brain-and-behavior disagreement rather than for selective loss.

options.text: Blindsight and the split between competence and performance, both of which show a capacity present but not displayed.
options.why: Neither is what this section uses, and competence and performance belong to the developmental misuses of §2.5.2.

items.stem: §2.5.3 says the characteristic misuse of this comparison has a familiar shape. What is it?

options.text: The ladder of §2.2.5 in miniature, with the typical mind as standard and other minds described purely as sets of deficits.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's line is that an autistic person is not a neurotypical person with pieces missing, any more than a frog is a defective human.

options.text: Anthropomorphism, since a mind that developed differently gets credited with capacities it has not been shown to have.
options.why: Over-attribution is not the risk the section identifies here; the misuse it names describes other minds by what they lack.

options.text: The recapitulation fallacy, since a mind that developed differently gets treated as an earlier stage of a typical one.
options.why: That misuse belongs to §2.5.2's developmental material, and the shape named here is the ranking of minds against a standard.

options.text: Reverse inference, since a difference in brain structure gets read as showing which process is absent from the atypical mind.
options.why: Reverse inference is §2.4.4's error about activation, and the misuse here concerns the framing of a difference as a deficit.

items.stem: §2.5.3 says deficit framing fails in two separate ways. What are they?

options.text: It hides whatever the difference makes possible, and it is usually wrong about the mechanism: a differently developing system is not a typical one minus a part.
options.why: Correct. The second is what makes the objection scientific rather than only ethical, and it is easy to under-weight.

options.text: It is unkind to the people described, and it discourages them from participating in research, which narrows the samples available.
options.why: Participation is a real practical concern and is not either of the two the section names, one of which is about mechanism.

options.text: It hides whatever the difference makes possible, and it prevents clinicians from identifying the impairments that need support.
options.why: The section does not argue against identifying impairments; its second objection is that the deficit picture misdescribes the mechanism.

options.text: It assumes a single ladder of ability, and it treats the typical mind as an average when in fact typical minds vary a great deal.
options.why: Variation among typical minds is true and is not the second objection; the section's is about how a differently developing system is organized.

items.stem: §2.5.3 says this is where §2.1.9's warning has done its worst historical damage. What does it point to?

options.text: Claims about whose mind counts as fully functioning have decided who could be educated, institutionalized, sterilized, or believed — "mental age" among them.
options.why: Correct. The section states the history plainly and then refuses the easy conclusion that the comparison should therefore stop.

options.text: Claims about whose mind counts have shaped which conditions receive research funding, so some differences are far better understood than others.
options.why: Funding disparities are real and are not what the section points to; its examples concern decisions made about people's lives.

options.text: Claims about whose mind counts have determined which patients are offered treatment, which is why diagnosis is now handled by standardized criteria.
options.why: Standardized diagnosis is not discussed, and the historical damage the section names is broader than access to treatment.

options.text: Claims about whose mind counts have led researchers to over-report deficits, which is why findings in this area replicate poorly.
options.why: Replication is not the section's concern, and the damage it describes was done to people rather than to a literature.

items.stem: Having stated that history, §2.5.3 refuses one conclusion. Which, and what does it put in its place?

options.text: It refuses the conclusion that the comparison should stop, since it is genuinely informative — asking instead that the people compared are people first, and that language is a choice with consequences.
options.why: Correct. The section defends the comparison while declining to defend the framing, which is what makes its position more than a caution.

options.text: It refuses the conclusion that the history matters, because the science can be assessed on its own terms independently of how it has been used.
options.why: The section insists the stakes are not an abstraction, and it treats the history as bearing directly on how the work should be done.

options.text: It refuses the conclusion that the comparison is informative, and recommends that differences be studied only where a person has asked for them to be.
options.why: The section is explicit that the comparison is genuinely informative and often helpful, so this reverses its position.

options.text: It refuses the conclusion that language matters, on the grounds that changing terminology does not change the underlying findings.
options.why: Language is precisely what the section says is a choice with consequences, so this inverts its closing point.

items.stem: §2.6 restates the one inferential logic that ran through the whole chapter. What is it, and what three questions were built around it?

options.text: A comparison never interprets itself, so the work is diagnosing the why first — and the questions are where the similarity came from, how deep it goes, how precisely it can be stated.
options.why: Correct. The close is written so that a reader leaves with one transferable procedure rather than a list of comparison types.

options.text: A comparison is only as good as its measurement, so the work is measuring precisely — and the three questions are what, how much, and how reliably.
options.why: Neither the logic nor the questions match the chapter, which locates the difficulty in interpretation rather than in measurement.

options.text: A comparison always has a moral dimension, so the work is naming the stakes — and the three questions are who benefits, who is harmed, and who decides.
options.why: The moral stakes run through the chapter as a warning alongside the method rather than as the inferential logic itself.

options.text: A comparison establishes a relationship, so the work is replicating it — and the three questions are whether it holds, how large it is, and where else it appears.
options.why: Replication and effect size are not the chapter's three questions, and its central claim is that a relationship does not interpret itself.

items.stem: §2.6 inventories six settings and says what form the questions take in three of them. Which grouping is right?

options.text: Across species the first question becomes homology against analogy; across the natural and artificial divide the second becomes behavioral against mechanistic equivalence; across conditions a confound is the wrong-why error.
options.why: Correct. Different domains use different words and keep coming back to the same three questions underneath them.

options.text: Across species the second question becomes homology against analogy; across the natural and artificial divide the first becomes behavioral against mechanistic equivalence; across conditions a control condition is the wrong-why error.
options.why: The first two are swapped, and a control condition is the remedy for the wrong-why error rather than the error itself.

options.text: Across species the third question becomes homology against analogy; across methods the second becomes converging operations; across ages a confound is the wrong-why error.
options.why: Homology and analogy answer the origin question, converging operations is a strategy rather than an answer, and the confound belongs to conditions.

options.text: Across species the first question becomes homology against analogy; across ages the second becomes competence against performance; across conditions chance is the wrong-why error.
options.why: Only the first is right; competence and performance are a misuse rather than a form of the depth question, and chance is not a wrong-why error.

items.stem: §2.6 names what the chapter has actually offered. What is it?

options.text: Not an inventory of comparisons but a way of handling any of them: cultures, individuals and historical periods run on the same logic.
options.why: Correct. That is the sentence the whole chapter exists to earn, and it is what makes the six settings illustrations rather than the content.

options.text: A complete inventory of the comparisons the field makes, so that a reader meeting a new study can identify which kind it belongs to.
options.why: The chapter names comparisons it did not have time to discuss, which is exactly why it does not claim to be an inventory.

options.text: A defence of cross-system comparison against the objection that most working scientists compare conditions instead.
options.why: The chapter concedes that asymmetry twice over rather than defending against it, and it teaches the condition contrast at length.

options.text: A method for deciding which of two competing explanations of a resemblance is correct in any given case.
options.why: The chapter's aim is to name the candidates and say what would separate them, which stops short of a decision procedure.

items.stem: §2.6 states what comparison can and cannot deliver. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Done carefully it licenses conclusions about origins, mechanisms, and the problems a capacity solved; it settles no question of what a creature is owed.
options.why: Correct. What it is truly like to be an octopus, an infant, or a machine is not a question this method answers.

options.text: Done carefully it licenses conclusions about origins and mechanisms and about what any creature is owed; what it cannot reach is the problem a capacity solved.
options.why: The moral question is explicitly what comparison does not settle, and the problem a capacity solved is squarely among what it licenses.

options.text: Done carefully it licenses conclusions about what a system does; it cannot reach origins or mechanisms, which need evidence from inside the system.
options.why: Origins and mechanisms are both named among what the method licenses, given the tree and the depth question respectively.

options.text: Done carefully it licenses conclusions about mechanisms alone; origins are a matter for the fossil record and the problems solved for theory.
options.why: The chapter derives origin claims from the distribution of traits across living species rather than from fossils.

items.stem: §2.6 separates two of the six settings from the rest. Which two, and why?

options.text: Cross-species and natural-versus-artificial: the evolutionary spine and the AI parallel are the two threads the book is woven from.
options.why: Correct. From Module 3 onward each module takes an evolutionary step and sets an artificial system beside it.

options.text: Across methods and across conditions, because they are what working scientists use most and therefore what a student will meet first.
options.why: Both are important and neither is a spine; the chapter is candid that the family it teaches least is the one most used.

options.text: Across ages and across typical and atypical minds, because both concern how a capacity comes into being or comes apart.
options.why: Both appear in §2.5 as comparisons the chapter gives a few paragraphs rather than as the organizing structure of the course.

options.text: Cross-species and across methods, because the first orders the modules and the second supplies the evidence each module rests on.
