options.why: The second thread named alongside cross-species comparison is the natural-versus-artificial one rather than comparison across methods.

items.stem: What does §2.6 say Module 3 takes up, and what is structurally new about it?

options.text: The neuron, the first cell specialized for carrying signals quickly over distance — and the first module giving each Marr level its own lecture.
options.why: Correct. The questions will be Marr's, with the comparative move added: what else in the world solves the same problem the same way.

options.text: The first simple nervous systems, paired with the robot vacuum — and it is the first module to run the AI parallel alongside the evolutionary one.
options.why: Simple nervous systems paired with the robot vacuum is Module 4's pairing, as §2.3.6 announces.

options.text: The neuron — and it is the first module to be organized around a single species rather than around a capacity shared across many of them.
options.why: The organizing structure announced is by evolutionary step and by Marr level rather than by species.

options.text: Learning and plasticity, paired with reinforcement-learning systems — and it is the first module to use an existing reading rather than a new chapter.
options.why: That describes Module 5's pairing, and §2.6 hands off to the neuron rather than to learning.

items.stem: Closing the module, lecture 2.3 summarizes what comparison buys. How does it put it?

options.text: Quite an accomplishment for a method whose entire requirement is looking at two things at the same time.
options.why: Correct. And what it does not do is settle what any creature is owed, or reach all the way into another mind.

options.text: Quite an accomplishment for a method that has been refined continuously since Darwin first applied it to the human mind.
options.why: The lecture's line is about how little the method requires rather than about how long it has been developed.

options.text: A modest return for a method that requires holding two entire systems in view at once and measuring both of them carefully.
options.why: The lecture treats the return as large relative to the requirement, which is the opposite of the framing here.

options.text: A reminder that the method's reach is limited, since two things looked at together can only ever yield a relationship between them.
options.why: That relationship is where the chapter starts rather than where the lecture ends, and the closing note is about how much follows from it.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 tells the room not to memorize the list of natural-and-artificial systems it has just given. What does it ask them to notice instead?

options.text: What the pairings are for: each is an instance of the three questions, and the answers come out differently every time.
options.why: Correct. The differences are what teach us — about the brain, and about the machine.

options.text: Which module each pairing belongs to, since the sequence is what makes the evolutionary spine legible as a single argument.
options.why: The ordering is announced and the lecture explicitly sets aside memorizing which pairing goes where.

options.text: That the artificial member of each pair was built after the natural one was understood, which is what makes the comparison fair.
options.why: No such historical claim is made, and several of the artificial systems predate any settled account of their natural counterpart.

options.text: That every pairing has turned out to show behavioral rather than mechanistic equivalence, which is the pattern across the course.
options.why: The lecture says the answers differ every time, so no standing pattern of that kind is claimed.

items.stem: A student asks whether the newborn speech-preference findings show that language is innate. In a short paragraph, answer using §2.5.2's reframing of the question and its account of what developmental evidence actually establishes.
items.answer: The findings do not answer the question as asked, because the question as usually posed does not survive contact with them. What the three accounts disagree about is not whether something is innate but what exactly is claimed to be innate, and the candidates are very different from one another: specific content, a general architecture, or a bias about what to attend to. A preference for speech at a few hours old is compatible with a modest built-in bias toward the low-frequency sounds that reach the womb, and Mehler's rhythm result shows that at least part of what looks built in was learned before birth, since which language it is depends on where the child developed. It also helps to see what the comparison actually did. Nobody watched a mind before and after learning; a preference was observed at one age, and the inference ran backwards from that age to what could and could not have produced it by then. That is the general shape of developmental evidence, and it constrains the candidates rather than selecting one.
rubric: Says the question as posed is the wrong one, and reframes it as what exactly is claimed to be innate.
Names at least two of the candidates: specific content, a general architecture, a bias about what to attend to.
Uses a specific finding — Mehler's rhythm result, or prenatal learning generally — to show part of the preference was learned.
States the shape of developmental evidence: a preference observed at an age, with the inference running backwards to what could have produced it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what a selective loss licenses that a general impairment does not, and say why §2.5.3 holds that describing a difference only as a lack is usually wrong about the mechanism as well as unfair.
items.answer: A selective loss is one where a capacity fails while everything around it remains intact — face recognition gone while vision and object recognition are unaffected, or fluent production lost while comprehension survives. That pattern is evidence that the capacity is a real component of the system rather than an incidental consequence of the whole thing working, because an incidental consequence would not be removable on its own. A general impairment cannot support that inference, since a loss that takes several capacities together is consistent with a shared resource, with a common cause, or with the system degrading as a whole. The deficit framing goes wrong on the science as well as on the description because it treats an atypical mind as a typical mind with a part removed, and a system that develops differently throughout is not built that way. The difference is distributed rather than subtracted, so an account written as a list of missing pieces will misdescribe the mechanism and will also hide whatever the difference makes possible.
rubric: States that a selective loss is a capacity failing while what surrounds it remains intact, with an example.
Says what it licenses: that the capacity is a real component rather than an incidental consequence.
Explains why a general impairment does not support that inference.
Explains the mechanism objection: a differently developing system is not a typical one with a part removed.

items.stem: Lecture 2.3 tells the room what they had at the start of the course and what they have now. How does it describe the change?

options.text: At the start there was a mind and a brain and no way to get from one to the other; now there are Marr's three levels for taking one system apart, and three questions for setting any two things side by side.
options.why: Correct. The lecture adds that everything from Module 3 onward is a matter of using that toolkit rather than adding to it.

options.text: At the start there was a set of disciplines with nothing in common; now there is a single evolutionary framework that unifies all of them.
options.why: The disciplines are Module 0's material, and the toolkit named here is the levels plus the three questions rather than a framework.

options.text: At the start there were three competing methods for studying a mind; now there is a strategy for combining them into one account.
options.why: Converging operations is one tool inside the toolkit rather than the summary the lecture gives of the first three weeks.

options.text: At the start there was a question about whether machines can think; now there is a criterion for deciding it in any particular case.
options.why: The lecture is explicit that the machine-mind question gets no clean yes or no, and offers no such criterion.
